3.q: Permits Online is in the 'starting up a project' process. The support contract for the council's permit database ends on 31 October next year and extending it is not affordable. Graham Pell, the executive, tells Hannah Okoro that because the project is unavoidable there is no need to compare options or document a business case: the online service named in the mandate should simply be built. How well does this apply the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because the end of support for the permit database means the council has no choice but to start a project.
It applies it well, because the executive is accountable for the business case and can decide that one is not needed.
It applies it poorly, because even an unavoidable project needs a business case showing that the chosen option gives the best value.
It applies it poorly, because the business case should be confirmed by a benefits review before initiation is authorized.
3.w: The principle applies to compulsory and unavoidable projects too: there must be a documented justification for the option chosen (for example replacing only the database versus a full online service), and it must be revalidated throughout (see manual 2.1 and 5.2.3). Dropping the business case because some project is unavoidable applies the principle poorly.

n.0: The deadline explains why some project is needed, but the principle still requires the chosen solution to be justified against the alternatives (manual 2.1).
n.1: The executive owns the business case, but owning it does not mean dispensing with it; principles cannot be tailored away.
n.3: Benefits are confirmed mainly after closure through benefits reviews; before initiation an outline business case is developed and checked, not confirmed.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'starting up a project' process. Hannah Okoro asks the PMO for the lessons report from the council's waste collection app, which went 40% over budget and launched without the contact centre being told. She also arranges a call with a neighbouring council that moved its parking permits online two years ago, and records what she learns in the lessons log. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Learn from experience, because the council has run few projects like this and is seeking lessons from its own and other organizations.
Ensure continued business justification, because the waste app overspend shows how actual costs can drift away from a business case.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the waste app went wrong partly because the contact centre was left out.
Tailor to suit the project, because the other council's experience will decide how far the method is adapted for Calderbrook.
3.w: Learn from experience: lessons are sought, recorded and acted on from the start, and when a project is new territory for an organization it is even more important to learn from others, including outside bodies (see manual 2.2). Reviewing lessons reports and consulting people with experience of similar projects is the 'assess previous lessons' activity, recorded in the lessons log (13.4.2).

n.1: Hannah is gathering lessons, not checking whether Permits Online is still desirable, viable and achievable; the overspend is a lesson rather than a test of this project's justification.
n.2: The contact centre point is one of the lessons gathered; the action itself is seeking and recording lessons, not agreeing roles or building relationships.
n.3: Tailoring is agreed in initiation to fit the method to the project; contacting another council for its lessons is learning from experience.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'starting up a project' process. Graham Pell proposes a project board made up of himself and Ruth Abernethy, head of parking services. He says Kestrel Lane Digital is a contractor that can be managed through its contract, and that the council's ICT team can be asked for help when it is needed. How well does this apply the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because the council is a thin client and the contract already sets out what Kestrel Lane must deliver.
It applies it well, because a smaller board reduces the time that senior managers spend directing the project.
It applies it poorly, because the head of parking services should be the executive, as she will run the service.
It applies it poorly, because the supplier interest of Kestrel Lane and the ICT team is not represented on the board.
3.w: The principle requires a project management team that engages the business, user and supplier interests, reflected in the make-up of the project board (see manual 2.3 and 6.2.1). Kestrel Lane and the council's ICT team supply the products, so a senior supplier role is needed; a contract does not replace supplier representation in decision-making.

n.0: A thin client model means the supplier does much of the work, which makes supplier representation more important; the contract does not give the supplier a voice in direction.
n.1: Board size should be proportionate, but leaving out one of the three project interests is not a valid way to reduce the burden.
n.2: Ruth Abernethy will use and run the service, which suits the senior user role; Graham Pell holds the budget and is named as accountable in the mandate, which suits the executive role.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'initiating a project' process. The plan has four stages: initiation, discovery and alpha, a private beta in the Old Town ward, and a public beta with migration. To reduce the number of board meetings, Graham Pell suggests merging the private and public beta into one 28-week stage. The private beta is the first time real permits will be issued online. How well does this apply the 'manage by stages' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because longer stages reduce the burden on senior management and the project still has more than two stages.
It applies it well, because the board can still be told about problems in the private beta through exception reports.
It applies it poorly, because each delivery stage should be the same length so that progress can be compared between stages.
It applies it poorly, because the end of the private beta is a key point to review real-user results before launching borough-wide.
3.w: Stages give the board decision points at which to judge whether to commit further, and shorter stages give more control (see manual 2.4). The end of the private beta is the natural point to decide, on evidence from real users and with a very low appetite for data and accessibility risk, whether to launch borough-wide and migrate every permit. Merging the stages removes that decision point.

n.0: It is true that longer stages reduce the board's burden and that two stages is the minimum, but the risk of going live borough-wide calls for a decision point after the private beta.
n.1: Exception reports deal with forecast tolerance breaches; they do not give the planned go or no-go decision that a stage boundary provides.
n.2: Stage length depends on the planning horizon, risk and decision points; there is no rule that stages must be of equal length.

3.q: Permits Online is in the discovery and alpha stage. The board has set stage tolerances of plus or minus two weeks and £25,000. Graham Pell asks Hannah Okoro to send him the notes of every sprint review and says he wants to approve personally any change to the order of work in Kestrel Lane's sprint backlog, even where it does not affect the stage plan. How well does this apply the 'manage by exception' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because the executive is accountable for the project's success and may choose how closely to control it.
It applies it well, because the council's low appetite for data risk means the executive should approve every backlog change.
It applies it poorly, because sprint reviews should be reported to the board in checkpoint reports from the team manager.
It applies it poorly, because within the agreed stage tolerances day-to-day decisions belong to the project manager and the team.
3.w: Manage by exception sets tolerances so that each level can work without interference while forecasts stay within them, and escalates when a breach is forecast (see manual 2.5). Graham's request pulls routine decisions inside tolerance back to the executive, adding burden without improving control.

n.0: The executive is ultimately accountable, but the principle expects that accountability to be exercised by setting tolerances and dealing with exceptions, not by approving routine work.
n.1: The low appetite for data risk shapes risk tolerances and controls; it does not mean every reordering of backlog items needs the executive's approval.
n.2: Checkpoint reports go from the team manager to the project manager, not to the board; the board receives highlight reports.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'initiating a project' process. Hannah Okoro, Tom Achebe and Ruth Abernethy write descriptions of the main products: the online application, the automatic eligibility checks and the telephone assisted route. Each sets out the product's purpose, its composition and how it will be checked, with WCAG 2.2 AA as a quality specification for every online screen. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Ensure continued business justification, because the products must enable the expected cut in processing time from 11 days to 2.
Learn from experience, because the accessibility specification comes from the council's digital service standard and past audits.
Focus on products, because what each product is and the quality it must meet are being agreed before work on it starts.
Manage by stages, because the product descriptions will be reviewed at the end of each stage before the next one is authorized.
3.w: Focus on products: a project defines its products and their quality requirements so that everyone knows what is to be delivered and how it will be checked (see manual 2.6). Product descriptions that set out purpose, composition and quality specifications are the main tool for this and also help control scope.

n.0: Products should lead to the benefits, but the action described is defining the products and their quality, not checking the project's justification.
n.1: The specification may draw on the service standard, but writing product descriptions is not the act of seeking and applying lessons.
n.3: Product descriptions may be updated at stage boundaries, but the situation is about defining products before delivery, not about stage-by-stage control.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'initiating a project' process. Kestrel Lane holds a sprint review every two weeks and keeps a burn-up chart. Hannah Okoro agrees with Tom Achebe that a short note issued after each sprint review, with the burn-up chart, new risks and issues and the work planned for the next sprint, will serve as the checkpoint report. This is recorded in the PID for the board to approve. Is this an appropriate application of the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
o: Yes, because a supplier that works in sprints need not follow the project's management products.
Yes, because the report's format suits the supplier's way of working and still gives the project manager what is needed.
No, because checkpoint reports should follow the standard PRINCE2 layout so that the board can compare them.
No, because tailoring must be decided by the project board rather than agreed between the project manager and a team manager.
3.w: Tailoring adapts management products (their names, formats and whether they are merged) to the project's context, such as a supplier's agile way of working, while keeping the purpose of the product (see manual 2.7). The note still reports work package status to the project manager, and the tailoring is documented in the PID, as 'agree the tailoring requirements' expects (15.4.1).

n.0: Suppliers need not use PRINCE2 internally, but the project still needs work package status reported; tailoring changes the form of the product, it does not remove the need for it.
n.2: Management products can be renamed, merged or given different formats; there is no required standard layout, and checkpoint reports go to the project manager rather than the board.
n.3: The project manager leads 'agree the tailoring requirements' and documents the tailoring in the PID, which the board approves when it authorizes the project.

3.q: Permits Online is in the discovery and alpha stage. Kestrel Lane's Scrum team works from its own offices 90 miles away, while Alan Briggs's ICT staff, who are building the council tax integration, work at the town hall. The two groups have met on video calls and are now blaming each other for integration delays. Hannah Okoro arranges for both groups to work together at the town hall for one day every sprint, starting with the sprint review. Is this an appropriate way to lead the project team, and why?
o: Yes, because working together in one place removes the need for checkpoint reports from Tom Achebe's team.
Yes, because teams that are not co-located need deliberate ways to build trust and cohesion across organizational silos.
No, because Kestrel Lane is responsible for its own staff and ways of working under its contract with the council.
No, because building the team is the team manager's responsibility and not part of the project manager's role.
3.w: Leading successful teams includes building social cohesion: co-located teams share information naturally, but remote or hybrid teams need deliberate methods, such as regular co-location days for key people, to build trust across project silos (see manual 3.3.3). The friction between the two groups shows this is needed.

n.0: Co-location days improve relationships; they do not replace the checkpoint reporting agreed in the work package.
n.2: Siobhan Kerr is accountable for Kestrel Lane's staff, but the project manager still leads the cross-organization project team and the relationships within it.
n.3: The project manager manages relationships across the project ecosystem; building cohesion between teams from two organizations falls to the project manager.

3.q: Permits Online is in the discovery and alpha stage. Under the contract, Calderbrook will own the product and set its priorities while Kestrel Lane designs and builds it. The permit officer chosen to prioritize the backlog has never worked with an agile supplier and keeps deferring decisions, which is slowing the sprints. Hannah Okoro decides to leave the role empty and let Tom Achebe's team set the priorities, as they are experienced in Scrum. Is this an appropriate way to manage the project team, and why?
o: Yes, because in a thin client model the supplier does most of the work, including much of the management.
Yes, because Kestrel Lane's team understands Scrum better than anyone at the council and will decide faster.
No, because the competency gap should be closed, for example by training or moving the role to someone suitable.
No, because role descriptions must be agreed before any team members are chosen for the project.
3.w: Roles should reflect people's capability, authority and availability; when a competency gap appears it should be identified and mitigated, for example by upskilling or shifting the responsibility to someone better suited (see manual 3.3.2). Handing the council's priority decisions to the supplier abandons the agreed model in which the council owns the product.

n.0: A thin client model does give the supplier much of the work, but this contract keeps product ownership and priority-setting with the council, so the user perspective would be lost.
n.1: Faster decisions do not make the supplier the right owner of the council's priorities; the gap should be closed rather than the responsibility moved to the supplier.
n.3: Role descriptions are reviewed as relationships shift; the problem here is a capability gap in a filled role, not the order in which roles were described.

3.q: Permits Online is in the discovery and alpha stage. Hannah Okoro needs the nine permit officers to help design how exceptions will be handled in the new service. Her stakeholder analysis lists Ruth Abernethy and the trade union. Ruth mentions that Joel Turner, a permit officer with 20 years' service, designed many of the team's workarounds and is the person colleagues go to for advice. Which action is MOST LIKELY to help the permit officers adopt the new way of working?
o: Invite Joel Turner to co-create the exception-handling process with Kestrel Lane and record him as a key influencer.
Ask Fiona McRae to tell the permit officers that the new process has been agreed with the trade union.
Wait until the public beta stage, when the service is stable, before involving the permit officers in its design.
Ask Ruth Abernethy to email the change management approach to the permit officers and invite their questions.
3.w: Leading successful change means identifying stakeholders and key influencers, who may hold no formal role, and co-creating products and ways of working with users so that they are adopted (see manual 3.2.2 and 3.3). Joel Turner is an informal leader trusted by colleagues who knows the current workarounds.

n.1: The union should be consulted, but announcing a finished process through it is telling rather than co-creating, and does not use the influence of the people who do the work.
n.2: Leaving users out until the service is stable increases resistance and handover risk; co-creation works best early in design.
n.3: Sending a management document informs people but does not engage the informal leaders who shape how the team actually works.

3.q: Permits Online is in the discovery and alpha stage. At each board meeting Ruth Abernethy, head of parking services, repeats her doubt that an online service will work for her customers. Graham Pell suggests recording her view in the minutes but no longer inviting her to sprint reviews, so that the work is not slowed down. Is this an appropriate way to lead the change, and why?
o: Yes, because the mandate from the chief executive's office has already decided that permits will move online.
Yes, because Ruth Abernethy's concern has been recorded and can be revisited at the end of the stage.
No, because the head of parking services should be the executive and so must attend every sprint review.
No, because the reasons for her doubts should be explored, and she will run the service once it is live.
3.w: Pockets of resistance show where engagement should be focused: the project should find out why a stakeholder resists rather than sideline them (see manual 3.2 and 3.4). Ruth manages the permit officers and will run the new service, so her concerns may reveal real user needs, such as residents without internet access, and her support is needed for adoption.

n.0: The mandate sets the direction, but leading change still means engaging the people affected and understanding resistance, not overriding it.
n.1: Recording a concern is not investigating it; excluding her from sprint reviews removes the chance to understand and address it.
n.2: Graham Pell, the budget holder named as accountable in the mandate, suits the executive role; Ruth's attendance as executive is not why this action is poor.

3.q: Permits Online is preparing for the private beta in the Old Town ward. The communication management approach plans to tell residents about the beta through the council website and social media. Sam Whitlock, chair of the Old Town Residents' Association, says that many older residents in the ward do not use the internet, and ward councillors share this worry. What should Hannah Okoro do to apply the communication management approach?
o: Post on social media more often in the weeks before the private beta so that more residents see the message.
Add channels that reach residents offline, such as letters and association meetings, to the communications schedule.
Ask Cllr Margaret Doyle to approve every message before it is sent, as she is councillor for the Old Town ward.
Keep the plan unchanged, since older residents can still use the telephone assisted route after the launch.
3.w: The communication management approach defines the means and frequency of communication with each stakeholder group, based on stakeholder analysis, and should be updated when feedback shows a group is not being reached (see manual 3.4). Choosing channels that reach residents without internet access is the effective response.

n.0: Posting more often does not reach people who do not use the internet; the channel, not the frequency, is the problem.
n.2: Approval of messages by one councillor does not close the gap in reach, which is the problem the feedback identified.
n.3: The telephone route lets residents apply, but it does not tell them about the private beta; the feedback shows a stakeholder group is being missed.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'initiating a project' process. Hannah Okoro has drafted this entry: 'Permit officers: today they key paper applications by hand; after the public beta they will handle cases flagged by the automatic checks, using a new case system, with revised job descriptions agreed with the trade union.' Where should this entry be recorded?
o: In the communication management approach, under the stakeholder analysis for the permit officers.
In the issue management approach, as a change to the project's baselined products.
In the change management approach, describing the current and target states for the permit officers.
In the business case, under the expected benefits of a smaller permit team.
3.w: The change management approach sets out the target organizational state and how the business will move to it from the current state, through any interim states, including the characteristics of each state such as processes, responsibilities and capabilities (see manual 3.2.1).

n.0: Stakeholder analysis identifies who is affected and how they can influence the project; it does not describe how their work will change between states.
n.1: The issue management approach covers how issues and changes to the project baseline are controlled, not organizational change: the classic change management versus change control trap.
n.3: Five posts saved is a benefit, but the entry describes how the team's work changes from the current to the target state, not a measurable benefit.

3.q: Matching set (business case). Hannah Okoro is preparing the full business case for Permits Online. Which heading of the business case should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 1 of 3: The project will run for 44 weeks from the start of initiation, and its benefits will be realized over the two years after launch.
o: Reasons
Expected benefits
Time
Costs
3.w: The time heading records the period over which the project runs and the period over which its benefits are expected to be realized (business case composition, manual chapter 5).

n.0: Reasons explain why the project is needed and how it supports business objectives, not how long the project and its benefits will take.
n.1: Expected benefits states the measurable improvements themselves; when they will be realized is recorded under time.
n.3: Costs covers project costs and ongoing running costs with their funding, not durations.

3.q: Matching set (business case). Hannah Okoro is preparing the full business case for Permits Online. Which heading of the business case should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 2 of 3: Support for the current permit database ends on 31 October next year, and the corporate plan commits the council to services that are digital by preference.
o: Reasons
Expected benefits
Time
Costs
3.w: The reasons heading explains why the project is needed and how it enables the organization's business objectives, here the end of support and the corporate plan's digital commitment (business case composition, manual chapter 5).

n.1: These are the drivers for the project, not measurable improvements that it will produce.
n.2: No duration or period of benefits realization is given; these explain why the project is needed.
n.3: No cost or funding information is given.

3.q: Matching set (business case). Hannah Okoro is preparing the full business case for Permits Online. Which heading of the business case should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 3 of 3: Kestrel Lane will charge £48,000 a year to host and support the live service, funded from the parking services budget.
o: Reasons
Expected benefits
Time
Costs
3.w: The costs heading includes ongoing operations and maintenance costs as well as project costs, together with how they will be funded (business case composition, manual chapter 5).

n.0: A running charge is not a reason for undertaking the project.
n.1: A charge is a cost of the investment, not an improvement it delivers.
n.2: The yearly charge is a cost of running the product; the time heading records the duration of the project and of benefits realization.

3.q: Matching set (organizing). The project management team for Permits Online is being appointed. Using the additional information about the people, which individual would be most appropriate for each role? Statement 1 of 3: Executive.
o: Graham Pell
Ruth Abernethy
Siobhan Kerr
Priya Lal
3.w: Graham Pell is the budget holder for parking services and is named in the mandate as accountable for Permits Online. The executive is the single point of accountability for the project, secures its funding and owns the business case (manual 6.2.4 and appendix B).

n.1: Ruth Abernethy runs the service that will use the products, which suits the senior user role; she does not hold the budget or the accountability named in the mandate.
n.2: Siobhan Kerr leads the supplier and represents its interests, which suits the senior supplier role; the executive represents the council's business interest.
n.3: Priya Lal has no role in parking services and no budget; her independent review role suits assurance.

3.q: Matching set (organizing). The project management team for Permits Online is being appointed. Using the additional information about the people, which individual would be most appropriate for each role? Statement 2 of 3: Senior supplier.
o: Graham Pell
Ruth Abernethy
Siobhan Kerr
Priya Lal
3.w: Siobhan Kerr is Kestrel Lane's delivery director, accountable for the agency's staff, its contract and the technical quality of what it builds. The senior supplier represents those delivering the products, commits supplier resources and is accountable for the quality of the supplier's products (manual 6.2.4).

n.0: Graham Pell is best placed as executive, holding the budget and named as accountable; he does not lead the organization delivering the products.
n.1: Ruth Abernethy runs the service that will use the products, so she represents users rather than suppliers.
n.3: Priya Lal reviews digital projects for the council; she does not lead the supplier or commit its staff.

3.q: Matching set (organizing). The project management team for Permits Online is being appointed. Using the additional information about the people, which individual would be most appropriate for each role? Statement 3 of 3: Project assurance, carried out by someone the board appoints to review the project on its behalf.
o: Graham Pell
Ruth Abernethy
Siobhan Kerr
Priya Lal
3.w: Project assurance must be independent of the project manager and is carried out for the board. Priya Lal already reviews digital projects against the council's service standard and has no role in parking services, so she can give the board an independent view (manual 6.2.4).

n.0: Graham Pell is best suited to be the executive, a board member, rather than someone the board appoints to assure the project for it.
n.1: Ruth Abernethy runs the service that the project changes and is best suited to be the senior user, a board member.
n.2: Siobhan Kerr is accountable for Kestrel Lane's delivery and suits the senior supplier role; she cannot give an independent view of her own agency's work.

3.q: Matching set (plans). Which role should carry out each of these planning actions on Permits Online? Statement 1 of 3: Set the tolerances for the project as a whole and document them in the project mandate.
o: Executive
Business layer
Team manager
Project manager
3.w: The business layer provides the planning standards and sets project tolerances, documenting them in the project mandate (plans roles, manual table 7.1). For Permits Online this is the chief executive's office.

n.0: The executive defines tolerances for each stage; project-level tolerances come from the business layer.
n.2: Team managers work within work package tolerances; they do not set project tolerances.
n.3: The project manager works within project tolerances set from above and sets work package tolerances.

3.q: Matching set (plans). Which role should carry out each of these planning actions on Permits Online? Statement 2 of 3: Define the tolerances for the private beta stage and approve the private beta stage plan.
o: Executive
Business layer
Team manager
Project manager
3.w: The executive defines the tolerances for each stage and approves stage plans (plans roles, manual table 7.1).

n.1: The business layer sets project tolerances, not stage tolerances, and does not approve stage plans.
n.2: Team managers prepare schedules and team plans for their work packages; they do not set stage tolerances.
n.3: The project manager prepares the stage plan but neither approves it nor sets its tolerances.

3.q: Matching set (plans). Which role should carry out each of these planning actions on Permits Online? Statement 3 of 3: Prepare the schedule for the work package that builds the automatic eligibility checks.
o: Executive
Business layer
Team manager
Project manager
3.w: Team managers prepare the schedules for each work package they take on, and team plans where needed (plans roles, manual table 7.1).

n.0: The executive approves stage plans and sets stage tolerances; work package schedules are below that level.
n.1: The business layer provides planning standards; it does not schedule work packages.
n.3: The project manager prepares the work package description; the schedule for the work package is prepared by the team manager.

3.q: Matching set (quality). Hannah Okoro is updating the quality register entry for the accessibility check on the online application form. Which heading of the quality register should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 1 of 3: Each screen tested by a panel of residents who use screen readers, followed by an automated WCAG 2.2 AA scan.
o: Quality method
Planned and actual dates
Responsibilities
Result
3.w: The quality method heading records how the product is checked, for example testing or inspection (quality register composition, manual chapter 8).

n.1: No dates are given; this describes how the check is carried out.
n.2: No reviewer or approver is named; this describes the method of checking.
n.3: No outcome is recorded; this is the method, not whether the form passed.

3.q: Matching set (quality). Hannah Okoro is updating the quality register entry for the accessibility check on the online application form. Which heading of the quality register should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 2 of 3: A tester from Tom Achebe's team carried out the check, and Ruth Abernethy approved the form.
o: Quality method
Planned and actual dates
Responsibilities
Result
3.w: The responsibilities heading records who carried out, reviewed and approved the quality activity (quality register composition, manual chapter 8).

n.0: This names people and their part in the check, not the method used.
n.1: No planned or actual dates are given.
n.3: No pass or fail outcome is given; this records who was involved.

3.q: Matching set (quality). Hannah Okoro is updating the quality register entry for the accessibility check on the online application form. Which heading of the quality register should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 3 of 3: Failed on two screens that could not be completed using a keyboard; the form will be fixed and checked again.
o: Quality method
Planned and actual dates
Responsibilities
Result
3.w: The result heading records the outcome of the quality activity, typically pass or fail, and what will happen after a failure, such as a repeat check (quality register composition, manual 8.2.2).

n.0: This is the outcome of the check, not the method used to carry it out.
n.1: A repeat check is mentioned, but no planned or actual dates are given; the entry records the outcome.
n.2: No reviewer or approver is named; the entry records the outcome and the follow-up.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'starting up a project' process. In the outline business case Hannah Okoro analyses one option, the full online service. She does not assess carrying on as now or replacing only the permit database, saying the mandate has already chosen the online service. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the outline business case in starting up is high level and is refined into the full business case in initiation.
Yes, because the mandate from the chief executive's office has already named the online service as the solution.
No, because a project that the council has to undertake should choose the do-minimum option to keep costs down.
No, because carrying on as now should be assessed as the baseline for measuring the benefits of the other options.
3.w: The business case technique compares business options, starting with doing nothing differently, which is the baseline for quantifying the others, then doing the minimum and doing more than the minimum; the difference between them is what the investment buys (see manual 5.3.1). Without that baseline the board cannot judge whether the online service is the best value.

n.0: The outline business case is high level, but it still needs enough options analysis to show that the project is worth initiating.
n.1: A mandate triggers starting up; it does not remove the need to justify the chosen option, even for an unavoidable project (manual 2.1).
n.2: Justification means choosing the option of best overall value, which may or may not be the do-minimum option.

3.q: Permits Online is nearing the end of the private beta stage. Online take-up in the Old Town ward is 35%, against the 70% assumed in the business case, so forecast savings are lower. Hannah Okoro updates the business case with actual costs, the take-up data and revised benefit forecasts, and the board reviews whether the project is still worth continuing before deciding on the public beta. Is this an effective way to apply the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the senior user is accountable for the business case and should present the revised forecasts.
Yes, because the business case is maintained at each stage end so the board can check it is still justified.
No, because benefits are confirmed after closure, so the board should not act on forecasts from a beta.
No, because project assurance, not the project manager, should update the benefit forecasts in the business case.
3.w: At the end of each stage the project manager maintains the business case with actual progress and the latest forecasts, and the board checks whether the project is still desirable, viable and achievable before authorizing the next stage (see manual 5.3.1). Falling take-up is exactly the evidence that check needs.

n.0: The executive, not the senior user, is accountable for the business case; the senior user specifies the benefits and shows they are on track.
n.2: Benefits are mostly confirmed after closure, but forecasts must be checked at each stage boundary so the board can decide whether to continue.
n.3: Project assurance monitors the business case for the board; the project manager prepares and maintains it on the executive's behalf.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'initiating a project' process. Before designing the project team structure, Hannah Okoro maps how the council makes decisions that will affect the project: cabinet approval for permit fee changes, consultation with the trade union and HR on job changes, and the ICT change board for integration work. Is this an appropriate application of the organizing practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the business layer must approve the project team structure before the initiation stage can start.
Yes, because the council's existing structures and approvals are understood before the project ecosystem is designed.
No, because mapping the council's governance is a task for the business layer rather than the project manager.
No, because the project ecosystem should be designed first and the council's structures then fitted around it.
3.w: The organizational design and development technique begins by understanding the organizational ecosystem: its existing structures, governance, the decisions that need business approval and its people management policies. Designing the project ecosystem follows (see manual 6.3.1).

n.0: The project management team is appointed in starting up, by the executive with the business layer accountable; that does not explain why mapping governance is useful here.
n.2: The business layer provides the mandate and appoints the executive; understanding the ecosystem in order to design the project's organization is part of the project's own organizing work.
n.3: The technique works the other way round: the existing ecosystem is understood first so that the project ecosystem fits it.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'initiating a project' process. The PMO's second officer will provide project support, maintaining the registers and planning tools. To save staff time, Graham Pell proposes that the same officer also carries out business assurance for him, as she already knows the project's documents well. Is this an effective way to apply the organizing practice, and why?
o: Yes, because board members may delegate their assurance work to someone in the business.
Yes, because the PMO already holds the council's project templates and its portfolio list.
No, because project assurance should be carried out by a firm from outside the council.
No, because project support and project assurance must be kept as separate roles.
3.w: Project assurance is the board's responsibility and must be independent of the project manager; it cannot be given to project support, and the two roles must be kept separate (see manual 6.2.4 and appendix B). The officer would be assuring work she maintains for the project manager.

n.0: Delegating assurance is allowed, but not to the person providing project support.
n.1: Familiarity with the templates does not make the support officer independent of the project manager.
n.2: Assurance can be carried out by board members, by people from the business or by external parties; an outside firm is not required.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'initiating a project' process. Before estimating anything, Hannah Okoro and Tom Achebe list the products needed: the online application, eligibility checks, council tax integration, migrated permit records, the telephone assisted route and staff guidance. They then draw how each depends on the others, showing that the integration depends on Alan Briggs's ICT team. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the products are identified and their dependencies mapped before estimates and a schedule are prepared.
Yes, because the product flow diagram can be used in place of a schedule for a supplier working in sprints.
No, because a supplier using Scrum plans its work in sprints and should not be asked to define products first.
No, because the product breakdown is prepared by the team manager in the 'managing product delivery' process.
3.w: Product-based planning starts by defining and analysing the products (project product description, product breakdown structure, product descriptions and product flow diagram), then organizes work packages, prepares estimates and schedules them (see manual 7.3.1). The flow diagram also exposes the dependency on the ICT team.

n.1: The product flow diagram shows sequence and dependencies; a schedule is still prepared to show timing and durations.
n.2: Iterative delivery uses a product backlog, but products are still defined; planning is product-based whatever the delivery approach.
n.3: Product-based planning for the project plan is led by the project manager in initiation; team managers plan their own work packages.

3.q: Permits Online must be live, with all permits migrated, before 31 October, when support for the old database ends. The leadership team will accept some risk to speed but very little to data and accessibility. Hannah Okoro recommends, and the chief executive's office agrees, no time tolerance on the go-live date and a scope tolerance that lets online applications for business permits follow after launch. Is this an effective way to apply the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager is responsible for setting the tolerances for the project as a whole.
Yes, because knowing which constraints take precedence shows where tolerance can be given and where it cannot.
No, because tolerances should be set for every aspect of performance using the same percentage range.
No, because scope tolerance is set in work package descriptions and not at the level of the project plan.
3.w: Using tolerances to manage constraints depends on understanding which constraints take precedence (see manual 7.2.4). With a date that cannot move, flexibility is placed in scope instead. Project tolerances are set by the business layer, here on Hannah's recommendation.

n.0: Project tolerances are set by the business layer, here the chief executive's office; the project manager recommends but does not set them.
n.2: Tolerances are set per aspect to reflect the project's constraints and priorities; there is no rule of a common range.
n.3: Tolerances exist at each level of plan, so scope tolerance can be set for the project plan as well as for stages and work packages.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'starting up a project' process. While Hannah Okoro drafts the project product description, Ruth Abernethy asks for 'permit calls to the contact centre halved within a year of launch' to be an acceptance criterion. Hannah records it as an expected benefit instead, and lists meeting WCAG 2.2 AA, passing the independent accessibility audit and passing the IT health check as acceptance criteria. Is this appropriate, and why?
o: Yes, because acceptance criteria are set by the project manager, who decides what the users will accept.
Yes, because acceptance criteria must be met before the product is accepted, and halving calls is a later benefit.
No, because the senior user specifies the benefits and so decides what the acceptance criteria will be.
No, because every acceptance criterion should be linked to a benefit that can be measured after launch.
3.w: Acceptance criteria are a prioritized list of measurable criteria that the project product must meet before the users will accept it, recorded in the project product description (see manual 8.1.1). Halving calls is a benefit realized after launch; it belongs in the business case and the benefits management approach.

n.0: The project manager documents acceptance criteria but agrees them with the users; it is the users, not the project manager, who accept the product.
n.2: The senior user provides quality expectations and acceptance criteria, but a benefit realized a year after launch cannot be a condition of accepting the product.
n.3: Acceptance criteria must be met at acceptance; a benefit measured after launch cannot be tested at that point.

3.q: Permits Online is in the discovery and alpha stage. Kestrel Lane runs accessibility and usability tests in every sprint and keeps the results in its own tool, which council staff cannot see. Hannah Okoro has no record of which products have passed their quality checks. At the end of the stage the board asks for evidence that quality control has been carried out. Is this an effective way to apply the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because quality control is carried out by the team, and the supplier's records are its own concern.
Yes, because Kestrel Lane uses Scrum, and agile teams can tailor out quality records for the project.
No, because a quality register should show the quality activities planned and done, so progress can be reviewed.
No, because test results should be recorded in the risk register so that failures can be managed as risks.
3.w: Quality control results are recorded in the quality register, which summarizes all quality activities planned or performed and is used by the project manager and project assurance to review progress (see manual 8.2.2). The supplier's tool could serve as that record if the project could see it, but here no usable record exists.

n.0: The team performs the quality checks, but the results must be visible to the project so that the project manager, board and assurance can rely on them.
n.1: Tailoring can change the form of the record, but not remove the need for evidence that quality control has been done.
n.3: Failed tests are recorded in the quality register and, where needed, raised as issues; the risk register holds uncertain future events.

3.q: Matching set (risk). Hannah Okoro is entering a new risk about the council tax integration in the risk register for Permits Online. Which heading of the risk register should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 1 of 3: Because the ICT team is supporting three other projects, the council tax integration may be finished late, which would delay the start of the private beta.
o: Risk owner
Risk description
Proximity
Risk action owner
3.w: A risk description sets out the cause (the ICT team's other commitments), the uncertain event (late integration) and the effect on objectives (a delayed private beta) (see manual 9.2.1 and 9.5).

n.0: No person is named; the statement describes what the risk is.
n.2: No timing is given for when the risk might occur.
n.3: No action or person carrying it out is named; this is the cause, event and effect.

3.q: Matching set (risk). Hannah Okoro is entering a new risk about the council tax integration in the risk register for Permits Online. Which heading of the risk register should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 2 of 3: The risk could occur in weeks 6 to 10 of the discovery and alpha stage, when the integration is due to be built.
o: Risk owner
Risk description
Proximity
Risk action owner
3.w: Proximity records how close in time the risk is likely to occur (see manual 9.5).

n.0: No person is named; this states when the risk might occur.
n.1: This states when the risk might occur, not its cause, event and effect.
n.3: No agreed action or person carrying it out is named.

3.q: Matching set (risk). Hannah Okoro is entering a new risk about the council tax integration in the risk register for Permits Online. Which heading of the risk register should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 3 of 3: Alan Briggs, ICT infrastructure manager, is responsible for managing this risk and its response.
o: Risk owner
Risk description
Proximity
Risk action owner
3.w: The risk owner is the person assigned to take responsibility for managing a risk and responding to it; a risk action owner carries out specific agreed actions on the owner's behalf (see manual 9.2 and the risk register composition).

n.1: This names who manages the risk, not what the risk is.
n.2: No timing is given for when the risk might occur.
n.3: A risk action owner carries out a specific agreed action for the risk owner; Alan Briggs is responsible for managing the risk as a whole.

3.q: Matching set (issues). The PMO's second officer provides project support for Permits Online, and Tom Achebe is the team manager for the build. Which role should carry out each action? Statement 1 of 3: Enter a new request for change from the Old Town Residents' Association in the issue register.
o: Senior user
Project manager
Team manager
Project support
3.w: Project support administers the issue and change control procedures by maintaining the issue register (issues roles, manual table 10.2).

n.0: The senior user decides on escalated issues; keeping the register is administration.
n.1: The project manager runs the issue procedure and keeps the register when there is no project support; here project support is in place.
n.2: Team managers implement corrective actions in their work packages; they do not keep the issue register.

3.q: Matching set (issues). The PMO's second officer provides project support for Permits Online, and Tom Achebe is the team manager for the build. Which role should carry out each action? Statement 2 of 3: Carry out the agreed rework of the payment page within the team's current work package after it failed an accessibility check.
o: Senior user
Project manager
Team manager
Project support
3.w: Team managers implement corrective actions within their work packages (issues roles, manual table 10.2).

n.0: The senior user decides on escalated issues; the rework itself is done by the team.
n.1: The project manager authorizes corrective action and creates new work packages where needed, but carrying out rework within the current work package falls to the team manager.
n.3: Project support administers the issue register; it does not rework products.

3.q: Matching set (issues). The PMO's second officer provides project support for Permits Online, and Tom Achebe is the team manager for the build. Which role should carry out each action? Statement 3 of 3: Decide on an escalated request for change, with a focus on protecting the expected cut in processing time.
o: Senior user
Project manager
Team manager
Project support
3.w: When issues are escalated, the senior user makes decisions with a focus on safeguarding the expected benefits (issues roles, manual table 10.2).

n.1: The project manager handles issues within delegated authority; an escalated request is decided above that level, where the senior user protects the expected benefits.
n.2: Team managers implement actions; they do not decide escalated issues.
n.3: Project support records the decision in the issue register; it does not make it.

3.q: Matching set (progress). Permits Online is in the private beta stage. Which report or log should each item be recorded in? Statement 1 of 3: Tom Achebe tells Hannah Okoro, at the interval set in his work package, what his team completed in the last sprint and what is planned next.
o: Checkpoint report
Highlight report
Exception report
Daily log
3.w: A checkpoint report is produced by the team manager for the project manager on the status of a work package, at the frequency set in the work package (see manual 11.5).

n.1: Highlight reports go from the project manager to the board on the status of the stage.
n.2: Nothing is forecast to exceed tolerance.
n.3: This is formal work package reporting from a team manager, not an informal note.

3.q: Matching set (progress). Permits Online is in the private beta stage. Which report or log should each item be recorded in? Statement 2 of 3: Hannah Okoro notes that Fiona McRae mentioned in confidence that two permit officers are thinking of retiring early, and that she will follow it up.
o: Checkpoint report
Highlight report
Exception report
Daily log
3.w: The daily log is the project manager's informal record of issues, actions and observations, including sensitive matters that would not suit open records (see manual 11.5).

n.0: This is not work package status from a team manager.
n.1: A sensitive, informal matter shared in confidence does not belong in a report to the board.
n.2: No tolerance breach is forecast.

3.q: Matching set (progress). Permits Online is in the private beta stage. Which report or log should each item be recorded in? Statement 3 of 3: Hannah Okoro tells the board that the integration delay is now forecast to exceed the stage time tolerance, and sets out options and a recommendation.
o: Checkpoint report
Highlight report
Exception report
Daily log
3.w: An exception report is produced by the project manager when a stage plan is forecast to exceed its tolerances, giving the options and a recommendation (see manual 11.3.1).

n.0: Checkpoint reports go from the team manager to the project manager.
n.1: A highlight report gives routine stage status; a forecast breach of stage tolerance calls for an exception report.
n.3: A forecast tolerance breach must be escalated formally, not noted informally.

3.q: Permits Online has a risk that the independent accessibility audit could find failures shortly before go-live, delaying the launch past 31 October. Hannah Okoro agrees with Tom Achebe that automated accessibility checks and testing with assistive technology users will run in every sprint, and that an interim audit will take place at the end of the private beta. Which type of risk response is this, and why?
o: Avoid, because the extra testing removes any chance that the final audit will find accessibility failures.
Reduce, because action taken now lowers the chance and impact of audit failures, though some risk remains.
Transfer, because Kestrel Lane will carry out the testing and so takes on the impact under its contract.
Prepare contingent plans, because the interim audit will be used if failures are found late in the project.
3.w: A reduce response takes definite action now to change the probability and/or the impact of a threat, leaving some residual risk (see manual 9.2.3.1). Testing in every sprint and an interim audit make late failures less likely and less damaging but cannot rule them out.

n.0: Avoid makes the threat certain not to happen, for example by removing its cause; testing lowers the likelihood, but the final audit could still find failures.
n.2: Transfer passes part of the financial impact to a third party; having the supplier test does not move the impact of a missed go-live date.
n.3: A contingent plan is prepared now and used if the risk occurs; the sprint testing and interim audit are planned to take place in any case.

3.q: Permits Online is in the discovery and alpha stage. In a risk workshop, Kestrel Lane's team says that moving 26,000 existing permits from the old database is low risk because their past migrations for other clients have gone well. Nobody challenges this, and the risk is scored as low probability without examining the quality of the council's old data. Is this an effective way to apply the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because Kestrel Lane is the supplier and is best placed to judge the risks in its own technical work.
Yes, because a risk workshop with the team is a recognized way to identify and assess the project's risks.
No, because migration risks belong to the business layer and should be recorded in its own register.
No, because optimism and groupthink may be hiding the risk, and data on the old records should inform the score.
3.w: Risk assessment can be distorted by decision bias such as optimism bias and groupthink, and data and analytics should be used to identify and assess risks (see manual 9.2.4 and 9.3.2.6). Testing a sample of the council's old records would give evidence for the probability score.

n.0: Supplier expertise is valuable, but success for other clients is not evidence about this council's data, and an unchallenged view is a sign of bias.
n.1: Workshops are a valid technique, but this one accepted an untested assumption, so the assessment is not effective.
n.2: The migration is project work; its risks are managed in the project's risk register.

3.q: The council's leadership team has a very low appetite for risks to residents' personal data. In the 'initiating a project' process, Hannah Okoro drafts the risk management approach. It proposes that the project board sets a tight risk tolerance for data protection, so that any data risk still assessed above 'low' after its response is escalated to the board straight away. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager sets the risk appetite for the project when writing the approach.
Yes, because the board sets risk tolerances from the business's appetite, and the approach says how they are applied.
No, because risk appetite and risk tolerance should both be set by the leadership team, not the project board.
No, because the specific data risks and their scores belong in the risk management approach itself.
3.w: Risk appetite is set by the business; risk tolerance is a measurable threshold set by the project board based on that appetite, and the risk management approach describes the procedures, techniques and responsibilities for managing risk on the project (see manual 9.2.1).

n.0: Risk appetite belongs to the business, here the leadership team; the project manager applies it but does not set it.
n.2: The business sets the appetite, but the risk tolerance for the project is set by the project board based on that appetite.
n.3: The risk management approach describes how risk is managed and holds no specific risks; individual risks go in the risk register.

3.q: Permits Online is in the private beta stage. At a sprint review, Tom Achebe reports that the payment page will not meet WCAG 2.2 AA, a quality specification in its product description, because of the card payment component used. Fixing it would need two extra sprints. How should Hannah Okoro classify this issue, and why?
o: As an off-specification, because a product is forecast not to meet one of its quality specifications.
As a request for change, because Kestrel Lane is asking for two more sprints to rework the payment page.
As a concern, because the effect of the failure on the go-live date has not yet been assessed.
As a risk, because the page might still pass the independent audit after further work in later sprints.
3.w: An off-specification is a product that will not meet, or is forecast not to meet, its quality specifications (see manual 10.2.3). It is handled through change control: the fix is approved, or a concession granted, by the board or the change authority.

n.1: A request for change proposes altering a baseline; here the baseline is unchanged and the product is failing to meet it.
n.2: Every issue is assessed for impact; the failure has already been found, so the more specific type, off-specification, applies.
n.3: The failure is already known, so it is an issue rather than an uncertain future event.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'initiating a project' process. Graham Pell proposes that Tom Achebe, Kestrel Lane's delivery manager, act as change authority for every request for change, with no cost limit and no change budget, because his team knows the backlog best. Is this an effective way to apply the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project board may delegate the approval of requests for change to a change authority.
Yes, because under a time-and-materials contract the supplier pays for any changes that it approves.
No, because delegated change authority should have defined limits, with a change budget, set by the board.
No, because the project board must decide every request for change itself and cannot delegate this.
3.w: The board is the ultimate authority for requests for change but may delegate approval to a change authority within defined limits, ideally with a change budget so that approved changes can be funded (see manual 10.2.4 and 10.2.5). Unlimited authority for the supplier's delivery manager removes the board's control over the baseline and over a capped contract.

n.0: Delegation is allowed, but within defined limits; unlimited authority with no budget is not effective delegation.
n.1: Under time and materials the council pays for the time used, so changes approved by the supplier would raise the council's costs.
n.3: The board may delegate approval of changes to a change authority or to the project manager.

3.q: Permits Online is in the discovery and alpha stage. This is Hannah Okoro's first project of this size, and Calderbrook has little experience of PRINCE2 or of working with an agile supplier. The board asks for a highlight report every week during this stage, moving to every two weeks once it is confident that reporting is reliable. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because weekly highlight reports mean that the board need not set tolerances for this stage.
Yes, because reporting frequency should match the control needed, and can be reduced as confidence grows.
No, because highlight reports are produced at the end of each stage to support the decision on the next stage.
No, because the frequency of highlight reports is set by the team manager in each work package description.
3.w: The frequency of reporting should reflect the level of control needed: inexperience calls for more frequent reports until confidence grows (see manual 11.2.4). The board sets the interval for highlight reports.

n.0: Reports inform the board but do not replace tolerances, which define the authority delegated to the project manager.
n.2: That describes the end stage report; highlight reports are time-driven reports at intervals set by the board.
n.3: Work package descriptions set checkpoint reporting from team manager to project manager; the board sets highlight report frequency.

3.q: Permits Online is in the private beta stage, which has a time tolerance of two weeks. A delay in the ICT team's integration work means Hannah Okoro forecasts the stage will finish six days late. She moves a testing work package earlier to recover some time, records the issue and reports both in her next highlight report. Is this an effective way to apply the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the forecast is within stage tolerance, so she can take corrective action and report it routinely.
Yes, because the business layer sets stage tolerances and will be told if they are breached.
No, because a delay affecting a fixed go-live date should be escalated to the board in an exception report.
No, because Alan Briggs, as manager of the delayed team, should raise an exception report to the board.
3.w: An exception is a forecast breach of tolerance. While the stage is forecast to finish within its tolerance, the project manager takes corrective action and reports through highlight reports; an exception report is needed when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded (see manual 11.2.6 and 16.4.6).

n.1: The project board, not the business layer, sets stage tolerances.
n.2: The go-live date matters, but the stage is still forecast within the tolerance the board set, so there is no exception to escalate.
n.3: Problems at team level are raised with the project manager as issues; exception reports go from the project manager to the board.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'starting up a project' process. Hannah Okoro meets Graham Pell, Ruth Abernethy and Siobhan Kerr to agree what the project will deliver. Together they draft the project product description, including the users' quality expectations and the go-live conditions as acceptance criteria. Is this an appropriate application of the 'prepare the outline business case' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the executive, senior user and senior supplier are consulted to define what the project will deliver.
Yes, because the outline business case must contain the detailed costs from the project product description.
No, because the project product description is created in initiation as part of preparing the project plan.
No, because the senior supplier should not be involved until the project has been authorized by the board.
3.w: In 'prepare the outline business case' the project manager consults the executive, senior user and senior supplier to understand what the project is to deliver and creates the project product description, including the quality expectations and acceptance criteria (see manual 13.4.3).

n.1: The outline business case is high level at this point; detailed costs come from the project plan in initiation.
n.2: The project product description is created in starting up a project; it is then used in initiation and when closing the project.
n.3: The senior supplier is consulted in starting up so that what is to be delivered is understood from the supplier side too.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'starting up a project' process. The chief executive's office has appointed Graham Pell as executive. Graham is now choosing the senior user and senior supplier and agreeing who will provide project assurance. Which role is accountable for the 'appoint the project management team' activity?
o: The executive, Graham Pell, who is choosing the other members of the board.
The project manager, Hannah Okoro, who will lead the project team day to day.
The project board, once all of its members have been appointed.
The business layer, here the chief executive's office that commissioned the project.
3.w: In the recommended RACI for 'appoint the project management team', the business layer is accountable and the executive is responsible for making the appointments; the project manager is not involved (see manual 13.4.4 and table 13.2).

n.0: Graham Pell is responsible for carrying out the appointments; accountability for them sits with the business layer.
n.1: The project manager is not involved in appointing the project management team.
n.2: The board cannot be accountable for appointing itself; the business layer that commissions the project is accountable.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'starting up a project' process. Worried about the fixed date of 31 October, Hannah Okoro asks Kestrel Lane to start building prototype screens straight away, before the project brief has been approved, so that the alpha stage can be shortened later. Is this an effective way to carry out starting up a project, and why?
o: Yes, because early prototypes help to show whether the project is viable before initiation is authorized.
Yes, because Kestrel Lane works iteratively and the project approach allows design work to begin early.
No, because starting up should do the minimum needed to decide whether initiation is worthwhile.
No, because the council's ICT team, not Kestrel Lane, should build any prototypes for the project.
3.w: Starting up a project is deliberately light: it does the minimum needed to decide whether there is a viable and worthwhile project to initiate, and it prevents resources being committed before that decision (see manual 13.1). Building prototypes is delivery work and should wait until the board has authorized it.

n.0: Viability at this point is judged from the outline business case and project brief, not from delivery work done before any authorization.
n.1: The project approach describes how the work will be delivered once authorized; it does not allow delivery to start before initiation.
n.3: Who builds the prototypes is not the problem: Kestrel Lane is the appointed supplier, but no delivery work should start before authorization.

3.q: The project brief and initiation stage plan for Permits Online have been sent to the board. Graham Pell, Ruth Abernethy and Siobhan Kerr each review them and agree by email that initiation should go ahead, without holding a meeting. Graham then emails Hannah Okoro a written instruction to start the six-week initiation stage. Is this an appropriate application of the 'authorize initiation' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager may begin initiation as soon as the project brief is complete.
Yes, because all board members agreed and the executive gave the project manager a documented instruction.
No, because initiation must be authorized at a formal board meeting at which minutes are taken.
No, because the business layer, not the project board, authorizes the start of the initiation stage.
3.w: Authorize initiation can be done with or without a formal meeting, as long as all board members agree and the project manager receives a documented instruction from the executive (see manual 14.4.1).

n.0: The project manager needs the board's authority to initiate; completing the brief leads to the request, not the start.
n.2: A formal meeting is not required for this decision.
n.3: Authorizing initiation is a project board decision in directing a project; the business layer provides the mandate.

3.q: Permits Online is in the private beta stage. Tom Achebe's team asks whether residents without a council tax account should be able to apply for visitor vouchers online. The answer depends on how residents will use the service, and Hannah Okoro asks the board for guidance through the 'give ongoing direction' activity. Which role should be responsible for giving this user-related direction?
o: The executive.
The senior supplier.
The senior user.
Project assurance.
3.w: In the recommended RACI for 'give ongoing direction', the senior user is responsible for user-related direction, with project assurance consulted (see manual 14.4.3 and table 14.2).

n.0: The executive gives direction on business matters such as justification and funding; user-related direction falls to the senior user.
n.1: The senior supplier directs on supplier and technical matters, not on how residents will use the service.
n.3: Project assurance is consulted and advises the board; it does not give the direction.

3.q: Permits Online is in the discovery and alpha stage. At a sprint review, Cllr Margaret Doyle, a member of the board, tells Tom Achebe's team to add a printable paper form to the online service for older residents, and the team starts work on it that afternoon. Hannah Okoro learns about it a week later. Is this an effective way for the board to direct the project, and why?
o: Yes, because individual board members may give ongoing direction at any time during a stage.
Yes, because the change helps residents without internet access, which ward councillors are worried about.
No, because Cllr Doyle is a councillor and so should not be a member of the project board.
No, because direction should go to the project manager, and new requirements go through issue control.
3.w: Board members, collectively or individually, give ongoing direction to the project manager rather than to the team; the team manager takes instructions from the project manager, and a new requirement is a request for change handled through the issue management approach (see manual 14.4.3 and 10.2.3).

n.0: Individual members can give direction, but to the project manager; instructing the team directly bypasses the project manager and change control.
n.1: The concern is valid, but a good idea still needs to be assessed against the baseline, the plan and the business case.
n.2: Being a councillor does not in itself rule her out of the board, and it is not why this way of directing is poor.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'initiating a project' process. Hannah Okoro drafts the digital and data management approach from the council's data protection policy and security standards, and asks the waste collection app team what they learned about data confidentiality. She then uses the approaches to set up the project controls and the project plan. Is this an appropriate application of the 'agree the management approaches' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the digital and data management approach replaces the need for a risk management approach.
Yes, because the approaches draw on the council's policies and standards and on lessons from similar projects.
No, because the management approaches should be prepared after the project plan so that they match it.
No, because the digital and data management approach belongs to Kestrel Lane, which will host the service.
3.w: In 'agree the management approaches' the approaches are derived from the business's strategies, standards and practices that the project must comply with, lessons are sought from similar projects (including on data confidentiality), and once they are defined the project controls and project plan follow (see manual 15.4.2).

n.0: Each approach has its own purpose; managing data does not replace the procedures for managing risk.
n.2: The order is the reverse: the approaches are agreed first, and the controls and project plan follow.
n.3: The digital and data management approach is part of the PID and covers data across the project ecosystem, whoever hosts the service.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'initiating a project' process. Hannah Okoro describes how residents' suggestions and problems found in testing will be captured, how their severity will be rated, and how changes to approved products will be assessed and decided. She also sets up a register for formal items of this kind. Which practice is being applied by the 'initiating a project' process?
o: Risk, because the register will hold uncertain events that may affect the project's objectives.
Issues, because an issue management approach and an issue register are being put in place.
Quality, because problems found in testing are results of quality control on the products.
Progress, because the register will be used to report status to the board at agreed intervals.
3.w: In initiating a project the issues practice is applied by developing the issue management approach, which sets out how issues are captured and how changes to the baseline are assessed and controlled, and by setting up the issue register (see manual table 15.3).

n.0: Problems already found and requested changes are issues, not uncertain future events.
n.2: Quality results are recorded in the quality register; capturing and deciding on issues and changes is the issues practice.
n.3: Progress reporting to the board uses highlight reports; the register described is for issues and changes.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'initiating a project' process. Hannah Okoro proposes combining the communication and change management approaches into one short document, as the same people are affected by both, while writing a detailed digital and data management approach because of the council's very low appetite for data risk. The tailoring is recorded in the PID for the board to approve. Is this an effective way to carry out initiation, and why?
o: Yes, because management products can be merged or scaled, giving most detail where the risk is greatest.
Yes, because the change management approach and the issue management approach cover the same subject.
No, because each of the nine management approaches must be written as a separate document.
No, because tailoring decisions are made in starting up and cannot be changed during initiation.
3.w: Tailoring lets management products be merged, split or given different formats, and keeps controls proportionate to the project's scale, complexity and risk (see manual 2.7 and 15.4.1). Detail is placed where the business's appetite for risk is lowest, and the tailoring is documented in the PID for approval.

n.1: The change management approach covers organizational transition and the issue management approach covers change control; they are different subjects.
n.2: Management products can be merged or combined; there is no requirement for nine separate documents.
n.3: Tailoring requirements are agreed in initiating a project, in 'agree the tailoring requirements', and can be revisited at stage boundaries.

3.q: Permits Online is in the discovery and alpha stage. Hannah Okoro and Tom Achebe draft the work package description for the eligibility checks together. They agree time and cost tolerances, a scope tolerance on optional features, checkpoint reports after each sprint review and how finished products will be handed over. Tom confirms his team can deliver it before Hannah authorizes the work. Is this an appropriate application of the 'authorize a work package' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the team manager sets the tolerances for the work package and the project manager records them.
Yes, because the project manager co-creates the work package with the team manager and confirms acceptance.
No, because the work package description should also set a benefits tolerance for processing time.
No, because work packages should be authorized by the project board as part of approving the stage plan.
3.w: In 'authorize a work package' the project manager defines the work package, co-creates and reviews it with the team manager, confirms that the team manager accepts it and then authorizes the work (see manual 16.4.1). Work package tolerances cover scope, cost and time.

n.0: The project manager sets work package tolerances; the team manager agrees to work within them.
n.2: Benefits and quality tolerances are not set in a work package description; its tolerances are scope, cost and time.
n.3: The board approves stage plans; authorizing work packages within the stage is the project manager's activity in controlling a stage.

3.q: Permits Online is in the private beta stage. While evaluating stage status, Hannah Okoro finds that the telephone assisted route is behind schedule but still within stage tolerance. She moves two Kestrel Lane developers onto the work through an amended work package. Which role is accountable for the 'take corrective action' activity?
o: The executive.
The project manager.
The team manager.
Project support.
3.w: In the recommended RACI for 'take corrective action', the executive is accountable, the project manager is responsible for selecting and triggering the action, and project support is informed (see manual 16.4.6 and table 16.2).

n.1: The project manager is responsible for taking the corrective action; accountability for the activity sits with the executive.
n.2: The team manager carries out the amended work package but is not accountable for the activity.
n.3: Project support is informed of corrective action, not accountable for it.

3.q: Permits Online is in the private beta stage and is forecast to finish within its tolerances. Dev Mistry tells Hannah Okoro that contact centre staff have not been briefed on the online service and are giving residents wrong advice. Without recording or assessing the problem, Hannah sends the board an exception report the same day. Is this an effective way to carry out controlling a stage, and why?
o: Yes, because the waste app lesson shows that contact centre problems must go straight to the board.
Yes, because the board should be alerted as early as possible to anything affecting residents.
No, because the issue should be captured and assessed first, and no stage tolerance breach is forecast.
No, because contact centre problems are business as usual and so lie outside the project's control.
3.w: In 'capture issues and risks' each issue is registered and assessed before a course of action is chosen (see manual 16.4.5). An exception report is for a forecast breach of stage tolerance (16.4.7); here the stage is within tolerance, so the project manager should handle the problem, for example by arranging briefings, and report it in the next highlight report.

n.0: The lesson is about telling the contact centre, which this problem shows is needed; it does not change how issues are escalated.
n.1: Alerting the board early applies to forecast exceptions; issues within tolerance are handled by the project manager.
n.3: Preparing the contact centre for the new service is part of the project's communication and change work, so this is a project issue.
