3.q: Permits Online is in the discovery and alpha stage. Tom Achebe receives the draft work package for the council tax integration interface. It relies on Alan Briggs's ICT team, who are free for two days a week, so the planned four sprints are not achievable. Before agreeing to it, Tom discusses the timescale and the dependency with Hannah Okoro, and they agree a revised work package. Is this an appropriate application of the 'accept a work package' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the team manager sets the tolerances for the work package once it has been accepted.
Yes, because the team manager agrees with the project manager what will be delivered and whether it is achievable.
No, because the team manager should accept the work package as authorized and report problems in checkpoints.
No, because Tom Achebe should take the dependency on the ICT team to the project board to resolve.
3.w: In 'accept a work package' the team manager agrees with the project manager what is to be delivered, the reporting requirements, constraints and procedures, and confirms that it is achievable before committing to it (see manual 17.4.1).

n.0: The project manager sets work package tolerances; the team manager agrees to work within them.
n.2: Acceptance is an agreement, not a formality; problems known at the start should be resolved before the team manager commits.
n.3: The team manager works with the project manager, not the board; the board is not involved in managing product delivery.

3.q: Permits Online is in the private beta stage. Tom Achebe's team is building and testing the permit renewal feature under an authorized work package, holding daily stand-ups and recording completed quality checks. Which role is accountable for the 'execute a work package' activity?
o: The team manager.
The senior supplier.
The project manager.
The executive.
3.w: In the recommended RACI for 'execute a work package', the project manager is accountable while the team manager leads the work; project assurance is consulted, and the business layer and executive are not involved (see manual 17.4.2 and table 17.2).

n.0: The team manager leads the work in the work package but is not accountable for the activity in the recommended RACI.
n.1: The senior supplier commits supplier resources at board level, but the board is not involved in managing product delivery.
n.3: The executive is not involved in executing work packages.

3.q: Permits Online is in the private beta stage. Tom Achebe's team finds that the vehicle record check fails for about 5% of lease cars. Tom decides to add a step where residents upload a lease agreement, which changes the agreed product description for the application form, and tells Hannah Okoro when he notifies completion of the work package. Is this an effective way to execute the work package, and why?
o: Yes, because the team manager may make decisions within the work package to deliver its products.
Yes, because the extra step solves the problem for residents and keeps the private beta on schedule.
No, because new issues should be raised with the project manager when found, not decided by the team.
No, because the team manager should have taken the issue to the senior user to decide.
3.w: In 'execute a work package' the team manager notifies the project manager of new issues, risks or lessons and takes any action the project manager requires (see manual 17.4.2). Changing a baselined product description is a change to be assessed through the issue management approach, not decided within the team.

n.0: Team managers decide within their work package tolerances, but altering an agreed product description goes beyond the work package and needs change control.
n.1: Solving the problem quickly does not justify changing the baseline without assessment and approval.
n.3: The team manager raises issues with the project manager, who escalates them if needed; the board is not involved in managing product delivery.

3.q: Permits Online is in the public beta stage. Hannah Okoro's exception report showed that migration problems would take the stage beyond its cost tolerance, and the board asked for an exception plan. Hannah records the request in the project log, prepares a plan from the current position to the end of the stage, and checks whether the business case and project plan need updating. Is this an appropriate application of the 'prepare exception plan' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because it replaces the stage plan from now to the end of the stage, and the PID is reviewed with it.
Yes, because an exception plan covers the rest of the whole project rather than the current stage.
No, because exception plans are prepared in controlling a stage as part of taking corrective action.
No, because the exception plan should replace the team plan for the migration work package.
3.w: When the board asks for an exception plan after an exception report, the project manager prepares it in managing a stage boundary: the request is recorded in the project log, the plan replaces the stage plan from the current position to the end of the stage, and the PID, including the business case and project plan, is reviewed and updated (see manual chapter 18 and 7.2.2.4). Its approval marks a stage boundary.

n.1: A stage-level exception plan covers the rest of the stage it replaces; a project-level plan would be needed for a forecast breach of project tolerance.
n.2: Corrective action within tolerance happens in controlling a stage; exception plans are prepared in managing a stage boundary.
n.3: Exception plans replace stage or project plans; they are not produced for team plans.

3.q: Permits Online is approaching the end of the discovery and alpha stage. As part of managing the stage boundary, Hannah Okoro reviews how the combined council and Kestrel Lane team has performed, including workload and well-being during the integration delays, and records lessons for the end stage report. Which practice is being applied by the 'managing a stage boundary' process?
o: Progress, because the findings will be summarized for the board in the end stage report.
Quality, because the team's performance is checked against the quality register for the stage.
Plans, because the team's workload will be used to prepare the next stage plan.
Organizing, because the team's performance, health and well-being are reviewed at the boundary.
3.w: In managing a stage boundary the organizing practice is applied by reviewing the project team's performance, health and well-being, both for lessons and for the end stage report (see manual table 18.3).

n.0: Progress is applied by creating and issuing the end stage report; reviewing the team's performance and well-being is organizing.
n.1: The quality register records quality activities on products, not team performance or well-being.
n.2: The next stage plan is prepared in this process, but reviewing the team's health and well-being is not the plans practice.

3.q: Permits Online is approaching the end of the discovery and alpha stage. The project plan, approved in initiation, already shows the private beta's main products and dates. To save time, Hannah Okoro asks the board to authorize the private beta stage on the basis of the project plan, without preparing a stage plan, although the alpha research has changed several user needs. Is this an effective way to manage the stage boundary, and why?
o: Yes, because the project plan already contains enough detail for the board to control each stage.
Yes, because the project manager can approve the start of the next stage within project tolerance.
No, because stage plans should be prepared during initiation for every stage of the project.
No, because the next stage plan is prepared near the end of this stage, reflecting what has been learned.
3.w: As only the near future can be planned in detail, each delivery stage plan is prepared near the end of the current stage, close to when the work happens, and approved by the board (see manual 7.2.2.2 and chapter 18). The alpha research has changed user needs, so a fresh stage plan is needed.

n.0: The project plan is high level; the detailed stage plan is the basis for the project manager's control within a stage.
n.1: A stage starts when the board authorizes it; the project manager cannot approve it.
n.2: The initiation stage plan is prepared in starting up; each later stage plan is prepared at the boundary before that stage.

3.q: Permits Online is in the closing part of the public beta stage. All permits are migrated and the paper process has ended. Hannah Okoro confirms with Ruth Abernethy that the service meets its acceptance criteria and has passed the audit and IT health check, transfers running of the service to parking services and checks that Kestrel Lane's hosting and support arrangements are in place. Is this an appropriate application of the 'confirm project acceptance' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because acceptance is confirmed and the products pass to the people who will operate and support them.
Yes, because handing the service over to parking services is the final post-project benefits review.
No, because acceptance should wait until benefits reviews confirm that permit calls have halved.
No, because the project should be closed as a separate stage once the public beta has finished.
3.w: Confirm project acceptance ensures that the products are passed into the operational and maintenance environment and that acceptance of the project product is confirmed against its acceptance criteria (see manual 19.4.3). Checking the support arrangements meets the objective that the business can support the products after closure.

n.1: Handover is not a benefits review; post-project benefits reviews are planned in the project and carried out by the business later.
n.2: Benefits such as halving calls are measured after closure in post-project benefits reviews; acceptance is judged against the acceptance criteria.
n.3: Closing a project is the last part of the final stage, not a separate stage.

3.q: Permits Online is in the 'closing a project' process. Hannah Okoro checks that every product listed for the project, from the online application to the staff guidance, has been delivered and approved, notes each product's final status and closes the register that tracks them. Which practice is being applied by the 'closing a project' process?
o: Quality, because the quality register is checked and closed to confirm every quality activity was completed.
Progress, because the end project report compares what was delivered with the baselined PID.
Issues, because the status of each product shows whether any changes to the baseline remain open.
Plans, because the product register is checked and closed as the record of the plan's products.
3.w: In closing a project the plans practice is applied by checking and closing the product register, the list of all products required by a plan and their status (see manual table 19.3).

n.0: Checking and closing the quality register is how quality is applied in closing; the register described lists products and their status, which is the product register.
n.1: The end project report applies the progress practice, but the action described is closing the product register.
n.2: Open issues are handled through the issue register and follow-on action recommendations; the product register is a plans record.

3.q: Permits Online has gone live and is in the 'closing a project' process. To show that permit calls to the contact centre halve within a year, Hannah Okoro proposes keeping the project open, with herself and two Kestrel Lane staff, for twelve months after launch to run the benefits reviews before asking for closure. Is this an effective way to carry out closing a project, and why?
o: Yes, because the senior user is responsible for the continued realization of benefits after closure.
Yes, because the business case cannot be confirmed until all of the expected benefits have been measured.
No, because the benefits management approach should be closed along with the other project records.
No, because post-project benefits reviews are planned by the project but carried out by the business after closure.
3.w: Closing a project updates the benefits management approach to plan the post-project benefits reviews; carrying them out is not a project activity but is done by the business after closure (see manual 19.2, 19.4 and 5.3.1). Keeping the project open would prolong its costs and blur the handover.

n.0: The senior user stays responsible for the continued realization of benefits after closure, which is why the project need not stay open to measure them.
n.1: Benefits are mostly confirmed after the project has closed; the project does not wait for them before closing.
n.2: The benefits management approach is not closed; it is updated in closing so that the business can run the post-project reviews.

4.q: Tarnside College's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'starting up a project' process. In the outline business case, Leah Whitfield compares leaving the warehouse empty, converting it for welding and electrical courses without the nacelle rig, and building the full centre. For each option she weighs the grant, the employers' apprentice pledges and the risk of grant clawback against the cost to the college. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Focus on products, because each option is defined by the products it would deliver, such as the welding bays and the nacelle rig.
Manage by exception, because the governors have limited spending on the centre to 3% above the approved budget.
Ensure continued business justification, because the options are compared to find the best balance of benefits, costs and risks.
Learn from experience, because the lab refurbishment showed that the college must plan its capital projects with more care.
4.w: Ensure continued business justification: there must be a justifiable reason for the project, documented in a business case, and the chosen option should give the best overall value. Comparing doing nothing, doing the minimum and doing more than the minimum, and weighing benefits against costs and risks, is how that justification is developed (see manual 2.1 and 5.3.1).

n.0: The options are described by what they deliver, but the purpose of the comparison is to justify the investment, not to define products and their quality requirements.
n.1: The 3% limit is a tolerance, which belongs to manage by exception; the action here is comparing options to justify the investment.
n.3: No previous lessons are being sought or applied in this action; Leah is analysing business options.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. In starting up, Leah Whitfield recorded the lab refurbishment lessons in the lessons log, including that changes had been agreed on site without anyone checking the budget. To keep the work moving, Mark Ostrowski now proposes that the contractor's site manager and Craig Dunmore agree design changes at weekly site meetings and tell Leah afterwards. How well does this apply the 'learn from experience' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because the lessons log was created in starting up, as the 'assess previous lessons' activity recommends.
It applies it well, because Craig Dunmore has managed many small works contracts and understands the college's budgets.
It applies it poorly, because the lessons log should be set up in initiation, once the board has authorized the project.
It applies it poorly, because the lessons were recorded but the proposal repeats the same mistake rather than acting on it.
4.w: Learn from experience means lessons are sought, recorded and acted on throughout the project (see manual 2.2). The lab refurbishment showed the danger of agreeing changes on site without checking the budget; agreeing design changes at site meetings and telling the project manager afterwards repeats it, so the lesson has been recorded but not applied.

n.0: Creating the lessons log in starting up is correct, but recording lessons is not enough: this proposal repeats the very mistake the lessons warned about.
n.1: Craig's experience does not change the lesson that site changes need their cost checked before they are agreed.
n.2: The lessons log is created in starting up a project ('assess previous lessons'), so recording the lessons then was correct.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the detailed design and procurement stage. Leah Whitfield sets up a group that meets every six weeks, bringing together Ade Okafor of Brackmoor Offshore Wind, the other wind operator, Sunita Rao and Bethany Cole. Its purpose is for the employers and the college to understand each other's priorities, agree who contacts whom on apprentice matters and keep the employers engaged as the design develops. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the project is building relationships with key external stakeholders.
Focus on products, because the group will set the quality specifications for the nacelle rig before it is ordered.
Ensure continued business justification, because the employers' pledges are the main source of the project's benefits.
Learn from experience, because the wind operators already train apprentices and can pass on lessons from their own centres.
4.w: The principle now covers relationships as well as roles: the project management team initiates and builds relationships with and between internal and external stakeholders (see manual 2.3). A regular group that helps the employers and the college understand each other and agree who contacts whom does exactly that.

n.1: The group exists to build understanding and agree contacts, not to write product descriptions or quality specifications.
n.2: The pledges matter to the business case, but the action described is building relationships, not checking that the project is still justified.
n.3: Nothing in the group's purpose is about seeking or recording lessons; it is about relationships and engagement.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is at the end of the detailed design and procurement stage, and the design-and-build contract is about to be signed. To save board time, Mark Ostrowski proposes treating stages 3, 4 and 5 as a single 13-month stage running to the opening day, because the contractor's programme covers all of that work. How well does this apply the 'manage by stages' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because longer stages reduce the burden on senior managers, and the contractor's programme has been agreed.
It applies it well, because the board will still receive highlight reports and can step in if a problem arises.
It applies it poorly, because a 13-month stage removes the points where the board reviews viability before committing more.
It applies it poorly, because commissioning and handover should be planned as part of a separate closing stage.
4.w: Manage by stages gives the board review and decision points at which it assesses viability before authorizing the next stage; shorter stages give more control, longer ones less burden (see manual 2.4). Merging the structural, fit-out and handover stages leaves no point between signing the contract and opening day at which the board decides whether to continue, despite the tight cost limit.

n.0: Stage length is a trade-off, but on a large build with a 3% cost limit and a fixed date, one 13-month stage gives up too much control; the contractor's programme does not replace board decision points.
n.1: Highlight reports keep the board informed, but they are not decision points at which the board reviews viability and authorizes the next commitment.
n.3: Closing a project is not a stage; it is the last part of the final stage, so commissioning and handover cannot move into a closing stage.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. The governors' limit of 3% above the approved budget and the fixed September opening are recorded as project tolerances. The board sets cost and time tolerances for each stage, Leah Whitfield agrees to raise an exception report as soon as a stage is forecast to go beyond them, and Mark Ostrowski will refer any forecast beyond the project tolerances to the governors. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Manage by stages, because the board sets separate cost and time tolerances for each of the five stages.
Ensure continued business justification, because a forecast overspend beyond 3% would threaten the college's reserves.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because Leah and Mark each have a defined part in escalating problems.
Manage by exception, because each level has limits of delegated authority and forecast breaches are escalated to the next level.
4.w: Manage by exception sets limits of delegated authority through tolerances, with escalation to the next level as soon as a breach is forecast: the business layer sets project tolerances, the board stage tolerances, and exceptions go upwards (see manual 2.5 and 11.2.1).

n.0: Tolerances are set per stage, but setting limits of authority and escalating forecast breaches is manage by exception.
n.1: An overspend would affect justification, but the arrangement described sets limits of delegated authority and escalation routes.
n.2: Roles are involved, but the core of the arrangement is tolerances at each level and escalation when they are forecast to be exceeded.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Before the architect starts the detailed design, Leah Whitfield arranges for Bethany Cole, Craig Dunmore and the architect to write the product description for the welding bays together. It sets out what each bay contains, the fume extraction performance it must achieve and who will review and approve it. How well does this apply the 'focus on products' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because Craig Dunmore holds a health and safety qualification and can approve the fume extraction design.
It applies it well, because defining each product and its quality requirements before design guides the work and avoids waste.
It applies it poorly, because product descriptions should be written by the supplier once the contract has been awarded.
It applies it poorly, because the vice principal's request for 30 bays must be decided before any product description is written.
4.w: Focus on products means defining products and their quality expectations before the work, so that the project is output-oriented and does no more than needed; product descriptions give purpose, composition, quality specifications and approval responsibilities, and co-creating them with users helps adoption (see manual 2.6 and 3.5.1).

n.0: Who approves is set out in the product description itself; Craig's qualification does not explain why defining the product first is good practice.
n.2: Product descriptions are prepared when planning, with input from users and suppliers; waiting for the contractor would leave the design without agreed requirements.
n.3: A request for change is handled through issue control; it does not stop the bays being described now, and the description can be updated if a change is approved.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Leah Whitfield proposes calling the project board the 'Skills Centre Steering Group', as the college names its capital project boards, using the college's capital project report template for highlight reports, and adding a site safety section to every highlight report, as one governor has asked. How well does this apply the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because the method can use the college's terms and formats and report the risks that matter here.
It applies it well, because tailoring lets the college set aside the principles that do not suit a building project.
It applies it poorly, because PRINCE2 names should be kept so that everyone can recognize the roles and products.
It applies it poorly, because tailoring is decided by the business layer before the project manager is appointed.
4.w: Tailoring adapts the method to the project's environment and risk: terminology can follow the organization's own, management products can take different formats, and controls such as reporting are shaped to the project's needs, here the safety risk next to the student entrance (see manual 2.7). The decisions are documented in the PID for the board to approve.

n.1: Principles cannot be tailored away; tailoring adapts processes, practices, roles, products and terminology.
n.2: Using the organization's own terminology is a recognized form of tailoring.
n.3: The project manager leads 'agree the tailoring requirements' in initiation, and the board approves the result in the PID.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage. The curriculum team designs courses in the main college building, while the contractor's site team, the Danish rig installers and Leah Whitfield, who works three days a week, are seldom on site together. Misunderstandings about room layouts are growing. Leah sets up a fortnightly site walk-round and lunch for Bethany Cole, the site manager and the installers, with a shared online board for questions in between. Is this an appropriate approach to leading the team, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager's role is to instruct each team on how its tasks should be carried out.
Yes, because regular purposeful contact builds trust and social cohesion between groups that rarely work together.
No, because the curriculum team belongs to the user community and so is not part of the project team.
No, because the contractor's staff work for their own company and so are outside Leah's leadership.
4.w: Bringing teams together means optimizing people's time and building social cohesion: people meeting purposefully and regularly, building trust across project silos; teams that are not co-located need deliberate methods to achieve this (see manual 3.3.3).

n.0: Instructing tasks is management; the action here is building trust and cohesion between groups, which is leadership.
n.2: People who use the products contribute to the project; the curriculum team is doing project work on the courses.
n.3: Leading across organizational boundaries is part of leading project teams; it calls for cultural intelligence, not exclusion.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the detailed design and procurement stage. Mark Ostrowski proposes that Craig Dunmore's estates team administer the design-and-build contract and check the contractor's monthly valuations, as they manage the college's small works contracts. Leah Whitfield notes that nobody in the team has handled a contract above £200,000, while Hamish Grant's firm checks valuations on large projects. Is this an appropriate approach to building the team, and why?
o: Yes, because the estates team will look after the building once it opens and so should own the contract.
Yes, because the college is acting as a thick client and should do most of the project work itself.
No, because contract administration is a project support task and so cannot be given to user representatives.
No, because roles should match capability, and the gap should be closed by upskilling or by giving the work to others.
4.w: Roles should reflect capability, authority and availability; the project manager identifies competency gaps and mitigates them, for example by upskilling or by shifting responsibilities to more suitable people, such as the cost consultant who already checks valuations (see manual 3.3.2).

n.0: Looking after the building later does not give the team the capability to administer a large contract now.
n.1: A thick client does much of the work itself, but roles should still go to people with the capability to fill them.
n.2: Contract tasks are not reserved to project support; the problem is the capability gap, not who the team represents.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the detailed design and procurement stage. Tenders show the budget is tight, and Mark Ostrowski suggests replacing the nacelle rig with a cheaper computer simulator. Before any recommendation goes to the board, Leah Whitfield meets Ade Okafor and the other wind operator to understand what their apprentices must be able to do on a real rig and how a simulator would affect their pledges. Is this an appropriate way to lead change with the people affected, and why?
o: Yes, because the wind operators are key influencers whose pledges rest on the rig, so their needs should shape the decision.
Yes, because the employers are paying for the rig and so have the authority to approve or reject the change.
No, because employers outside the college are not project stakeholders and can be informed after the board has decided.
No, because the change is a request for change, which the board decides without consulting stakeholders.
4.w: Stakeholder engagement means identifying stakeholders and key influencers and building relationships so that all impacted areas are involved as the project progresses (see manual 3.2.2). The wind operators say the rig is the main reason they are committing apprentices, so their needs should shape any recommendation.

n.1: The rig is funded by the grant and college reserves; the employers have influence, not authority over project decisions.
n.2: Stakeholders include organizations outside the business that can affect or be affected by the project; the employers are key ones.
n.3: Assessing a change is best done cooperatively; understanding its effect on stakeholders informs the recommendation to the board.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage. Three of the college's current electrical instructors, who will move into the new centre, keep objecting to the planned teaching timetable and have stopped attending design workshops. Sunita Rao suggests leaving them out of the remaining workshops so that decisions can be made faster. Is this an appropriate way to lead the change, and why?
o: Yes, because co-creation works best with people who support the change and will promote it to others.
Yes, because the instructors' line manager can direct them to accept the timetable once the centre opens.
No, because their resistance shows where engagement is needed, so the reasons behind it should be explored.
No, because each instructor is a senior user and must approve the course timetable before the centre opens.
4.w: Pockets of resistance show where communication and engagement should be focused: find out why people resist rather than sidelining them, and involve users in co-creating the ways of working they will adopt (see manual 3.2 and 3.4).

n.0: Co-creation involves users and key influencers, including doubters; excluding them makes adoption less likely.
n.1: Directing people to comply does not deal with the cause of resistance or help them move to the target state.
n.3: The instructors are users, but they do not hold the senior user role; Sunita Rao represents the users on the board.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is about to start the asbestos removal and strip-out. Site traffic will use a new gate, and the student pedestrian route will move for four months. About 1,800 students aged 16 to 18 use the main campus each day, and many arrive by bus. Leah Whitfield is updating the communication management approach. Which action BEST applies it?
o: Ask the main contractor to post notices on the site hoarding, as it is responsible for safety on its own site.
Plan messages for students, parents and bus operators through channels they use, with a way to raise concerns.
Add the route change to the next highlight report, so that the board and governors know about it first.
Send one email to all students and staff from the principal on the day before the strip-out starts.
4.w: The communication management approach sets the means and frequency of communication with, and feedback from, each stakeholder group, based on stakeholder analysis of who is affected (see manual 3.4). Students, parents and bus operators are directly affected by the moved route, so messages should reach them through suitable channels before and during the work, with a way to respond.

n.0: Site notices reach people who are already at the site; they do not plan messages for each affected group or allow feedback.
n.2: The highlight report informs the board about stage status; it does not reach the students and others who are affected.
n.3: A single late message with no route for feedback does not give a controlled, two-way flow of information.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Leah Whitfield drafts this entry for the communication management approach: 'Rachel Tse, sustainability manager: reports on the climate targets to the governors and the combined authority; strong influence on grant compliance scoring; worried that the heat pumps could be cut to save money.' Under which heading should this entry be recorded, and why?
o: Communications schedule and procedures, because it sets out how Rachel will report to the combined authority.
Supporting tools and techniques, because Rachel uses reporting tools to track the climate emergency targets.
Stakeholder analysis, because it records who is affected by or can influence the project and their current views.
Resources, because Rachel's time is needed for the project's communication activities on sustainability.
4.w: Stakeholder analysis identifies who is impacted by the project's outcome or delivery and who can influence its success or failure, with their interests and concerns (see manual 3.4). Rachel's role, influence on grant scoring and concern about the heat pumps belong there; the schedule and procedures then plan the messages for her.

n.0: The entry does not set out when or how messages will be sent; it describes Rachel's interest, influence and position.
n.1: No tool or platform for communication is described; the entry is about a stakeholder.
n.3: The entry does not commit Rachel's time to communication work; it analyses her as a stakeholder.

4.q: Matching set (business case). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Which management product, or heading of the business case, should each piece of information be recorded in? Statement 1 of 3: Sunita Rao's team will count apprentice enrolments each September for three years after opening and report the figures at planned benefits reviews.
o: Business case: expected benefits
Benefits management approach
Business case: costs
Sustainability management approach
4.w: The benefits management approach defines the benefits management actions and benefits reviews, including how and when benefits are measured and who is responsible, so that realization can be confirmed after the project (manual 5.5 and 5.3.1).

n.0: The expected benefits heading states the measurable benefits themselves; the measurement actions, timing and reviews belong in the benefits management approach.
n.2: No cost is described; this is how and when a benefit will be measured and reviewed.
n.3: Apprentice numbers are a benefit measure, not a sustainability performance target.

4.q: Matching set (business case). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Which management product, or heading of the business case, should each piece of information be recorded in? Statement 2 of 3: The heat pumps and solar panels will add £38,000 a year to the centre's running and maintenance costs, met from the estates budget.
o: Business case: expected benefits
Benefits management approach
Business case: costs
Sustainability management approach
4.w: The costs heading of the business case covers project costs and the ongoing operations and maintenance costs of the products, with their funding arrangements (business case composition, manual chapter 5).

n.0: This is a cost of owning the products, not an improvement they bring.
n.1: A running cost is not a benefits management action or review.
n.3: The sustainability management approach sets the actions, reviews and controls for sustainability targets; the running cost of the equipment and its funding belong under costs.

4.q: Matching set (business case). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Which management product, or heading of the business case, should each piece of information be recorded in? Statement 3 of 3: Construction waste diverted from landfill will be checked monthly from the contractor's waste records, with a tolerance of two percentage points below the 90% target.
o: Business case: expected benefits
Benefits management approach
Business case: costs
Sustainability management approach
4.w: Sustainability performance targets and tolerances are documented in the sustainability management approach, which defines the actions, reviews and controls needed to achieve them (manual 5.2.2).

n.0: Diverting waste is a sustainability target for the work, not an expected benefit of the centre.
n.1: Waste diversion is a sustainability target, not one of the project's benefits; its tolerance and checks belong in the sustainability management approach.
n.2: No cost is described; this is a target, a tolerance and a control.

4.q: Matching set (organizing). Greystack Build Ltd has won the design-and-build contract, and the project board for Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre is being confirmed. Using the additional information about the people, which individual would be most appropriate for each role? Statement 1 of 3: Executive.
o: Paul Kettering
Mark Ostrowski
Owen Pryce
Sunita Rao
4.w: Mark Ostrowski controls the college budget and reserves that part-fund the project and has led a major capital project. The executive is the single point of accountability, owns the business case and secures funding (manual 6.2.4 and appendix B).

n.0: Paul Kettering is a governor and chairs the finance and resources committee, which belongs to the business layer that sets project tolerances; he is not part of the college's management with the budget to commit.
n.2: Owen Pryce represents the contractor, which suits the senior supplier role; the executive represents the college's business interest.
n.3: Sunita Rao is responsible for the apprenticeship programmes that will use the centre, which suits the senior user role.

4.q: Matching set (organizing). Greystack Build Ltd has won the design-and-build contract, and the project board for Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre is being confirmed. Using the additional information about the people, which individual would be most appropriate for each role? Statement 2 of 3: Senior user.
o: Paul Kettering
Mark Ostrowski
Owen Pryce
Sunita Rao
4.w: Sunita Rao is responsible for the apprenticeship programmes that will run in the centre and for recruiting its instructors. The senior user represents those who will use the products, specifies the benefits and is responsible for showing that forecast benefits are on track and for their realization after closure (manual 6.2.4.2 and appendix B).

n.0: Paul Kettering is a governor in the business layer and will not use the centre's products.
n.1: Mark Ostrowski holds the budget and accountability for value, which suits the executive role.
n.2: Owen Pryce represents the organization delivering the building, not the people who will use it.

4.q: Matching set (organizing). Greystack Build Ltd has won the design-and-build contract, and the project board for Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre is being confirmed. Using the additional information about the people, which individual would be most appropriate for each role? Statement 3 of 3: Senior supplier.
o: Paul Kettering
Mark Ostrowski
Owen Pryce
Sunita Rao
4.w: Owen Pryce is contracts director at Greystack Build, which will design and build the centre. The senior supplier represents those delivering the products, commits supplier resources and is accountable for the quality of supplier products (manual 6.2.4 and appendix B).

n.0: Paul Kettering is a governor and a retired construction director; he does not represent or commit any supplier's resources.
n.1: Mark Ostrowski represents the college's business interest as executive.
n.3: Sunita Rao represents the users of the centre.

4.q: Matching set (plans). Leah Whitfield is writing the work package description for the asbestos removal in stage 3, to be carried out by a licensed subcontractor. Under which heading of the work package description should each piece of information be recorded? Statement 1 of 3: Site vehicles must not cross the student pedestrian route, and no removal work may take place while students are arriving or leaving.
o: Techniques and procedures
Constraints
References
Targets and tolerances
4.w: Constraints in a work package description cover restrictions on how the work is done, such as permitted hours, safety and security requirements (plans practice, work package description composition, manual chapter 7).

n.0: These are restrictions on when and where work may happen, not the methods to be used for removal.
n.2: References list the documents the work package draws on, such as higher-level plans; these are restrictions.
n.3: No target or permitted deviation for time, cost or scope is stated.

4.q: Matching set (plans). Leah Whitfield is writing the work package description for the asbestos removal in stage 3, to be carried out by a licensed subcontractor. Under which heading of the work package description should each piece of information be recorded? Statement 2 of 3: Complete the removal in five weeks at a cost of £140,000, plus or minus three days and £7,000.
o: Techniques and procedures
Constraints
References
Targets and tolerances
4.w: A work package description sets the targets and the time, cost and scope tolerances within which the team manager works; benefits and quality tolerances are not set at this level (manual 11.2.1).

n.0: Duration, cost and permitted deviation are targets and tolerances, not techniques.
n.1: These are targets with permitted deviations rather than restrictions on how the work is done.
n.2: Figures for time and cost with a permitted deviation are tolerances, not references to other documents.

4.q: Matching set (plans). Leah Whitfield is writing the work package description for the asbestos removal in stage 3, to be carried out by a licensed subcontractor. Under which heading of the work package description should each piece of information be recorded? Statement 3 of 3: The stage 3 plan, the asbestos survey report and the product description for the cleared warehouse.
o: Techniques and procedures
Constraints
References
Targets and tolerances
4.w: References identify the documents the work package relies on, such as the stage plan it comes from and related product descriptions (plans practice, work package description composition, manual chapter 7).

n.0: These are documents to refer to, not the methods the subcontractor will use.
n.1: No restriction on the work is described; these are source documents.
n.3: No time, cost or scope targets are given.

4.q: Matching set (quality). Leah Whitfield, Bethany Cole and Craig Dunmore are writing the product description for the welding bays. Under which heading of the product description should each piece of information be recorded? Statement 1 of 3: Twenty-four bays, each with a screened booth, a fume extraction hood, a gas supply point and a welding power source.
o: Quality specifications
Quality responsibilities
Composition
Derivation
4.w: Composition lists the parts the product is made up of (product description composition, manual chapter 8).

n.0: No measurable level the product must meet is stated; this lists its parts.
n.1: No producer, reviewer or approver is named.
n.3: Derivation says what the product is developed from; this lists what it contains.

4.q: Matching set (quality). Leah Whitfield, Bethany Cole and Craig Dunmore are writing the product description for the welding bays. Under which heading of the product description should each piece of information be recorded? Statement 2 of 3: Each extraction hood must achieve a capture velocity of at least 0.5 metres per second at the welding position.
o: Quality specifications
Quality responsibilities
Composition
Derivation
4.w: Quality specifications set the measurable levels the finished product must meet, which quality control checks against (manual 8.2 and product description composition).

n.1: No person responsible for producing, reviewing or approving the bays is named.
n.2: This is a measurable performance level, not a list of the product's parts.
n.3: This is not a source the product is derived from; it is a measure it must meet.

4.q: Matching set (quality). Leah Whitfield, Bethany Cole and Craig Dunmore are writing the product description for the welding bays. Under which heading of the product description should each piece of information be recorded? Statement 3 of 3: The architect's approved layout drawings and the fume extraction design produced in stage 2.
o: Quality specifications
Quality responsibilities
Composition
Derivation
4.w: Derivation identifies the source products from which the product is developed, here the approved drawings and extraction design (product description composition, manual chapter 8).

n.0: Drawings and a design are sources for the product, not measures of its quality.
n.1: No responsibilities for quality are described.
n.2: These are inputs the bays are built from, not parts of the bays.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the detailed design and procurement stage. Tender prices put the project close to its budget, and Mark Ostrowski suggests replacing the heat pumps with gas boilers to save £280,000, saying this must improve the business case. Leah Whitfield instead updates the business case to show both the saving and the effect on the combined authority's grant compliance scoring and on the college's climate targets, so the board can compare the options. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because justification is about overall value, and outcomes must stay aligned with business objectives, including ESG goals.
Yes, because the sustainability management approach fixes the heat pumps as a requirement that the board cannot change.
No, because sustainability targets are recorded in the sustainability management approach, not in the business case.
No, because the executive chooses between business options, so the project manager should not analyse alternatives.
4.w: Business justification is about value, not cost alone: outcomes and benefits must align with business objectives, which can include ESG goals, and the sustainability management approach supports the business case (see manual 5.2.2 and 5.2.3). A saving that put grant compliance and the climate targets at risk could reduce overall value, so both effects must be shown.

n.1: The sustainability management approach sets targets and controls, but the board can still decide on options; the reason the analysis is right is that value, not cost alone, decides justification.
n.2: The targets sit in the sustainability management approach, which supports the business case; the effect of dropping them on grant scoring and objectives is part of the justification.
n.3: The project manager prepares and maintains the business case on the executive's behalf, including assessing options for the board.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. The draft benefits management approach says that Sunita Rao, as senior user, will specify the apprenticeship benefits, show the board at each stage end that the forecast is on track, and remain responsible for the continued realization of the benefits after opening. Benefits reviews are planned at the end of the first and second academic years after opening. Is this an effective way to apply the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project board will carry out the reviews itself, as it is accountable for the benefits.
Yes, because the senior user specifies the benefits and is responsible for their realization, including after closure.
No, because the executive owns the business case and so should demonstrate that the forecast benefits are on track.
No, because benefits reviews should take place before the board authorizes closure, while the team is in place.
4.w: The senior user specifies the benefits, demonstrates that forecast benefits are on track and is responsible for their continued realization after the project closes (see manual 6.2.4.2). The benefits management approach plans the reviews that will confirm them, which the business carries out after closure (see manual 5.5 and 5.3.1).

n.0: Post-project benefits reviews are carried out by the business; the project board does not continue after closure.
n.2: The executive is accountable for the business case, but demonstrating that forecast benefits are on track is a senior user responsibility.
n.3: Most benefits arise after the project; reviews are planned during the project and carried out by the business after closure.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Leah Whitfield works three days a week. Mark Ostrowski proposes that Craig Dunmore act as project manager on her two non-working days, with each of them authorizing work packages and taking decisions on their own days. Is this an appropriate application of the organizing practice, and why?
o: Yes, because PRINCE2 roles can be shared between people when the workload is too great for one person.
Yes, because Craig Dunmore holds a health and safety qualification and knows the college site well.
No, because Craig Dunmore represents the users and so cannot hold any project role other than senior user.
No, because the project manager role should not be shared, so that day-to-day management keeps a single focus.
4.w: The project manager role should not be shared, so that day-to-day management has a single point of focus; depending on scale and capacity the project manager may take on team manager and project support roles, but two people should not each act as project manager (see manual 6.2.4).

n.0: Some roles, such as senior user, can be shared, but the project manager role should not be.
n.1: Craig's knowledge may make him useful to the project, but it does not justify splitting the project manager role.
n.2: One person can hold more than one role within the rules, for example user assurance or team manager; the problem is sharing the project manager role.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Mark Ostrowski, as executive, asks the college's head of internal audit to provide business assurance by reviewing cost reports and forecasts independently of Leah Whitfield. Sunita Rao, as senior user, asks Craig Dunmore to provide user assurance that the building can be run and maintained. Mark and Sunita remain answerable for assurance in their areas. Is this an effective way to apply the organizing practice, and why?
o: Yes, because assurance can go to suitable people independent of the project manager, while accountability stays with the board.
Yes, because delegating assurance moves accountability for each area from the board members to the people appointed.
No, because project assurance has to be carried out by the board members themselves and cannot be delegated.
No, because assurance should come from project support, so that the registers can be checked at the same time.
4.w: Board members are accountable for assurance of their own areas, business, user and supplier, but may delegate it to people in the business or outside it, who must be independent of the project manager; delegating does not move the accountability (see manual 6.2.4 and appendix B).

n.1: Board members remain accountable for assurance of their areas even when they delegate the work.
n.2: Assurance can be delegated to people from the business or to external parties.
n.3: Project support must be kept separate from project assurance; it cannot assure the project.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. In the product flow diagram, Leah Whitfield shows the nacelle training rig as an external product from the Danish manufacturer. Working back from the opening date, its 30-week lead time and installation in stage 4 mean the order must be placed during stage 2, before the building contract is signed. She schedules the order accordingly. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the product flow diagram shows the sequence and dependencies of products, including those from outside.
Yes, because the rig is a must-have product for the wind operators and so is scheduled ahead of every other product.
No, because products supplied from outside the project are outside its control and are left out of its plans.
No, because committing to the rig before stage 4 is authorized conflicts with the manage by stages principle.
4.w: Product-based planning includes a product flow diagram showing the sequence of development and the dependencies between products, including external products; the schedule is then built from it, which reveals when long-lead items must be ordered (see manual 7.3.1).

n.1: The rig's importance does not set its place in the schedule; its dependencies and lead time do.
n.2: External products are shown in the product flow diagram because the project depends on them.
n.3: The order is placed within stage 2 under a plan the board has authorized; scheduling for lead times is part of planning.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. The governors have set a zero time tolerance on the September opening and a cost tolerance of 3% above budget. In the project plan, Leah Whitfield ranks the products, marks the visitor viewing gallery and the external landscaping as lower priority, and proposes a scope tolerance, for the governors to confirm, that allows them to be dropped if time or cost come under pressure. Is this an effective way to apply the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager sets the project tolerances in the project plan for the board to approve.
Yes, because with time fixed and cost capped, a scope tolerance on lower-priority products gives room to manage.
No, because scope tolerance is set for work packages, not for the project plan or the stage plans.
No, because tolerances should be set equally across all seven aspects so that none takes precedence.
4.w: Tolerances are used to manage constraints, and understanding which constraints take precedence is crucial when setting them (see manual 7.2.4). With no time tolerance and a tight cost limit, a scope tolerance based on prioritized products is what allows the plan to flex.

n.0: Project tolerances are set by the business layer, here the governors; the project manager proposes and plans within them.
n.2: Scope tolerance is set for project and stage plans as well as work packages.
n.3: Knowing which constraints take precedence is crucial to setting tolerances; they are not set equally.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage. The combined authority wants confidence that the project's checks on the fume extraction and the electrical installation are adequate. Mark Ostrowski asks the college's quality and compliance unit, which sits outside the project management team, to review whether the planned inspections and tests are appropriate and to report its findings to the board. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because quality assurance is done independently of the project management team, checking that quality controls are suitable.
Yes, because the quality and compliance unit is part of project assurance, which the project manager is responsible for.
No, because quality assurance should be done by the senior supplier, who is accountable for the quality of supplier products.
No, because checking the tests is part of quality control, which team managers carry out within their work packages.
4.w: Quality assurance is a planned, systematic activity, performed independently of the project management team, often by a business function, that gives confidence the project's quality control measures are appropriate (see manual 8.2.3). It differs from project assurance, which is the board's responsibility.

n.1: Project assurance is the board's responsibility, not the project manager's, and a unit outside the project management team is providing quality assurance.
n.2: The senior supplier is accountable for supplier products, but quality assurance is independent of the project management team.
n.3: Quality control checks the products themselves; reviewing whether the controls are appropriate is quality assurance.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the commissioning and handover stage. The contractor's commissioning engineer tests the fume extraction, finds four bays below the specified capture velocity, adjusts the fans and retests them the next day. Only the passing retest results are entered in the quality register, so it shows every bay passing first time. Is this an effective way to apply the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because a failed check may be repeated where a pass is expected, and the final result is what counts.
Yes, because the quality register is a record for the team, and the board relies on the end stage report instead.
No, because the register should record each quality activity and its result, including failures and the response.
No, because the failed bays are off-specifications that must be accepted as concessions by the project board.
4.w: The quality register records all quality activities planned and performed, with dates, responsibilities and results, including failures and the response to them; a failed check may be repeated, but the record must be complete so that progress and quality can be reviewed (see manual 8.2.2 and 8.3.1.2).

n.0: Repeating a failed check is allowed, but the register should still record the failure and the response to it.
n.1: The quality register is used by the project manager and project assurance to review progress, and its records feed the end stage report.
n.3: After adjustment the bays meet their specification, so there is no off-specification needing a concession.

4.q: Matching set (risk). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is recording risk information as it moves from starting up into initiation and delivery. Which product should each piece of information be recorded in? Statement 1 of 3: During starting up, before any registers have been set up, Leah Whitfield notes a possible threat that contamination under the warehouse floor could delay the structural works.
o: Risk register
Daily log
Issue management approach
Risk management approach
4.w: In starting up a project, an initial set of key risks is identified and recorded in the daily log, because the risk register is not set up until initiation (manual table 13.3 and 4.3.2).

n.0: The risk register is set up in initiating a project; until then early risks are kept in the daily log.
n.2: The issue management approach describes how issues and changes are handled; it holds no specific risks.
n.3: The risk management approach describes procedures and scales and contains no specific risks; it is also not written until initiation.

4.q: Matching set (risk). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is recording risk information as it moves from starting up into initiation and delivery. Which product should each piece of information be recorded in? Statement 2 of 3: In initiation, Leah Whitfield sets out the five-point probability and impact scales the project will use, and that threats scoring 15 or more will be reported to the board.
o: Risk register
Daily log
Issue management approach
Risk management approach
4.w: The risk management approach describes how risk will be managed: the procedures, techniques, standards and responsibilities, such as scoring scales and when risks are escalated (manual 9.2.1 and chapter 9 products).

n.0: The risk register records specific risks and their status, not the scales and procedure for assessing them.
n.1: These are agreed procedures for the whole project, not informal notes.
n.2: Probability and impact scales for risks belong in the risk management approach, not the approach for issues and change control.

4.q: Matching set (risk). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is recording risk information as it moves from starting up into initiation and delivery. Which product should each piece of information be recorded in? Statement 3 of 3: In stage 2, Leah Whitfield records that, as the Danish manufacturer has a full order book, the rig may be delivered late, delaying the opening, with Sunita Rao as risk owner.
o: Risk register
Daily log
Issue management approach
Risk management approach
4.w: The risk register records each identified risk with its description as cause, event and effect, its owner and its status (manual chapter 9 products).

n.1: Once the risk register exists, formal risks are recorded there with an owner, not in the daily log.
n.2: This is a specific uncertain event, not a procedure for handling issues.
n.3: The risk management approach holds procedures and scales, never individual risks.

4.q: Matching set (issues). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage, and Leah Whitfield is recording new issues in the issue register. Which type of issue should each be recorded as? Statement 1 of 3: Craig Dunmore asks for the plant room to be enlarged so that the heat pumps are easier to maintain, which would change the approved design.
o: Off-specification
Request for change
Business opportunity
Event external to the project
4.w: A request for change is a proposal for a change to a baseline, here the approved design (manual 10.1 and issue types).

n.0: Nothing has failed to meet its specification; Craig wants the specification itself changed.
n.2: This is a proposed change to the baseline, not an unexpected positive consequence for the organization.
n.3: The request comes from within the project team about its own design, not from an event outside the project.

4.q: Matching set (issues). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage, and Leah Whitfield is recording new issues in the issue register. Which type of issue should each be recorded as? Statement 2 of 3: Testing shows that the electrical installation in two classrooms will not meet the earthing specification in its product description.
o: Off-specification
Request for change
Business opportunity
Event external to the project
4.w: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications (manual 10.1 and issue types).

n.1: No one is proposing to change the baseline; the product is forecast to fall short of it.
n.2: A shortfall against specification is not a positive opportunity.
n.3: The failure is in the project's own product, not an event outside the project.

4.q: Matching set (issues). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage, and Leah Whitfield is recording new issues in the issue register. Which type of issue should each be recorded as? Statement 3 of 3: Bethany Cole points out that the welding bays could also host paid evening courses for local adults, bringing the college extra income.
o: Off-specification
Request for change
Business opportunity
Event external to the project
4.w: A business opportunity is an unanticipated positive consequence for the project or the user organization, here extra income for the college (manual 10.1 and issue types).

n.0: No product is failing to meet its specification.
n.1: No change to an approved product is proposed; the idea is a new way for the college to benefit.
n.3: The idea comes from within the project, from a user, not from an event outside it.

4.q: Matching set (progress). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the asbestos removal, strip-out and structural works stage. Which report or log should each item be recorded in? Statement 1 of 3: Leah Whitfield's monthly summary to the board of the stage's status, including site safety incidents, as one governor has asked.
o: Highlight report
Checkpoint report
Lessons log
End stage report
4.w: The highlight report is the project manager's regular, time-driven summary of stage status to the project board, at an interval the board sets (manual chapter 11 products).

n.1: Checkpoint reports go from a team manager to the project manager about a work package.
n.2: This is a status report to the board, not a note of a lesson.
n.3: The end stage report is produced once, at the end of the stage, not every month.

4.q: Matching set (progress). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the asbestos removal, strip-out and structural works stage. Which report or log should each item be recorded in? Statement 2 of 3: Leah Whitfield notes that the contractor's weekly written reports give a far clearer picture of progress than the verbal reports on the lab refurbishment did.
o: Highlight report
Checkpoint report
Lessons log
End stage report
4.w: The lessons log is the informal repository for lessons that could be applied on this or future projects (manual chapter 11 products).

n.0: The observation is a lesson about reporting, not a summary of stage status for the board.
n.1: A checkpoint report gives work package status; this is a lesson learned.
n.3: Lessons may later feed the end stage report, but the note is first recorded in the lessons log.

4.q: Matching set (progress). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the asbestos removal, strip-out and structural works stage. Which report or log should each item be recorded in? Statement 3 of 3: At the end of the stage, Leah Whitfield summarizes its performance and the overall project position so the board can decide whether to authorize the fit-out stage.
o: Highlight report
Checkpoint report
Lessons log
End stage report
4.w: The end stage report, produced in managing a stage boundary, summarizes the stage's progress and the overall project situation so the board can decide what to do next (manual chapter 11 products).

n.0: Highlight reports are routine during a stage; the event-driven report at the stage end is the end stage report.
n.1: Checkpoint reports cover a work package, not the stage and the project.
n.2: This is a formal report to the board, not an informal record of lessons.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the detailed design and procurement stage. There is a risk that the nacelle rig, with its 30-week lead time, arrives after opening day. Leah Whitfield agrees with Ade Okafor that, if this happens, first-term apprentices will train on Brackmoor's own rig at its base, and she sets aside money in the risk budget for transport, to be spent if the rig is late. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because it is a transfer response, passing the financial impact of a late rig to Brackmoor Offshore Wind.
Yes, because it prepares a contingent plan now, funded by the risk budget, for use if the risk occurs.
No, because money for responding to risks should come from the change budget rather than the risk budget.
No, because late delivery depends on a supplier in Denmark, so the risk should be accepted and watched.
4.w: Preparing contingent plans means planning actions now that will be used only if the risk occurs; the risk budget funds specific responses to risks, such as contingent plans (see manual 9.2.3.1 and table 9.1).

n.0: Transfer passes the financial impact to a third party such as an insurer; here the college plans actions and pays for them itself.
n.2: The change budget funds approved changes; responses to risks, including contingent plans, are funded from the risk budget.
n.3: A risk outside the project's direct control can still have a response planned; acceptance is one option, not a requirement.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. At a risk workshop, Craig Dunmore raises the threat of a site vehicle striking a student on the pedestrian route. The group rates it as very unlikely because the expected contractor has worked safely for the college before, and Mark Ostrowski says he does not want safety worries to delay the start. Nobody challenges this, and the threat is accepted with no action. Is this an effective way to apply the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because data on past performance predicts future performance and so supports the low rating.
Yes, because the project board sets risk tolerance, so the workshop can accept threats that fall within it.
No, because optimism bias and groupthink are distorting the assessment, despite the lab project's vehicle incident.
No, because threats to safety should be transferred to the contractor through the design-and-build contract.
4.w: Decision bias can harm risk management: optimism bias discounts unfavourable risks and assumes success, and groupthink values group cohesion over dissent (see manual 9.2.4). The lab refurbishment's reportable incident with a contractor's van shows the threat is real, so the assessment and response need to be revisited.

n.0: Past data can help, but here it is used selectively: the college's own last project had a reportable vehicle incident.
n.1: Tolerance is set by the board, but that does not excuse an assessment distorted by bias.
n.3: Transfer deals with the financial impact; it does not remove the need for an honest assessment and suitable action on a safety threat.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the detailed design and procurement stage. Sunita Rao asks for 30 welding bays instead of 24. Leah Whitfield records it as a request for change, assesses with Hamish Grant and the architect its effect on cost, space, fume extraction, timescale and the business case, and sends the board an issue report setting out options, a recommendation and the consequences of approving or rejecting it. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the vice principal is the senior user and can approve changes to user requirements herself.
Yes, because the request is captured and assessed, then a recommendation goes to those with authority to decide.
No, because a request raised informally by a board member should be recorded in the daily log instead.
No, because a request that adds cost must be escalated to the board in an exception report.
4.w: The issues technique captures the issue, assesses its effect on targets, the business case and other products, recommends options to whoever holds the authority with the consequences of each made clear, then records the decision and implements it (see manual 10.3.1).

n.0: The senior user represents the users, but requests for change are decided by the board or a delegated change authority.
n.2: A request to change the approved design needs formal handling in the issue register, however it was raised.
n.3: An exception report is for a forecast breach of stage or project tolerance; a request for change is presented in an issue report.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. The board delegates to Leah Whitfield the authority to approve requests for change costing up to £10,000 each. It does not set a change budget, saying that approved changes can be paid for from the risk budget held for asbestos and ground conditions. Is this an effective way to apply the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the board is the ultimate authority for changes and may delegate approval to the project manager.
Yes, because one shared budget gives Leah more flexibility to deal with the asbestos and ground risks.
No, because the project manager cannot be a change authority, as approving changes is a board role.
No, because delegated change authority needs a change budget, and the risk budget is for responses to risks.
4.w: The board may delegate authority to approve changes, but it should come with a change budget so that approved changes can be funded and implemented; the risk budget is for responses to risks, not for changes (see manual 10.2.4, 10.2.5 and chapter 9).

n.0: Delegation to the project manager is allowed, but without a change budget the approved changes cannot properly be funded.
n.1: Spending the risk budget on changes would leave the asbestos and ground risks without the funds set aside for them.
n.2: The board may delegate approval of changes to a change authority or to the project manager.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the commissioning and handover stage. On a walk-round, instructors make 60 minor comments, such as scuffed paint and a sticking cupboard door, all of which the contractor has agreed to put right under the contract. Leah Whitfield records each one as a formal issue in the issue register and prepares an issue report on each for the board. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because comments from instructors are concerns, and each concern should be assessed and decided by the board.
Yes, because a full record of every snag will be needed for the end project report at closure.
No, because judgement is needed on what to record formally, and minor snags under the contract can be handled informally.
No, because snagging items are risks rather than issues and should go in the risk register.
4.w: Judgement is needed on which issues to record formally: too many trivial issues swamp decision-making, and informal issues can be managed in the daily log (see manual 10.2.2 and 10.1). Minor snags the contractor is already obliged to fix do not need board decisions.

n.0: Concerns are assessed by the project manager first; the board decides on issues beyond the project manager's authority.
n.1: The end project report reviews products and off-specifications; it does not need each minor snag raised formally.
n.3: The snags already exist, so they are not uncertain events; they are minor issues.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. The finance and resources committee meets every two months but wants to know at once about any forecast overspend. Leah Whitfield agrees monthly highlight reports for the board and weekly written checkpoint reports from the contractor. She also agrees to send an exception report as soon as a stage is forecast to exceed its cost tolerance, and Mark Ostrowski will pass any forecast project overspend to the committee. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because regular time-driven reports are combined with event-driven escalation when a breach is forecast.
Yes, because highlight reports should go straight to the finance and resources committee instead of the board.
No, because exception reports should be timed to match the committee's meetings every two months.
No, because weekly checkpoint reports are more frequent than a project of this size needs.
4.w: Progress control combines time-driven controls, such as highlight and checkpoint reports at agreed intervals, with event-driven controls, such as an exception report raised as soon as a breach of tolerance is forecast (see manual 11.2.2 and 11.2.6).

n.1: Highlight reports go to the project board; the committee, as part of the business layer, is told about project-level exceptions.
n.2: Exception reporting is event-driven: it happens as soon as a breach is forecast, not at fixed intervals.
n.3: Reporting frequency reflects the control needed; written weekly reports also address the lab project's lesson about verbal reporting.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage. Heat pump prices have risen, and Leah Whitfield's exception report forecasts that the project will finish 5% over budget, beyond the governors' 3% limit. Mark Ostrowski asks her to prepare an exception plan funded by a further £150,000 from college reserves, and the board approves it at its next meeting without referring it to the governors. Is this an effective way to apply the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project board decides how to respond to exception reports raised by the project manager.
Yes, because Mark Ostrowski controls the college's reserves and so can provide the extra funding.
No, because the exception plan should have been prepared before the exception report was sent to the board.
No, because a forecast breach of project tolerance is for the business layer, here the governors, to decide.
4.w: Under exception management the board decides on forecast breaches of stage tolerance, but forecast breaches of project tolerance are decided by the business layer, which set those tolerances (see manual 11.2.1 and 11.3.1). Here the governors set the 3% limit, so they must decide.

n.0: The board decides on breaches of stage tolerance; a forecast breach of project tolerance goes to the business layer.
n.1: Controlling reserves does not give the executive authority to exceed tolerances set by the governors.
n.2: The exception report comes first; the board then decides whether to request an exception plan.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'starting up a project' process. With Hamish Grant, Leah Whitfield compares three ways of delivering the centre: the estates team managing separate trade contracts, a traditional design-then-build contract, and the architect's design followed by a design-and-build contract. She recommends the last, with the college as a relatively thick client, and records the reasons in the project brief. Is this an appropriate application of the 'select the project approach' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because this activity decides how the work will be delivered, such as in-house or by third parties, before initiation.
Yes, because the project approach is first set out in the PID, which the board approves when it authorizes the project.
No, because the procurement route belongs in the commercial management approach, which is written in initiation.
No, because choosing the delivery method is a decision the project board takes in 'authorize initiation'.
4.w: 'Select the project approach' decides how the work will be approached, for example in-house or through third parties, build or buy, and which delivery method, so that alternatives are evaluated before initiation and recorded in the project brief (see manual 13.4.5).

n.1: The project approach is selected in starting up and recorded in the project brief; it is not first set out in the PID.
n.2: The commercial management approach later details procurement procedures, but the choice of delivery approach is made in starting up.
