n.3: The board approves the project brief in 'authorize initiation'; evaluating and selecting the approach is work done in starting up.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'starting up a project' process. Acting for the college's leadership, which forms the business layer, Dr Elaine Fairbairn has asked Mark Ostrowski to be the executive. Mark is now agreeing Leah Whitfield's fixed-term appointment as project manager. Using the recommended RACI for 'appoint the executive and the project manager', which statement is correct?
o: Mark Ostrowski, as executive, is accountable, and Leah Whitfield, as project manager, is responsible.
The project board is accountable, and the business layer, here Dr Fairbairn, is consulted.
The business layer, here Dr Fairbairn, is responsible, and the governors are accountable.
The business layer, here Dr Fairbairn, is accountable, and Mark Ostrowski, as executive, is responsible.
4.w: In the recommended RACI for 'appoint the executive and the project manager', the business layer is accountable and the executive is responsible; the project manager then manages the project day to day on the executive's behalf (see manual 13.4.1 and table 13.2).

n.0: The executive is responsible for this activity rather than accountable, and the business layer is accountable.
n.1: The project board is not yet formed; the business layer is accountable for these appointments.
n.2: The executive, not the business layer, is responsible for the activity; the business layer is accountable.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'starting up a project' process. Because the opening date cannot move, Mark Ostrowski asks Leah Whitfield to use starting up to prepare a full cost plan, a detailed risk register and the full business case, so that the board can authorize the whole project in one step. Starting up is now planned to take ten weeks. Is this an effective way to carry out starting up a project, and why?
o: Yes, because detailed work in starting up reduces the risk of missing the fixed opening date.
Yes, because the board can authorize initiation and the project together when the end date is fixed.
No, because starting up should do the minimum needed to decide whether initiation is worthwhile.
No, because the cost plan and risk register should be prepared by project assurance, not the project manager.
4.w: Starting up a project answers whether there is a viable and worthwhile project; it is a lighter process than initiation, doing the minimum necessary to decide whether initiation is worthwhile and to prevent poorly conceived projects being initiated (see manual 13.1). The full business case and detailed plans are prepared in initiating a project.

n.0: Detailed planning belongs in initiation, after the board has confirmed that initiation is worthwhile; starting up stays light.
n.1: Authorizing initiation and authorizing the project are separate decisions in directing a project, whatever the deadline.
n.3: Project assurance reviews for the board; it does not prepare the project's plans and registers.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the asbestos removal, strip-out and structural works stage. The contractor offers to work on Saturdays at no extra cost to recover four days lost to bad weather, but site traffic would then pass the campus on Saturday enrichment days. Leah Whitfield asks the board for advice. Mark Ostrowski consults Sunita Rao by phone and confirms the board's view to Leah in writing the same day. Is this an appropriate application of the 'give ongoing direction' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the executive can approve changes to the stage plan without involving the other board members.
Yes, because board members can give informal guidance in answer to requests for advice at any time in a stage.
No, because the board should give direction at stage boundaries, through its response to the end stage report.
No, because advice from the board has to be agreed at a formal meeting attended by all of its members.
4.w: 'Give ongoing direction' lets the board, collectively or through individual members, give informal guidance and respond to requests for advice at any time during the project (see manual 14.4.3).

n.0: No change to the stage plan is being approved; Mark is responding to a request for advice, after consulting the senior user.
n.2: Ongoing direction can be given at any time during a stage, not only at stage boundaries.
n.3: Ongoing direction can be given informally, collectively or by individual board members.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is at the end of the detailed design and procurement stage. The board is reviewing the end stage report and the plan for stage 3, which includes signing the design-and-build contract. Using the recommended RACI for 'authorize a stage or exception plan', which statement is correct?
o: The executive is accountable, and the project manager is informed of the decision.
The project board as a whole is accountable, and the business layer is informed.
The business layer is accountable, and the executive is consulted on the decision.
The project manager is accountable, and the senior user and project assurance are informed.
4.w: In the recommended RACI for 'authorize a stage or exception plan', the executive is accountable and responsible, the senior user and project assurance are consulted, and the project manager is informed (see manual 14.4.4 and table 14.2).

n.1: The RACI makes the executive, as the single point of accountability, accountable for this decision.
n.2: Authorizing a stage is a project board decision, with the executive accountable; the business layer is not accountable for it.
n.3: The project manager prepares the plan but is informed of the decision; the senior user and project assurance are consulted.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Leah Whitfield submits the project initiation documentation for authorization. The board approves the full business case, the project plan and the other management approaches, but says it will look at the benefits management approach at closure, as apprentices will not start until the centre opens. Is this an effective way to carry out directing a project, and why?
o: Yes, because benefits are realized after the project, so how they are measured is planned in closing a project.
Yes, because the senior user specifies the benefits and so is the one who approves the benefits management approach.
No, because 'authorize the project' includes reviewing how and when the benefits will be measured and confirmed.
No, because the board should carry out the benefits reviews itself before it authorizes the first delivery stage.
4.w: In 'authorize the project' the board confirms that the business case shows a viable project, approves the PID and reviews the benefits management approach, so that it knows how benefits will be measured and confirmed (see manual 14.4.2 and table 14.3).

n.0: The benefits management approach is updated in closing, but it is created in initiation and reviewed when the project is authorized.
n.1: The senior user specifies the benefits, but the benefits management approach is reviewed and approved by the board in directing a project when it authorizes the project.
n.3: Benefits reviews take place mainly after closure; at authorization the board reviews how they will be done.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. While assembling the project initiation documentation, Leah Whitfield cross-checks the project plan against the business case and the grant agreement. She finds that the planned spending profile would leave £600,000 of grant unclaimed by 31 March of the second year, and revises the plan before requesting authorization. Is this an appropriate application of the 'assemble the project initiation documentation' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the parts are checked for consistency before the version used for authorization is baselined.
Yes, because grant claims are a project benefit and so must be recorded in the benefits management approach.
No, because the project plan is fixed before the PID is assembled and can then change through change control.
No, because the business case should be adjusted to fit the project plan rather than the other way round.
4.w: In 'assemble the project initiation documentation' the project manager cross-checks the elements for compatibility; the version used to gain authorization is then baselined and placed under change control (see manual 15.4.6).

n.1: Grant income is funding, not a benefit of the centre; the point is that the PID's parts must be consistent.
n.2: The PID is not baselined until it is authorized; inconsistencies found while assembling it are fixed before then.
n.3: Either part may need to change; what matters is that they are compatible, and here the plan was at fault.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Mark Ostrowski is the executive and Leah Whitfield the project manager. The outline business case is being developed into the full business case, using costs from the project plan and the risks in the project log. Using the recommended RACI for 'prepare the full business case', which statement is correct?
o: Dr Elaine Fairbairn, as the business layer, is accountable, and Mark Ostrowski is responsible.
Mark Ostrowski is accountable, Leah Whitfield is responsible and project assurance is consulted.
Leah Whitfield is accountable, and Hamish Grant, who prepares the cost plans, is responsible.
The project board is accountable, and Mark Ostrowski and Sunita Rao are jointly responsible.
4.w: In the recommended RACI for 'prepare the full business case', the executive is accountable, the project manager is responsible, project assurance is consulted and the business layer is not involved (see manual 15.4.5 and table 15.2).

n.0: The business layer is not involved in this activity; the executive is accountable and the project manager responsible.
n.2: The project manager is responsible, not accountable; the executive is accountable for the business case.
n.3: The executive alone is accountable, and the project manager prepares the business case on the executive's behalf.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. To save time, Mark Ostrowski proposes not writing a communication management approach: the governors already receive the college's monthly finance report, and Leah Whitfield can tell other people about the project as the need arises. Is this an effective way to carry out initiating a project, and why?
o: Yes, because tailoring allows management products to be merged with reports the college already uses.
Yes, because highlight reports will tell all stakeholders about progress at a frequency agreed by the board.
No, because each management approach has to be a separate document that the board reviews and approves on its own.
No, because stakeholders from governors to students have distinct needs, so how and when to communicate must be agreed.
4.w: In 'agree the management approaches' the communication management approach defines the means and frequency of communication with, and feedback from, the project ecosystem (see manual 15.4.2 and 3.4). Here the governors want safety reports, the finance committee wants immediate overspend warnings, and students and employers are affected, so communication cannot be left to chance.

n.0: Products can be merged or reformatted, but the governors' finance report does not cover the project's other stakeholders' needs.
n.1: Highlight reports go to the board; they do not reach students, employers or the combined authority.
n.2: Management approaches can be combined or tailored; the problem is that communication would not be planned at all.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the asbestos removal, strip-out and structural works stage. More asbestos is found behind a wall lining. Leah Whitfield captures and assesses the problem: it adds two weeks and £35,000, within the stage tolerances of three weeks and £60,000, and can be funded from the risk budget held for asbestos. She issues a revised work package to the removal subcontractor and reports the action in her next highlight report. Is this an appropriate application of the 'take corrective action' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because asbestos is a safety matter, which the project manager may resolve without involving the board.
Yes, because within stage tolerance the project manager selects a solution and applies it through a work package.
No, because the extra cost should be referred to the board in an exception report before the work is changed.
No, because the subcontractor's team manager should decide the response and revise the work package.
4.w: 'Take corrective action' collects information about a deviation, identifies and selects solutions that keep the stage within tolerance, and puts them into effect through 'authorize a work package' (see manual 16.4.6). The board is kept informed through the highlight report.

n.0: Safety is not what gives Leah authority to act; it is that the deviation is forecast to stay within stage tolerance.
n.2: An exception report is needed when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded; this deviation stays within it.
n.3: The team manager raises the problem and carries out the revised work, but the project manager decides corrective action and authorizes work packages.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage. Remembering the lab refurbishment, Leah Whitfield writes into each work package description how the contractor's team must raise problems and requests for change, so that nothing is agreed on site without assessment, and she updates the issue register as they arrive. Which practice is being applied by the 'controlling a stage' process?
o: Progress, because the contractor will report problems to the project manager through its checkpoint reports.
Plans, because the work package descriptions are prepared, agreed and then authorized by the project manager.
Organizing, because each team's responsibilities for raising problems are defined in the work packages.
Issues, because the issue management approach is built into the work packages and the issue register is kept current.
4.w: In controlling a stage the issues practice is applied by including the issue management approach in work package descriptions and keeping the issue register up to date (see manual table 16.3).

n.0: Checkpoint reports carry progress information, but the action described applies the issue management approach.
n.1: Work package descriptions are plans products, but their content here is how issues and changes are handled.
n.2: Responsibilities are mentioned, but the procedure for capturing problems and changes belongs to the issues practice.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage. Greystack's site manager tells Leah Whitfield by phone that the welding bays work package is finished. As the stage is behind schedule, she marks it complete in the stage plan and authorizes the next work package, although the product description says the bays must pass the fume extraction test and be approved by Craig Dunmore. Is this an effective way to carry out controlling a stage, and why?
o: Yes, because the team manager is responsible for the quality of the products in the work package.
Yes, because the quality checks can be carried out during commissioning and handover in stage 5.
No, because a work package is received as complete once each product has the approvals in its product description.
No, because completion of a work package should be notified to the project board by the senior supplier.
4.w: In 'receive completed work package' the project manager makes sure each product has the approval required by the quality and sustainability responsibilities in its product description, then updates the product register and stage plan (see manual 16.4.3).

n.0: The team manager delivers to the product descriptions, but the project manager must confirm the required approvals before accepting the work package as complete.
n.1: The product description sets when and by whom the bays are approved; delaying the checks leaves an unapproved product treated as complete.
n.3: Work package completion is notified by the team manager to the project manager; the board is not involved in managing product delivery.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage. Greystack's site manager is leading the fit-out work package. After the fire-stopping inspection passes, his team records the result in the quality register. He also notices that the planned heat pump compound may block the delivery route for the nacelle rig, and reports this new risk to Leah Whitfield in his weekly checkpoint report. Is this an appropriate application of the 'execute a work package' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the team manager reports new risks to the project manager and keeps quality records up to date.
Yes, because the team manager owns all the risks within the work package and decides how to respond to them.
No, because new risks should be raised directly with the senior supplier, who represents the contractor.
No, because project support, not the team, should update the quality register with inspection results.
4.w: In 'execute a work package' the team manager manages development of the products, notifies the project manager of new issues, risks or lessons, takes any action the project manager requires, records completed quality activities in the quality register and reports through checkpoint reports (see manual 17.4.2).

n.1: The team manager notifies new risks to the project manager and takes any action the project manager requires.
n.2: In managing product delivery the team manager deals with the project manager, not with board members.
n.3: In managing product delivery the team records completed quality activities and updates the quality register.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the asbestos removal, strip-out and structural works stage. Greystack's site manager has finished the strip-out work package and is notifying Leah Whitfield, the project manager. Using the recommended RACI for 'notify work package completion', which other role should be informed?
o: The business layer, so that the governors know the strip-out has been completed.
The senior user, so that Sunita Rao can plan the next curriculum activities.
Project support, so that the project's records and registers can be updated.
The senior supplier, so that Owen Pryce can confirm the completed work to the board.
4.w: In the recommended RACI for 'notify work package completion', project support is informed, while the business layer, senior user and senior supplier are not; the board is not involved in managing product delivery (see manual 17.4.4 and table 17.2).

n.0: The business layer is not informed of work package completion; it receives project-level information through the board.
n.1: The recommended RACI does not inform the senior user of work package completion.
n.3: The recommended RACI does not inform the senior supplier; completion is a matter between the team manager and the project manager.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage. Ingrid Sorensen's installation team is installing the nacelle rig under a work package. Visiting the site, Ade Okafor of Brackmoor asks the team to add a second control panel like the one on Brackmoor's turbines. The team agrees, as the change is small and Brackmoor is a key employer, and tells Leah Whitfield once it is done. Is this an effective way to carry out managing product delivery, and why?
o: Yes, because Brackmoor's support is the main reason the wind operators are committing apprentices.
Yes, because a team manager may agree minor product changes directly with key stakeholders during installation.
No, because changes to the rig have to be approved by Sunita Rao as senior user before work starts.
No, because the team should work under the project manager's direction and raise the request as an issue.
4.w: Managing product delivery controls the link between the project manager and the team manager: the team works to the agreed work package, notifies the project manager of new issues and takes action required by the project manager, not by others (see manual 17.1 and 17.4.2). A request to change the product goes through issue control.

n.0: Brackmoor's importance makes the request worth assessing, but it does not authorize the team to change the product.
n.1: A change to an agreed product is a request for change: the team raises it with the project manager for issue control, and the team manager does not agree it directly with stakeholders.
n.2: Requests for change are decided by the board or a delegated change authority, not by the senior user acting alone.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is near the end of the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage. Leah Whitfield briefs the board on the stage's performance, gives an overview of the commissioning and handover stage, confirms that the eight instructors have been recruited, and highlights that four welding bays were accepted under a concession because their screens differ slightly from the specification. Is this an appropriate application of the 'request next stage' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the board needs the stage's performance, readiness for the next stage and any concessions to decide.
Yes, because the project manager authorizes the next stage once the board has read the end stage report.
No, because concessions should be reported in the end project report at closure rather than at a stage end.
No, because instructor recruitment is business as usual and lies outside the scope of the project.
4.w: In 'request next stage' the project manager briefs the board on current stage performance, gives an overview of the next stage and the people and resources it needs, confirms readiness to proceed and highlights any concessions for off-specifications in the stage (see managing a stage boundary, manual chapter 18).

n.1: The next stage starts only when the board authorizes it in directing a project; the project manager requests it.
n.2: Concessions granted in a stage are highlighted when requesting the next stage, as well as being reviewed at closure.
n.3: Course and staff readiness is part of the project's final stage, so instructor recruitment is relevant to readiness.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is near the end of the asbestos removal, strip-out and structural works stage, and Leah Whitfield is preparing the end stage report. Using the recommended RACI for 'evaluate the stage', which roles should she consult?
o: The executive and the senior user, who will decide whether to authorize the next stage.
The team manager, project support and project assurance, who hold the information and checks needed.
The business layer and the senior supplier, as the contractor's work makes up most of the stage.
The senior user, the senior supplier and the business layer, to agree what the report will say.
4.w: In the recommended RACI for 'evaluate the stage', the project manager is responsible for preparing the end stage report, and the team manager, project support and project assurance are consulted (see managing a stage boundary, manual chapter 18).

n.0: The RACI for 'evaluate the stage' consults the team manager, project support and project assurance; the board decides later in directing a project.
n.2: The business layer is not consulted in this activity, and the senior supplier is not among the roles consulted.
n.3: The project manager is responsible for the report; the roles consulted are the team manager, project support and project assurance.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is near the end of the asbestos removal, strip-out and structural works stage. Leah Whitfield updates the project plan with actual progress and prepares the fit-out stage plan. Heat pump quotes have risen by £120,000 and Brackmoor has cut its pledge from 40 to 25 apprentice places a year, but she leaves the business case unchanged because the grant amount has not changed. Is this an effective way to manage the stage boundary, and why?
o: Yes, because the business case is updated in initiation and is then confirmed after the centre has opened.
Yes, because changes in costs and pledges should be handled as issues within controlling a stage, not at the boundary.
No, because the fall in pledges should be referred to the combined authority before the stage boundary.
No, because the business case should show the new costs and benefit forecasts so the board can confirm justification.
4.w: In managing a stage boundary the business case is updated to reflect changes in the project and its environment, with revised costs, benefit forecasts and aggregated risk, so that the board can confirm continued business justification before authorizing the next stage (see manual chapter 18 and 5.3.1).

n.0: The business case is maintained at every stage boundary, not left until benefits are confirmed after closure.
n.1: Issues are captured during the stage, but their effect on justification is brought together in the business case at the boundary.
n.2: The combined authority is the funder, not part of the project's decision-making; the board needs the updated business case.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the asbestos removal, strip-out and structural works stage. After a funding review, the combined authority withdraws the grant, and the board instructs Leah Whitfield to close the project early. She records the instruction, makes the site safe and secure, agrees with the contractor which completed work is kept and which is abandoned, and makes sure the project's records are archived. Is this an appropriate application of the 'prepare premature closure' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager decides when the project should close once its business case is no longer valid.
Yes, because a premature close still needs an orderly closure, with useful work salvaged and products made safe.
No, because when the grant is withdrawn the board closes the project in directing a project, without closing a project.
No, because an exception plan should be prepared first to show how the project could continue with less money.
4.w: When the board orders a premature close, closing a project is still used: 'prepare premature closure' records the request, salvages anything useful, makes products safe and agrees what is completed or abandoned, so that the project is closed in an orderly way rather than abandoned (see manual 19.3 and 19.4.2).

n.0: Premature closure is triggered by the project board, not by the project manager.
n.2: Closing a project is still run, tailored as needed, when the board orders a premature close.
n.3: The board has already decided to close the project; preparing an exception plan would ignore that decision.

4.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'closing a project' process. Leah Whitfield is preparing the end project report and the lessons report, comparing the project's performance with the baselined project initiation documentation. Using the recommended RACI for 'evaluate the project', which statement is correct?
o: The executive is accountable, the project manager responsible, and the senior supplier and project assurance consulted.
The project manager is accountable, project support is responsible, and the business layer is consulted on the report.
The senior user is accountable, the project manager responsible, and the team managers informed of the findings.
The business layer is accountable, the executive responsible, and the project manager consulted on the findings.
4.w: In the recommended RACI for 'evaluate the project', the executive is accountable, the project manager is responsible, and the senior supplier and project assurance are consulted (see manual 19.4.4 and table 19.2).

n.1: The project manager is responsible for this activity and the executive accountable; the business layer is not consulted.
n.2: The executive, not the senior user, is accountable for evaluating the project.
n.3: The project manager, not the executive, is responsible for evaluating the project, with the executive accountable.

4.q: The Engineering Skills Centre opened on time, and the project is in the 'closing a project' process. Leah Whitfield proposes keeping the project open for six months after opening, so that the project team can deal with snags during the contractor's defects period and check that 300 apprentices have enrolled before the project closes. Is this an effective way to carry out closing a project, and why?
o: Yes, because benefits have to be confirmed before the project closes, so the project should stay open until enrolment is known.
Yes, because defects found in the first months of use are part of the project's scope and need its team to resolve them.
No, because a clear end is needed: open matters go to follow-on actions and the business reviews benefits after closure.
No, because closing a project should be planned as a separate stage after the commissioning and handover stage.
4.w: Closing a project gives a fixed point at which acceptance is confirmed; a clear end is better than a slow drift into use. Open issues and risks are passed on as follow-on action recommendations, and post-project benefits reviews are planned in the benefits management approach and carried out by the business (see manual 19.1 to 19.3).

n.0: Benefits are mostly confirmed after closure by the business, through reviews planned in the benefits management approach.
n.1: Defects handled under the contract can be passed on as follow-on actions; they do not justify keeping the project running.
n.3: Closing a project is not a stage; it is part of the final stage, so planning it as a separate stage is wrong.

5.q: Wenmoor's single point of access (SPA) project is at the boundary between the Eastfield pilot stage and the evaluation and roll-out stage. The commissioner has just confirmed that it will no longer withhold contract value if the SPA is late, and pilot data show referral to first contact falling to seven days, not the three days in the business case. Karen Lindqvist, the executive, says that because staff are trained and much of the budget is spent, the roll-out should go ahead without revisiting the business case. How well does this apply the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because stopping after the pilot would waste the money already spent on backfill and training.
It applies it well, because the executive owns the business case and decides when it needs to be reviewed.
It applies it poorly, because the benefits should be confirmed in a post-project review before the roll-out is authorized.
It applies it poorly, because the business case should be checked at the stage boundary to confirm the roll-out is still worth doing.
5.w: The justification for a project must remain valid and be revalidated throughout, and the board checks the business case at every stage boundary before authorizing the next stage (see manual 2.1 and 5.3.1). A change in the contract position and a much weaker benefit forecast are exactly what that check is for; if the roll-out is no longer justified it should be changed or stopped.

n.0: Money already spent cannot be recovered whatever is decided; the decision should rest on whether the remaining investment is still justified by the remaining benefits.
n.1: The executive is accountable for the business case, but that accountability includes having it checked at each stage end, not skipping the check.
n.2: Benefits are mainly confirmed after closure; at a stage boundary the business case is updated and checked using forecasts, not confirmed.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'starting up a project' process. Ellie Chandran, the project manager, finds that nobody recorded why the 2021 attempt to introduce central booking in Moorside was abandoned. She arranges to talk to Gareth Pugh, who took part in it, and to the managers of another community health provider that already runs a single point of access, and she records what she learns in the lessons log. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because Gareth Pugh is an informal leader whose support the project will need.
Ensure continued business justification, because the 2021 failure suggests the board must prove the SPA is worth doing.
Learn from experience, because lessons are being sought from an earlier attempt and from another organization.
Manage by stages, because the 2021 attempt ran for four months without a point at which it could be reviewed.
5.w: Learn from experience: lessons are sought, recorded and acted on from the start of a project, and where an organization has little relevant experience it is even more important to learn from others, including outside organizations (see manual 2.2). Consulting people with experience of similar work and recording it in the lessons log is the 'assess previous lessons' activity (13.4.2).

n.0: Gareth's influence matters for engaging Moorside nurses, but here Ellie is drawing on his experience of the earlier attempt, not defining his role or relationships.
n.1: Ellie is collecting lessons, not testing whether the SPA is desirable, viable and achievable; its justification rests on the commissioner's condition and the expected benefits.
n.3: The scenario does not say how the 2021 attempt was controlled; Ellie's action is seeking and recording lessons, not dividing this project into stages.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'starting up a project' process. Karen Lindqvist, the executive, first proposes Moira Healy, head of nursing for Eastfield, as the only senior user. Moira points out that she has no authority over the Moorside and Holtby nursing teams, which will have to change how they work during the roll-out. Karen therefore also appoints the heads of nursing for Moorside and Holtby as senior users. How well does this apply the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because users in all three localities are represented by people with authority over the teams affected.
It applies it well, because a larger board shares the executive's accountability for the project among more people.
It applies it poorly, because a project board should have a single senior user so that user decisions are not delayed.
It applies it poorly, because Gareth Pugh, whose views many Moorside nurses follow, should be their senior user.
5.w: The principle requires a project management team in which the business, user and supplier interests are properly represented by people with the authority to commit their area (see manual 2.3 and 6.2.1). The senior user role can be held by more than one person, so adding the Moorside and Holtby heads of nursing gives every locality that must adopt the SPA a voice in directing it.

n.1: There is one executive, whose accountability cannot be shared or delegated; adding senior users does not change that.
n.2: The senior user role can be shared by several people; leaving two localities unrepresented would weaken user commitment to the roll-out.
n.3: Gareth is a key influencer to engage, but he is an informal leader rather than the manager of the Moorside teams; the senior user needs authority to commit user resources.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Moira Healy, head of nursing for Eastfield, says her team is overstretched and asks to open the triage hub in Eastfield now, using draft triage criteria, rather than wait for the project to be authorized. Karen Lindqvist, the executive, agrees so that benefits start sooner, and asks Ellie Chandran to finish the project initiation documentation alongside. How well does this apply the 'manage by stages' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because an early start in Eastfield will give the board real data with which to judge the business case.
It applies it well, because the senior user may start using products in her own locality once she judges them fit.
It applies it poorly, because delivery work should not begin until the board has authorized the project and the next stage.
It applies it poorly, because each stage should be the same length so that the board reviews the project at regular intervals.
5.w: Manage by stages makes sure a project is properly initiated before delivery work starts, and each stage begins when the board authorizes it (see manual 2.4 and 14.4.4). Opening the hub during initiation, with criteria that have not been signed off, bypasses that decision point in a trust with a low appetite for clinical safety risk.

n.0: Pilot data are useful, but the plan already provides a controlled Eastfield pilot after the design stage; wanting data does not justify skipping the authorization decision.
n.1: The senior user accepts products against agreed criteria but has no authority to start delivery; work begins when the project and the stage are authorized.
n.3: Stage lengths vary with risk, complexity and decision points; the SPA plan already has stages of 8, 12, 16 and 24 weeks.

5.q: The SPA project is in the Eastfield pilot stage. Ellie Chandran authorizes the triage hub work package with tolerances of three days and £4,000. Within those limits, the team manager, the hub's lead nurse, decides how to cover rota gaps and reports this in her weekly checkpoint report; if she forecasts that the limits will be exceeded, she raises it with Ellie straight away. How well does this apply the 'manage by exception' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because the team manager reports the hub's progress to the project manager at regular intervals.
It applies it well, because authority is delegated within tolerances to the people who know the work, and forecast breaches are escalated.
It applies it poorly, because rota decisions during the pilot should be referred to the project board, which is accountable for it.
It applies it poorly, because the work package should also carry a benefits tolerance to protect the three-day target.
5.w: Manage by exception sets limits of delegated authority through tolerances, so each level decides within its limits and escalates as soon as a breach is forecast (see manual 2.5 and 11.2.1). Decisions are best made at the most local level where the knowledge sits (3.5.1): here the lead nurse decides rota cover and raises a forecast breach with the project manager.

n.0: Regular checkpoint reporting is time-driven progress control; it does not explain the delegation within tolerances and escalation on which manage by exception relies.
n.2: The board manages by exception; day-to-day decisions inside the work package belong to the team manager, within the tolerances the project manager has set.
n.3: Work package tolerances cover scope, cost and time; a benefits tolerance is not set in a work package description.

5.q: The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage. Before any triage criteria are drafted, Ellie Chandran and Moira Healy meet nurses and therapists from all three localities to agree a description of the 'triage criteria' product: what it is for, what it must contain, and that every criterion must be signed off by the clinical safety officer and the medical director before use. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Focus on products, because the team is agreeing what the triage criteria must contain and the quality they must meet before work starts.
Tailor to suit the project, because the clinical sign-off is a trust rule added to the standard PRINCE2 method for this project.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the description names who must approve the triage criteria.
Manage by exception, because the clinical safety officer's sign-off limits what the triage hub may change by itself.
5.w: Focus on products: the project defines its products, including their purpose, composition and quality requirements, before doing the work, so that the work delivers what users need and no more (see manual 2.6). Writing the product description with staff from every locality also co-creates the product, which helps adoption (3.5.1).

n.1: The sign-off rule is a quality requirement written into the product description, not an adaptation of the method to suit the project.
n.2: Naming approvers is one part of a product description; the action as a whole is defining the product before it is built.
n.3: Manage by exception concerns tolerances and escalation between management levels; an approval requirement for a product is part of defining that product.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Ellie Chandran proposes that project documents use the trust's own term 'senior responsible owner' for the executive role, and that highlight reports become a one-page summary posted fortnightly on the trust's collaboration platform, where board members can comment, because most of them work on rotas and meet online at lunchtime. Is this appropriate tailoring, and why?
o: Yes, because terminology and the format of reports can be adapted to the trust while the controls they provide are kept.
Yes, because tailoring allows the board to drop highlight reports when its members can see progress on the platform.
No, because PRINCE2 role names must be used in all project documents so that the method is applied consistently.
No, because the board should meet in person at each reporting interval to review the highlight report together.
5.w: Tailoring adapts the method to the project's environment and people: the organization's own terms can replace PRINCE2 terms, and the format and frequency of reports can suit the way the board works, while the principles and the controls the reports provide are kept (see manual 2.7). A short online highlight report suits a dispersed board that works on rotas.

n.1: The proposal keeps highlight reports and changes their format; it does not remove the time-driven reporting control.
n.2: Using the organization's own terms is a recognized form of tailoring; what cannot be tailored away are the principles.
n.3: PRINCE2 does not require the board to meet in person to receive highlight reports; virtual reporting to a dispersed board is acceptable tailoring.

5.q: The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage. Design team members work part-time or on rotas across the three localities and meet online at lunchtime. Ellie Chandran notices that Moorside and Eastfield staff rarely build on each other's ideas. She arranges a half-day design workshop each month, held in each locality in turn, for the key designers, with their clinical time backfilled from the budget, while keeping the short online meetings. Is this an appropriate way to lead the team, and why?
o: Yes, because co-located teams share information more easily, so the design team should now be moved to one site.
Yes, because a dispersed, part-time team needs deliberate chances to meet so that trust and cohesion can form.
No, because team-building is a matter for the line managers in each locality rather than for the project manager.
No, because the backfill budget pays for clinical time and should not be used for workshops away from patients.
5.w: Virtual, remote or hybrid teams do not build social cohesion by chance: deliberate methods, such as regular and purposeful in-person sessions for key people, build trust across project silos (see manual 3.3.3). Building the temporary project team is part of leading it, so Ellie is right to arrange this.

n.0: The workshops are held in each locality in turn and the team keeps working in its own localities; nobody is being moved to one site.
n.2: Leading and building the temporary project team is part of the project manager's and the board's responsibility; line managers do not lead the project team.
n.3: The workshops release clinicians from patient work, which is what backfilling clinical time pays for.

5.q: The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage. Hub nurses complain that Medivault's configuration team does not understand clinical language, and Medivault says the nurses' requests are vague. Ellie Chandran arranges for two Medivault configurers to spend a day in the Eastfield referral office, and for nurses to join Medivault's planning sessions, so that each side learns how the other works. Is this an appropriate way to lead the team, and why?
o: Yes, because leading across organizational boundaries depends on understanding how each organization works.
Yes, because the senior supplier is accountable for the quality of the products that the supplier delivers.
No, because Medivault is a contracted supplier, so working practices should be set by its support contract.
No, because the configurers' time should go on configuration work rather than on visits to the referral office.
5.w: Projects bring together people from different organizations with different cultures; leading across those boundaries calls for cultural intelligence, the ability to relate to and work across those cultures (see manual 3.3.1). Letting each side see how the other works builds shared understanding and better working relationships.

n.1: This is true of the senior supplier, but it does not explain why the joint visits help the two teams work together.
n.2: A contract sets what is supplied, but the project still has to build working relationships across organizations; the contract does not resolve misunderstandings between the teams.
n.3: Time spent understanding the users' work reduces rework from misunderstood requests; it supports the configuration rather than competing with it.

5.q: The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage. Many Moorside district nurses believe the triage hub will remove their professional judgement about which patients they see first. Gareth Pugh, a senior district nurse whose views many of them follow, shares this concern. Ellie Chandran invites Gareth to co-lead the working group that designs the triage criteria for rural visits. Is this an appropriate way to lead the change, and why?
o: Yes, because Gareth's long service makes him the right person to be the senior user for the Moorside locality.
Yes, because involving a key influencer in designing the new ways of working helps the people affected to adopt them.
No, because Gareth holds no formal role, so the project should work with Moorside nurses through their line managers.
No, because the loss of control over referrals is a dis-benefit already in the business case, so it has been accepted.
5.w: Leading change means identifying key influencers, including people with no formal role, and co-creating products and ways of working with users and influencers so that they are adopted (see manual 3.2.2 and 3.3). Giving Gareth a real part in designing rural triage can turn a likely source of resistance into ownership.

n.0: The action is about co-creating the criteria, not about board roles; the senior user needs authority to commit user resources, which an informal leader does not hold.
n.2: Projects should involve key people who are critical to success even when they hold no formal role; line management alone will not address an informal leader's influence.
n.3: Recording a dis-benefit in the business case does not remove the need to lead the people affected through the change.

5.q: The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage. Several Moorside GP practices say they will keep faxing referrals to the nurses they know, and Dr Anita Kapoor, chair of the Moorside GP federation, has publicly questioned whether the SPA suits a rural area. Ellie Chandran proposes that Karen Lindqvist, the executive, writes to the practices instructing them to stop faxing, and that Dr Kapoor is left out of the design work because she opposes the project. Is this an appropriate way to lead the change, and why?
o: Yes, because the commissioner has made the SPA a contract condition, so the support of GP practices is not needed.
Yes, because a clear instruction from the executive saves time that would otherwise go on stakeholders who disagree.
No, because GP practices are independent organizations and so fall outside the project's stakeholders.
No, because Dr Kapoor is a key influencer whose concerns about rural access should be understood and addressed.
5.w: Stakeholder engagement identifies key influencers and builds relationships with them; resistance shows where engagement should be focused, and its causes should be explored rather than the stakeholder sidelined (see manual 3.2.2 and 3.4). Dr Kapoor can sway the Moorside practices, so understanding her concerns is central to adoption there.

n.0: A contract condition makes the SPA necessary but does not make GP practices use it; referrers' cooperation is needed for the benefits.
n.1: Sidelining people who disagree tends to deepen resistance; PRINCE2 7 asks the project to find out why they resist.
n.2: Stakeholders include anyone who can affect or be affected by the project, inside or outside the business; referring GP practices clearly are.

5.q: The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage. New rotas for the triage hub have been drafted. Lorraine Fenwick, the union representative for nursing staff, has asked to see them before they are agreed, and most nurses work shifts and join meetings online at lunchtime. Which action BEST applies the communication management approach?
o: Email the final rotas to all nursing staff and to the union once the project board has approved them.
Publish the draft rotas on the trust intranet and ask nurses to raise any concerns through their line managers.
Share the draft rotas with Lorraine Fenwick and hold online lunchtime sessions for nurses' feedback before they are agreed.
Present the draft rotas at the next board meeting and invite the union to raise concerns through formal consultation later.
5.w: The communication management approach sets the means and frequency of communication with, and feedback from, each stakeholder group, as a controlled two-way flow (see manual 3.4). Sharing drafts with the union before agreement, and using the lunchtime online slot that staff can attend, gives the people affected a voice while it can still shape the rotas.

n.0: Sending rotas after approval is one-way and does not meet the union's request to see them before they are agreed.
n.1: Posting on the intranet is passive, and routing concerns through line managers gives no planned feedback channel to the project or the union.
n.3: Deferring the union's input until after the board has seen the rotas fails its request and limits two-way communication.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Ellie Chandran is drafting the communication management approach and has written this entry: 'Moorside GP practices: send referrals by fax to nurses they know; strongly influenced by Dr Kapoor; doubt that a single point of access suits a rural area; their cooperation will decide whether the Moorside roll-out succeeds.' Under which heading of the communication management approach should this entry be recorded, and why?
o: Communications schedule and procedures, because it sets out how the project will contact these practices.
Supporting tools and techniques, because it identifies fax as the channel that these practices currently use.
Resources, because it shows that extra staff effort will be needed to win over the Moorside practices.
Stakeholder analysis, because it records how this group is affected and how it could influence success.
5.w: Stakeholder analysis identifies who is affected by the project and who can influence its success or failure, with their position and influencers (see manual 3.4). The entry describes the Moorside practices' interests, attitude and influence, so it belongs there; the schedule of messages to them would follow from it.

n.0: The entry sets out no message, channel or timing for contacting the practices; it analyses their interests and influence.
n.1: Supporting tools and techniques covers tools the project uses, such as communication platforms or analytics; fax is mentioned as the practices' current behaviour.
n.2: Resources covers the people and budget for communication activities; the entry says nothing about the effort the project will provide.

5.q: Matching set (business case). The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process, and Ellie Chandran is preparing the full business case and the management approaches. Which product should each piece of information be recorded in? Statement 1 of 3: The project will cost £650,000, mostly to backfill clinical time and pay for training, funded from the commissioner's transformation money; the running cost of the triage hub rota will be met from the community services budget.
o: Project brief
Sustainability management approach
Business case
Benefits management approach
5.w: Project costs, ongoing running costs and how they are funded are recorded under the costs heading of the business case, which is completed as the full business case during initiation (see manual 5.5, business case composition).

n.0: The project brief, with its outline business case, was the basis for authorizing initiation and is superseded by the project initiation documentation; full costs belong in the business case now being prepared.
n.1: The sustainability management approach sets out actions, reviews and controls for sustainability targets, not the project's costs and funding.
n.3: The benefits management approach covers how benefits will be measured and reviewed, not what the project costs.

5.q: Matching set (business case). The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process, and Ellie Chandran is preparing the full business case and the management approaches. Which product should each piece of information be recorded in? Statement 2 of 3: The target is three days from referral to first contact; a result of up to four days is acceptable, and anything above that must be escalated to the trust's executive team.
o: Project brief
Sustainability management approach
Business case
Benefits management approach
5.w: Benefits tolerance, the permitted deviation from a benefit target before escalation, is documented in the benefits management approach (see manual 5.2.2).

n.0: The project brief set out the outline position for initiation; benefits tolerance is documented in the benefits management approach.
n.1: Referral waiting time is a service benefit rather than a sustainability performance target, so its tolerance is not recorded in the sustainability management approach.
n.2: The business case states the expected benefits, but the tolerance on a benefit target is documented in the benefits management approach.

5.q: Matching set (business case). The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process, and Ellie Chandran is preparing the full business case and the management approaches. Which product should each piece of information be recorded in? Statement 3 of 3: Moira Healy's team will count lost and duplicated referrals each month after each locality goes live, and a benefits review will be held 12 months after the final roll-out.
o: Project brief
Sustainability management approach
Business case
Benefits management approach
5.w: The benefits management approach defines the benefits management actions and the benefits reviews, including who measures what and when, so that realization can be confirmed, including after the project closes (see manual 5.5).

n.0: The project brief is superseded at initiation and does not plan benefits measurement after closure.
n.1: Lost referrals are a service benefit; the sustainability management approach covers sustainability targets and their controls.
n.2: The business case says which benefits are expected; the actions and reviews that measure them belong in the benefits management approach.

5.q: Matching set (organizing). The SPA project is in the 'starting up a project' process and the project management team is being appointed. Using the additional information about the people, which individual would be most appropriate for each role? Statement 1 of 3: Executive.
o: Karen Lindqvist
Moira Healy
Dr Samuel Adeyemi
Neil Ashworth
5.w: Karen Lindqvist holds the budget for community services, sits on the trust's executive team and reports to the commissioner on contract performance, so she can secure funding and be accountable for the business case (see manual 6.2.4 and appendix B).

n.2: Dr Samuel Adeyemi's part is to approve changes to the clinical triage criteria; he does not hold the community services budget that the executive needs to secure funding.
n.3: Neil Ashworth is independent of operational services and holds no budget for them, which suits assurance rather than the accountable executive role.

5.q: Matching set (organizing). The SPA project is in the 'starting up a project' process and the project management team is being appointed. Using the additional information about the people, which individual would be most appropriate for each role? Statement 2 of 3: Senior user.

Moira Healy
Dr Samuel Adeyemi
Neil Ashworth

5.q: Matching set (quality). In the design and pilot preparation stage, Ellie Chandran is writing the product description for the triage criteria. Composition
Derivation
Quality specifications

Quality specifications

5.q: Matching set (quality). In the design and pilot preparation stage, Ellie Chandran is writing the product description for the triage criteria. Composition
Derivation

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'starting up a project' process. In the outline business case, Ellie Chandran compares three options: keep the 14 referral routes and accept the loss of part of the contract value; set up one phone number that forwards calls to the three localities; or the full single point of access with a triage hub. She uses the first option as the baseline against which the other two are measured. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because even a required project should show that its chosen option gives best value against doing nothing differently.
Yes, because the outline business case gives detailed costs of every option so the board can authorize the project.
No, because the commissioner has made the SPA a contract condition, so the full SPA is the one option to cost.
No, because keeping the current 14 routes is not a valid option to analyse once the commissioner has made the SPA compulsory.
5.w: Developing the business case includes options analysis: 'do nothing differently' always comes first and is the baseline for measuring the others, followed by 'do the minimum' and 'do more than the minimum' (see manual 5.2.3 and 5.3.1). Compulsory projects still need to justify the option chosen.

n.1: The outline business case in starting up is high-level and supports the decision to authorize initiation; the project is authorized later on the full business case.
n.2: A contract condition may make some change unavoidable, but the chosen solution must still be justified against the alternatives.
n.3: Keeping things as they are ('do nothing differently') is analysed first even for a required project, because it is the baseline against which the other options are measured.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. In the draft benefits management approach, Ellie Chandran names herself as responsible for measuring the fall in unnecessary home visits for 12 months after the final roll-out. No one in the nursing service is named, and Moira Healy, the senior user, has not been asked about the measures. Is this an effective way to apply the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager prepares the benefits management approach on behalf of the executive of the project.
Yes, because the project manager is best placed to compare the home visit data with the figures in the business case.
No, because the senior user is responsible for showing that benefits are on track and for their realization after closure.
No, because benefits should be measured before closure, while the project team is still in place to do the work.
5.w: The senior user specifies the benefits and is responsible for demonstrating that forecast benefits are on track and for their continued realization after the project closes, when the project manager's role has ended (see manual 6.2.4.2). Leaving Moira and the nursing service out of the measures weakens the business's ownership of the benefits.

n.0: The project manager may draft the approach for the executive, but that does not make her the right person to measure benefits after the project has closed.
n.1: The project team disbands at closure; measurement over the following 12 months must be owned by the business through the senior user.
n.3: Most benefits are realized after the project closes, so measurement has to continue after closure; the flaw is that nobody in the nursing service owns it.

5.q: The SPA project is approaching the end of the Eastfield pilot stage. For the roll-out stage, Ellie Chandran plans how Moorside and Holtby nurses will join the triage rota, which Eastfield pilot staff will hand over and return to their teams, and when Medivault's configurers will leave. She updates the role descriptions and arranges an induction for new hub staff. Is this an appropriate application of the organizing practice, and why?
o: Yes, because 17% staff turnover means the project management team must be redesigned at every stage boundary.
Yes, because the people needed change during a project, so moving people on and off it should be managed.
No, because the project management team structure is fixed at authorization and changes through an exception plan.
No, because moving staff between rotas is a line management matter for the business and lies outside the project.
5.w: The organizational design and development technique includes managing ongoing changes to the project ecosystem: the capabilities needed change over the lifecycle, so people are moved on and off the project and new members are inducted (see manual 6.3.1). Role descriptions and the team structure are adapted at stage boundaries.

n.0: Turnover is a reason to plan succession, but the technique does not require a full redesign at every boundary; these changes follow the move from pilot to roll-out.
n.2: The team structure and role descriptions are reviewed and adapted at stage boundaries; they do not need an exception plan to change.
n.3: Line managers release their staff, but planning who joins and leaves the project team, and inducting them, is part of the project's organizing work.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Moira Healy is the senior user. To save her time, she proposes that one of the hub nurses who is writing the triage criteria also carries out user assurance on her behalf, as the nurse knows the criteria in detail. Ellie Chandran agrees. Is this an effective way to apply the organizing practice, and why?
o: Yes, because board members may delegate their assurance work to people from within the business.
Yes, because delegating assurance passes Moira's accountability for user assurance to the nurse.
No, because user assurance should be carried out by an organization from outside the trust.
No, because assurance should not be given to a team member who produces the products being assured.
5.w: Project assurance is the board's responsibility and must be independent of the project manager; it cannot be assigned to team members, the project manager or project support (see manual 6.2.4 and appendix B). A nurse writing the triage criteria would be assuring her own work.

n.0: Delegating assurance within the business is allowed, but not to someone doing the work being assured.
n.1: Board members stay accountable for assurance of their area even when they delegate the work.
n.2: Assurance can be carried out by board members, by people from the business or by external parties; an outside organization is not required.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Before estimating, Ellie Chandran and Josie Barker draw a product breakdown structure for the SPA, then a product flow diagram showing that the hub rotas cannot be finalized until the triage criteria are signed off. The diagram also shows the commissioner's approval of the new referral pathway, which the project needs but does not produce. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the flow diagram shows the sequence and dependencies of products, including external ones.
Yes, because the product breakdown structure lists the activities each team will carry out in the stage.
No, because products from outside the project are beyond its control and should be left out of its plans.
No, because the schedule should be drawn up first so the 18-month deadline decides which products are included.
5.w: Product-based planning defines and analyses the products first: the project product description, product breakdown structure, product descriptions and a product flow diagram showing sequence and dependencies, including external products. Work packages, estimates and the schedule follow (see manual 7.3.1).

n.1: A product breakdown structure is a hierarchy of products, not activities; the work is derived from the products later.
n.2: External products and dependencies should be shown so the plan reflects what the project relies on.
n.3: Scheduling comes after the products are defined and estimated; the deadline is a constraint, but the products drive the plan.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. The draft project plan has four stages: initiation, design and pilot preparation, the Eastfield pilot, and evaluation and roll-out. To reduce the number of board meetings, Karen Lindqvist, the executive, asks Ellie Chandran to merge the design stage and the pilot into one 28-week stage. The trust has a low appetite for clinical safety risk. Is this an effective way to apply the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because longer stages reduce the burden on senior managers, and the trust's directors have limited time for the project.
Yes, because the medical director can sign off the triage criteria during the merged stage without involving the board.
No, because the start of the pilot is a key decision point, and the board should check readiness before patients are triaged.
No, because the stages of a project should be equal in length so that progress can be compared from one stage to the next.
5.w: The number and length of stages depend on decision points, risk and complexity, and shorter stages give more control (see manual 2.4 and 7.2.3). Starting to triage real patients is a major, safety-critical commitment, so a stage boundary before the pilot lets the board decide whether the criteria, rotas and system are ready.

n.0: Longer stages do reduce the board's burden, but that trade-off does not suit a safety-critical step in a trust with a low appetite for clinical safety risk.
n.1: Clinical sign-off of the criteria is still required, but it does not replace the board's decision to commit to a live pilot.
n.3: Stage lengths vary with risk, complexity and decision points; equal length is not a requirement.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. In the quality management approach, Ellie Chandran states that the trust's quality team, which is independent of the project, will audit whether the project's quality checks on the triage criteria and the system configuration are suitable and are being carried out. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because this is project assurance, which the board carries out independently of the project.
Yes, because quality assurance gives independent confidence that the project's controls are suitable.
No, because the senior user should check the quality controls, as she will accept the products.
No, because quality checks should be assured by the teams that produce and test the products.
5.w: Quality assurance is performed independently of the project management team, typically by a business function such as a quality team, and checks that the project's quality control measures are appropriate (see manual 8.2.3).

n.0: Project assurance is the board's responsibility and is part of the project, though independent of the project manager; an audit by a business function independent of the project is quality assurance.
n.2: The senior user accepts the project product; independent review of the project's quality controls is quality assurance.
n.3: Producing and testing products is quality control; assurance of those controls comes from outside the project management team.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'starting up a project' process. While drafting the project product description, Ellie Chandran records Moira Healy's statement 'referral to first contact within three days' as the first of the SPA's acceptance criteria. Moira, the senior user, agrees with the wording. Is this an effective way to apply the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because acceptance criteria should be measurable, and the three-day target can be measured.
Yes, because the senior user is responsible for providing quality expectations and acceptance criteria.
No, because it is a benefit that depends on use after handover, not a test the SPA can be accepted against.
No, because acceptance criteria are set by the project board when it authorizes the project, not in starting up.
5.w: Acceptance criteria are prioritized, measurable criteria that the project product must meet before the users accept it, recorded in the project product description (manual chapter 8). An outcome or benefit, such as a shorter wait from referral to first contact, is not a quality expectation or acceptance criterion; it belongs in the business case.

n.0: Being measurable is necessary but not enough: the criterion must be something the delivered product can meet at acceptance, not a benefit that emerges from use.
n.1: The senior user does provide expectations and criteria, but that does not turn a benefit into an acceptance criterion.
n.3: Acceptance criteria are captured in the project product description during starting up.

5.q: Matching set (issues). The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage, and Ellie Chandran is capturing new issues. Which type of issue is each of the following? 5.q: Matching set (issues). The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage, and Ellie Chandran is capturing new issues. Which type of issue is each of the following? 5.q: Matching set (progress). The trust's executive team has set project tolerances of plus or minus 10% on cost and one month on time; beyond those, the trust board decides. Which role should decide how to respond to each situation? Statement 1 of 3: During the roll-out, the Moorside go-live is forecast to slip so far that the project will finish six weeks after its target date.
o: Business layer
Project board
Project manager
Team manager
5.w: A forecast breach of project tolerance, here one month on time, is outside the project board's authority and is decided by the business layer, which set the project tolerances (see manual 11.2.1 and 11.3.1).

n.1: The board decides on stage-level exceptions; a forecast breach of project tolerance goes to the business layer.
n.2: The project manager escalates exceptions to the board; deciding on a project-level exception is not within her authority.
n.3: The team manager works within work package tolerances and escalates to the project manager.

5.q: Matching set (progress). The trust's executive team has set project tolerances of plus or minus 10% on cost and one month on time; beyond those, the trust board decides. Which role should decide how to respond to each situation? o: Business layer
Project board
Project manager
Team manager
5.w: The project manager sets work package tolerances; a forecast breach is raised by the team manager as an issue and handled by the project manager in controlling a stage (see manual 11.2.1 and 11.2.6).

n.0: Project tolerances are not threatened, so the business layer is not involved.
n.1: Exceptions to stage or project plans go to the board; this one is at work package level.
n.3: The team manager raises the forecast breach with the project manager rather than deciding on it herself.

5.q: Matching set (progress). The trust's executive team has set project tolerances of plus or minus 10% on cost and one month on time; beyond those, the trust board decides. Which role should decide how to respond to each situation? Statement 3 of 3: Ellie Chandran forecasts that the Eastfield pilot stage will exceed its cost tolerance, although the project as a whole is still forecast to stay within 10%.
o: Business layer
Project board
Project manager
Team manager
5.w: The project board sets stage tolerances and decides how to respond to an exception report about a forecast breach of them, for example by asking for an exception plan (see manual 11.2.1 and 11.3.1).

n.2: The project manager cannot authorize work beyond stage tolerance; she escalates it to the board in an exception report.
n.3: The team manager has no authority over stage tolerances.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. At a risk workshop attended mostly by Eastfield staff, Moira Healy, who is widely respected, rates the risk that Moorside nurses will not adopt the triage hub as low, and nobody challenges her. Ellie Chandran is concerned that the group is agreeing too readily, so she holds a second session with Gareth Pugh and two Moorside nurses and asks them how the hub could fail. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because groupthink can distort the assessment of risks, and dissenting views help to counter it.
Yes, because risks should be identified by people outside the project team rather than by its own members.
No, because the risk has already been assessed as low and should now be accepted and monitored.
No, because the risk owner assesses the risk, and Moira Healy has already given her assessment of it.
5.w: PRINCE2 7 recognizes that decision bias can distort risk decisions; groupthink values agreement within a group over dissent or the right answer (see manual 9.2.4). Seeking the views of people likely to disagree, here the Moorside nurses most affected, is a practical counter-measure.

n.1: Project team members are a main source of risk identification; the point here is to widen the range of views, not to exclude the team.
n.2: An assessment made under bias is unreliable; reassessing it is part of managing the risk.
n.3: A risk owner manages the response to a risk; that does not make one person's rating final, especially when bias is suspected.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. The trust has a low appetite for risk to clinical safety and a moderate appetite for risk to administrative processes. Ellie Chandran's draft risk management approach uses one set of scales and one risk tolerance for every risk, so a threat that a triage criterion might miss a red-flag symptom is handled in the same way as a threat that a rota spreadsheet is late. Is this an effective way to apply the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because a single set of scales keeps risk scoring simple for a project manager who is new to PRINCE2 7.
Yes, because risk appetite is set by the business, so the project's own approach does not need to reflect it.
No, because the risk management approach should list each clinical safety risk together with its owner and its response.
No, because the board should set risk tolerances that reflect the trust's different appetites for clinical and administrative risk.
5.w: Risk appetite is set by the business, and risk tolerance, a measurable threshold for each objective at risk, is set by the project board based on that appetite (see manual 9.2.1). A trust with a low appetite for clinical safety risk needs tighter thresholds and faster escalation for those risks than for administrative ones.

n.0: Simplicity helps, but treating clinical safety risks like administrative ones disregards the trust's stated appetite.
n.1: The appetite is set by the business precisely so that the board can set tolerances that apply it.
n.2: Specific risks, owners and responses go in the risk register; the approach sets procedures, scales and responsibilities.

5.q: The SPA project is in the Eastfield pilot stage. The patients' forum's request for carers to refer directly has been captured as an issue. Ellie Chandran assesses that it would cost £8,000 and add a week, within the stage tolerances, but the board has not delegated any authority to her to approve changes. What should Ellie produce to obtain a decision, and why?
o: An exception report, because the request falls outside the approved scope of the project.
A highlight report entry, because the cost and delay can be met within the stage tolerances.
An updated work package description, so that the change can be passed to the team manager.
An issue report, setting out the impact of the request and recommending a decision to the board.
5.w: An issue report describes an issue's impact on the baseline, sets out options and recommends a decision; it is used for requests for change that need a formal decision. Within tolerance, an issue report rather than an exception report is the right product (see manual 10.2.3 and 10.3.1).

n.0: An exception report is for a forecast breach of stage or project tolerance; this change is within tolerance.
n.1: Staying within tolerance does not give Ellie authority to approve a change; the board has kept that authority.
n.2: Work packages are updated after a change is approved; no decision has yet been made.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. The board proposes that Ellie Chandran may approve requests for change costing up to £5,000 each, from a change budget of £30,000. Any request affecting the triage criteria must first be signed off by the clinical safety officer and the medical director and then go to the board for a decision. Is this an effective way to apply the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the change budget can also pay for responses to clinical safety risks found during the pilot.
Yes, because delegating minor changes with a budget speeds decisions, while clinically sensitive ones go higher.
No, because the project board is the change authority, and so it may not delegate the approval of changes.
No, because a change authority should also carry out the changes it approves through its own work packages.
5.w: The board is the ultimate authority for requests for change but may delegate approval, within limits, to a change authority or the project manager, with a change budget so that approved changes can be funded (see manual 10.2.4 and 10.2.5). Keeping changes to triage criteria at board level, after clinical sign-off, respects the trust's low appetite for clinical safety risk.
