n.0: Responses to risks are funded from a risk budget; the change budget funds approved changes.
n.2: The board may delegate approval of changes within limits; it remains the ultimate authority.
n.3: Delegation concerns approving changes; approved changes are implemented through work packages authorized by the project manager.

5.q: The SPA project is close to the end of the Eastfield pilot stage. Ellie Chandran needs to give the board a summary of how the pilot stage performed, the overall position of the project and enough information for the board to decide whether to go ahead with the roll-out. Which product should she prepare, and why?
o: A highlight report, because it gives the board a regular summary of the stage's status at the interval the board set.
A lessons report, because the trust board has asked for a written record of what the project learns as it goes.
An end stage report, because it reviews the stage and the project's position so the board can decide what to do next.
An exception report, because the board must decide whether to change the plan for the roll-out stage.
5.w: The end stage report, prepared when evaluating the stage near its end, summarizes progress to date and the overall project situation and gives the board the information it needs to decide what to do next (see manual chapter 11 and chapter 18).

n.0: Highlight reports are time-driven updates during the stage; the decision to go ahead is supported by the event-driven end stage report.
n.1: A lessons report passes on lessons; it does not give the stage summary the board needs for the next-stage decision.
n.3: An exception report is used when a plan is forecast to exceed tolerance; nothing here says tolerances are threatened.

5.q: The SPA project is in the Eastfield pilot stage. The triage hub team has just been formed and has never worked to a work package before, while Medivault's configuration team has switched on the same referral module for other providers. Ellie Chandran sets weekly checkpoint reports in the hub work package and fortnightly ones in Medivault's. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because reporting should be more frequent for an inexperienced team until confidence in its work grows.
Yes, because Medivault is an external supplier, so it reports to the senior supplier rather than to the project manager.
No, because checkpoint reports should be at the same interval in every work package so the highlight report is consistent.
No, because the frequency of checkpoint reports is set by the project board in the communication management approach.
5.w: Reporting frequency should reflect the level of control needed: an inexperienced team reports more often until confidence grows, an experienced one less often (see manual 11.2.4). Checkpoint frequency is set in each work package description.

n.1: Checkpoint reports go from the team manager to the project manager, whoever the supplier is.
n.2: Each work package sets its own reporting frequency; the highlight report draws them together whatever their intervals.
n.3: The board sets the interval for highlight reports; checkpoint frequency is agreed in the work package between the project manager and the team manager.

5.q: The SPA project is in the evaluation and roll-out stage. Ellie Chandran has been compiling progress by hand from 14 spreadsheets. She now has the e-rostering and training systems feed data automatically into a weekly progress view showing referral routes switched over, staff trained and triage shifts filled, which board members can open on their phones. Is this an effective way to apply the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the system can then set each locality's tolerances from its own past performance.
Yes, because data and systems can remove manual collation and present progress in the format people prefer.
No, because highlight reports are written by the project manager and should not draw on automated data.
No, because these figures measure benefits, which are reviewed after the project has closed.
5.w: Using data and systems in progress management can remove manual consolidation of separate sources, use past performance to help forecast and present progress in the format stakeholders prefer (see manual 11.2.7). It supports, rather than replaces, the project manager's reporting.

n.0: Data can inform forecasts, but tolerances are set by the management levels, not by systems.
n.2: The project manager still owns the highlight report, but drawing on automated data makes it more timely and accurate.
n.3: Routes switched over, staff trained and shifts filled measure progress on the stage's work, not benefits.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'starting up a project' process. Ellie Chandran and Karen Lindqvist, the executive, compare buying a new referral system with switching on the unused referral module, which Medivault would configure under its existing support contract. They also decide that the trust's own staff will design the SPA and that it will be piloted in one locality before roll-out. Is this an appropriate application of the 'select the project approach' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because it decides how the work will be delivered, such as buy or configure and in-house or supplier, before initiation.
Yes, because selecting the approach confirms that the business case shows a viable project for the board.
No, because the project approach is chosen in initiating a project, once the project plan has been prepared.
No, because the supplier must be chosen through the commercial management approach before an approach is selected.
5.w: Selecting the project approach decides how the work will be approached, for example in-house or by third parties, building or buying, and the delivery method, so that initiation can be planned on that basis (see manual 13.4.5).

n.1: Viability is confirmed by the board when it authorizes the project on the full business case, not by selecting an approach.
n.2: The project approach is selected in starting up and recorded in the project brief; the project plan prepared in initiation builds on it.
n.3: The commercial management approach is agreed in initiation; the broad choice of how to deliver comes first, in starting up.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'starting up a project' process. The trust's executive team names Karen Lindqvist as executive, and Karen then appoints Ellie Chandran as project manager, using a role description that Karen drafted herself. Which role is accountable for the 'appoint the executive and the project manager' activity, and why?
o: The business layer, because it commissions the project and answers for these first appointments.
The executive, because Karen chose the project manager and wrote her role description herself.
The project board, because it will direct the project manager once the project is authorized.
The senior user, because the project manager will be delivering a new service for the users.
5.w: In the starting up a project RACI, the business layer is accountable for appointing the executive and the project manager, and the executive is responsible for carrying the activity out (see manual 13.4.1).

n.1: Karen is responsible for the activity, but accountability sits with the business layer that commissions the project.
n.2: The project board does not yet exist; its members are appointed later in starting up.
n.3: Accountability for these appointments rests with the business layer; the senior user is appointed later, with the rest of the project management team.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'starting up a project' process. Keen to impress the commissioner, Ellie Chandran spends ten weeks drawing up detailed rotas, a full cost model and product descriptions for every SPA product before asking the board for authority to initiate the project. Is this an effective way to carry out the starting up a project process, and why?
o: Yes, because the trust's low appetite for clinical safety risk means detailed plans are needed before any decision.
Yes, because a full cost model lets the board authorize the whole project at the end of starting up.
No, because starting up should do the minimum needed to decide whether the project is worth initiating.
No, because detailed planning of the SPA products is the senior supplier's job rather than the project manager's.
5.w: Starting up a project is lighter than initiation: it does the minimum necessary to decide whether initiation is worthwhile and to stop poorly conceived projects starting (see manual 13.1). Detailed products and plans belong to initiation and the later stages.

n.0: Safety-critical detail is planned and assured in initiation and the design stage; the decision at the end of starting up needs an outline, not detailed rotas.
n.1: At the end of starting up the board authorizes initiation, not the whole project; the project is authorized on the full business case after initiation.
n.3: The project manager prepares plans and product descriptions; the senior supplier commits supplier resources and is accountable for supplier products.

5.q: The SPA project is at the end of its final stage. The board reviews the end project report and checks that the updated benefits management approach plans reviews of referral times, lost referrals and unnecessary visits after closure, including whether nursing teams' loss of control over referrals has had unexpected effects. It then notifies the trust's executive team that the project is closing. Is this an appropriate application of the 'authorize project closure' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the board carries out the post-project benefits reviews itself once the project has closed.
Yes, because the board makes sure post-project reviews will cover the service in use, including side-effects.
No, because the benefits reviews should be completed by the project before the board authorizes closure.
No, because the closure notification should be sent by the project manager once the end project report is ready.
5.w: In authorizing project closure the board confirms closure, makes sure post-project benefits reviews are planned in the updated benefits management approach and will cover performance in operational use, including beneficial and adverse side-effects, and notifies the business layer (see manual 14.4.5).

n.0: Post-project benefits reviews are carried out by the business after the project has closed, not by the project board.
n.2: Most benefits are realized after closure; the project plans the reviews but does not carry them out.
n.3: The closure notification to the business layer is issued by the board in directing a project.

5.q: The SPA project is in the Eastfield pilot stage. Before each board meeting, Karen Lindqvist, the executive, and Moira Healy, the senior user, compare the figures in Ellie Chandran's highlight report with data from the referral module, to be sure the report gives a fair picture of the stage. Which practice is the board applying in directing a project, and why?
o: Quality, because the board is checking that a management product meets its quality specification.
Organizing, because checking the project manager's work is part of the board's assurance role.
Risk, because inaccurate reporting is a threat to the board's ability to control the stage.
Progress, because the board is making sure that progress reporting to it is fair and reliable.
5.w: In directing a project, the progress practice is applied when the board assures itself of fair reporting by validating highlight and end stage reports (see manual table 14.3).

n.0: Quality concerns the project's products and their specifications; validating progress reports applies the progress practice.
n.1: Assurance is a board responsibility set up under organizing, but checking that progress reports are fair applies the progress practice.
n.2: Unreliable reporting might create risk, but the action is validating reports, which applies the progress practice.

5.q: The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage. Because Ellie Chandran is new to PRINCE2 7, the board decides to meet every week, review every work package before Ellie authorizes it and approve each change to the draft rotas. Is this an effective way to carry out the directing a project process, and why?
o: Yes, because a project manager new to PRINCE2 7 needs the board to approve her work packages until she is trained.
Yes, because giving ongoing direction allows the board to take part in the project's decisions whenever it wishes.
No, because the board should not meet during a stage and should review the project at stage boundaries.
No, because the board should leave day-to-day management to the project manager and control the stage by exception.
5.w: Directing a project lets the board stay accountable while delegating day-to-day management to the project manager; it manages by exception through stage tolerances, highlight reports and exception reports (see manual 14.1 and 14.4.3). Concern about inexperience is better met by more frequent reporting and stronger assurance than by taking over the project manager's decisions.

n.0: Authorizing work packages is a project manager activity in controlling a stage; the board can ask for more frequent reports and stronger assurance instead.
n.1: Ongoing direction is guidance and responses to requests or exceptions; it does not mean the board makes day-to-day decisions.
n.2: The board can give ongoing direction and respond to exception reports during a stage; it is not limited to stage boundaries.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Ellie Chandran agrees with the board that it will receive a fortnightly online highlight report and make its decisions at the end of each stage, and she sets out how she will control the team managers' work through work packages and checkpoint reports. Is this an appropriate application of the 'establish project controls' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because establishing controls lets the board set the project's cost and time tolerances.
Yes, because it agrees the board's level of control after initiation and how the team managers' work is controlled.
No, because project controls are set in each delivery stage plan rather than during initiation.
No, because reporting arrangements belong in the communication management approach, agreed in starting up.
5.w: Establishing project controls agrees the level of control the board needs after initiation and the mechanism for it, and how the project manager will control the team managers' work (see manual 15.4.3).

n.0: Project tolerances are set by the business layer, here the trust's executive team; the board sets stage tolerances.
n.2: Project controls are agreed in initiation for the whole project; stage plans then apply them.
n.3: The communication management approach is agreed in initiation, not starting up, and it does not replace agreeing the board's controls.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Ellie Chandran updates the outline business case with the time and cost figures from the project plan and the aggregated risks from the project log, and asks for the views of Neil Ashworth, who carries out business assurance. Which role is accountable for the 'prepare the full business case' activity, and why?
o: The project manager, because Ellie is preparing the full business case from the project plan.
The executive, because the executive is accountable for the business case on behalf of the business.
The business layer, because the commissioner's transformation money is funding the project.
Project assurance, because Neil Ashworth reviews the business case independently for the board.
5.w: In the initiating a project RACI, the project manager is responsible for preparing the full business case, the executive is accountable, project assurance is consulted and the business layer is not involved (see manual 15.4.5).

n.0: Ellie is responsible for doing the work; accountability rests with the executive.
n.2: The business layer is not involved in this activity, whatever the source of the funding.
n.3: Project assurance is consulted on the full business case; it is not accountable for it.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. In the draft digital and data management approach, Ellie Chandran states that, to win over doubtful Moorside GP practices, weekly pilot referral data including patient details will be emailed to them as spreadsheets. The trust allows patient data to be shared through approved systems and no other way. Is this an effective way to carry out the initiating a project process, and why?
o: Yes, because sharing pilot results is a good way to win support from practices that doubt the SPA.
Yes, because the digital and data management approach belongs to the progress practice and covers reporting.
No, because the approach should set out how data will be kept secure, in line with the trust's rules on sharing.
No, because sharing information with GP practices should be covered in the communication management approach.
5.w: Agreeing the management approaches draws on the business's policies and standards; the digital and data management approach sets out how data will be created, used and managed, including how it is kept secure and private (see manual 15.4.2 and chapter 11). Emailing patient-level spreadsheets breaks the trust's rule that patient data is shared through approved systems.

n.0: Winning support matters, but not by a method that breaks the trust's data rules.
n.1: The approach does sit in the progress practice, but it must still set out how data is kept secure, which this plan fails to do.
n.3: The communication management approach plans communication with stakeholders, but how patient data is handled and kept secure belongs in the digital and data management approach.

5.q: The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage. The team manager hands over the completed triage criteria work package. Before updating the product register and the stage plan, Ellie Chandran checks that each set of criteria has been signed off by the clinical safety officer and the medical director, as their product description requires. Is this an appropriate application of the 'receive completed work package' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because each product should have the approvals its product description requires before it is treated as complete.
Yes, because receiving a completed work package is when the board accepts the project product on behalf of users.
No, because the senior user accepts each product when the work package is received, so Moira's approval is enough.
No, because checking approvals is a task for project assurance rather than for the project manager.
5.w: In receiving a completed work package the project manager makes sure each product has the requisite approval defined by the quality and sustainability responsibilities in its product description, then updates the product register and the stage plan (see manual 16.4.3).

n.1: Acceptance of the project product is confirmed in closing a project; this is receipt of one work package's products.
n.2: Who approves a product is set in its product description; here that requires the clinical safety officer and the medical director.
n.3: Project assurance may check on the board's behalf, but confirming approvals when receiving the work package is the project manager's activity.

5.q: The SPA project is in the Eastfield pilot stage. When the patients' forum asks for carers to be able to refer patients directly, Ellie Chandran records the request formally, works out its effect on the stage plan, the business case and the risks, and sets out the options. Which practice is she applying in controlling a stage, and why?
o: Business case, because she is judging whether the change would still leave the project justified.
Risk, because the request creates uncertainty about the cost and timescale of the stage.
Issues, because she is capturing and assessing a request to change the approved scope.
Progress, because she is forecasting the effect of the request on the stage plan.
5.w: Capturing a request for change and assessing its impact on plans, the business case and risks are the first steps of the issues technique, which controls changes to the project's baseline (see manual 10.3.1 and table 16.3).

n.0: The business case is one of the things assessed, but handling a request for change applies the issues practice.
n.1: The request is an issue that has arisen, not an uncertain event; its effect on risks is part of assessing it.
n.3: Forecasting belongs to progress, but the action as a whole is capturing and assessing a request for change.

5.q: The SPA project is in the Eastfield pilot stage, which has a time tolerance of two weeks. Training for hub nurses is running late, and Ellie Chandran forecasts that the stage will finish one week behind plan. Wanting the board to feel involved, she sends it an exception report asking it to choose between adding training sessions and shortening the induction. Is this an effective way to carry out the controlling a stage process, and why?
o: Yes, because an exception report keeps the board informed of any forecast deviation from the stage plan.
Yes, because a project manager new to PRINCE2 7 should refer decisions on corrective action to the executive.
No, because the delay is within stage tolerance, so she should take corrective action and report it to the board.
No, because the team manager should have sent the exception report to the board from the training work package.
5.w: If a deviation can be resolved within stage tolerance, the project manager takes corrective action in controlling a stage and reports it in the highlight report; an exception report is raised when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded (see manual 11.2.6, 16.4.6 and 16.4.7).

n.0: Exception reports are for forecast breaches of tolerance, not any deviation; using them within tolerance wastes the board's time.
n.1: Corrective action within tolerance is the project manager's activity; inexperience is addressed through support and assurance, not by passing decisions up.
n.3: Team managers raise work package problems with the project manager as issues; they do not send exception reports to the board.

5.q: The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage. Josie Barker, team manager for the referral form configuration, receives a draft work package from Ellie Chandran. Because one of her three analysts is leaving, she checks with her team whether the four-week timescale is achievable, agrees the reporting arrangements with Ellie and prepares a team plan before agreeing to deliver. Is this an appropriate application of the 'accept a work package' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because accepting a work package lets Josie change its tolerances to suit her team's capacity.
Yes, because the team manager agrees what will be delivered and confirms it is achievable before committing.
No, because the team plan should be approved by the project board before Josie accepts the work.
No, because the work package should be accepted by the senior supplier on behalf of Josie's team.
5.w: In accepting a work package the team manager agrees with the project manager what is to be delivered, the reporting requirements, constraints and procedures, and whether it is achievable, producing a team plan if needed, before agreeing to deliver (see manual 17.4.1).

n.0: Tolerances are agreed with the project manager; if they are not achievable Josie should say so, not change them herself.
n.2: Team plans are optional and produced by the team manager; the board is not involved in managing product delivery.
n.3: The team manager accepts the work package from the project manager; the senior supplier commits resources at board level.

5.q: The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage. After accepting the configuration work package, Josie Barker sets out which analyst will configure each referral form, in what order, and the date by which each form will be ready for testing. Which practice is she applying in managing product delivery, and why?
o: Organizing, because she is assigning responsibilities to the members of her team.
Progress, because the dates will be used to monitor the team's progress against plan.
Quality, because the dates show when each form will be ready for its quality check.
Plans, because she is developing a team plan for the products in her work package.
5.w: In managing product delivery the plans practice is applied when the team manager develops a team plan for the work package and updates the product register (see manual table 17.3).

n.0: Organizing defines the project's structure of accountability; setting out who does which product, and when, within a work package is team planning.
n.1: Progress will later be monitored against this plan, but producing the plan applies the plans practice.
n.2: The dates link to quality checks, but setting out who does what and when is the team plan.

5.q: The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage. Josie Barker's team finds that the referral module cannot receive faxes, which several Moorside practices still send. Tim Rawlings, the senior supplier, tells Josie to build a workaround at once. It will take her team two weeks beyond the work package's time tolerance, and she starts it without telling Ellie Chandran. Is this an effective way to carry out managing product delivery, and why?
o: Yes, because the senior supplier is accountable for the supplier's products and may direct the team's work.
Yes, because a team manager may go beyond tolerance where the change protects referrals from being lost.
No, because Josie should send an exception report to the project board, as the work package will overrun.
No, because Josie should raise the forecast breach with Ellie as an issue and act on Ellie's instructions.
5.w: In executing a work package the team manager notifies the project manager of new issues and risks and takes the action the project manager requires, not instructions from board members; a forecast breach of work package tolerance is raised with the project manager as an issue (see manual 17.4.2 and 11.2.1).

n.0: The senior supplier is accountable for supplier products at board level, but team managers take their instructions from the project manager.
n.1: Protecting referrals matters, but going beyond tolerance needs the project manager's decision.
n.2: Team managers escalate to the project manager, who decides whether stage tolerance is threatened and an exception report is needed.

5.q: The SPA project is approaching the end of the design and pilot preparation stage. Ellie Chandran briefs the board on how the stage went, gives an overview of the pilot stage and the backfill needed for the hub rota, shows that the triage criteria are signed off and the union has reviewed the rotas, and highlights a concession for a referral form field that was accepted without correction. Is this an appropriate application of the 'request next stage' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because it covers stage performance, the next stage, the resources needed, readiness and any concessions.
Yes, because requesting the next stage gives Ellie authority to start the pilot once she has briefed the board.
No, because concessions should be reported in the end project report rather than at a stage boundary.
No, because readiness for the pilot should be confirmed by the business layer, which set the project tolerances.
5.w: Requesting the next stage briefs the board on the current stage's performance, an overview of the next stage, the people and resources needed, readiness to proceed and any concessions for off-specifications in the stage, so the board can decide whether to authorize it (see manual chapter 18).

n.1: The next stage starts when the board authorizes it in directing a project; the briefing is a request.
n.2: Concessions in the stage are highlighted when requesting the next stage, as well as later in the end project report.
n.3: The board decides on the next stage; the business layer is involved in project-level tolerances and exceptions.

5.q: The SPA project is approaching the end of the Eastfield pilot stage. The end stage report must draw on the updated business case, project plan and project log, and the team managers, project support and Neil Ashworth, who carries out business assurance, will all contribute to it. Which role is responsible for the 'evaluate the stage' activity, and why?
o: Project assurance, because it reviews the stage's results independently for the board.
The project manager, because she prepares the end stage report for the board.
The team managers, because their teams delivered the products of the stage.
Project support, because it maintains the project log that the report draws on.
5.w: In the managing a stage boundary RACI, the project manager is responsible for evaluating the stage and preparing the end stage report; team managers, project support and project assurance are consulted (see manual chapter 18).

n.0: Project assurance is consulted on the evaluation; it does not prepare the report.
n.2: Team managers are consulted on their work packages' results; they are not responsible for the report.
n.3: Project support is consulted and may help compile information; the project manager is responsible.

5.q: The SPA project is approaching the end of the Eastfield pilot stage. Pilot data show referral to first contact falling to four days instead of the three in the business case, which is within the benefits tolerance in the benefits management approach. Ellie Chandran prepares an exception plan for the roll-out stage so that the board can approve the lower forecast. Is this an effective way to carry out managing a stage boundary, and why?
o: Yes, because any reduction in forecast benefits must be approved through an exception plan before the next stage.
Yes, because the exception plan replaces the project plan and resets the benefits targets for the roll-out.
No, because an exception plan is prepared when the board asks for one after a forecast breach of tolerance.
No, because benefits should not be reforecast until the post-project benefits review after closure.
5.w: An exception plan is prepared when the board requests one in response to an exception report about a forecast breach of tolerance. A change in benefit forecasts within tolerance is handled by updating the business case at the stage boundary for the board to review (see manual chapter 18 and 11.3.1).

n.0: Changes in forecast benefits within tolerance are dealt with by updating the business case, not by an exception plan.
n.1: No exception has been raised, so there is nothing for an exception plan to respond to.
n.3: The business case is updated with revised benefit forecasts at every stage boundary; confirmation of benefits comes later.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'closing a project' process at the end of the roll-out stage. Ellie Chandran obtains confirmation from Moira Healy, the senior user, that users accept the SPA, and confirms that community services management is ready to run the triage hub rota and that Medivault will support the module under its contract. Is this an appropriate application of the 'confirm project acceptance' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because confirming acceptance includes carrying out the post-project benefits reviews before the team disbands.
Yes, because acceptance is confirmed and the business is shown to be able to support the products after closure.
No, because each locality accepted the SPA at its go-live, so acceptance need not be confirmed again at closure.
No, because Medivault, as the supplier, should confirm acceptance of the configured module on the users' behalf.
5.w: Confirming project acceptance passes the products to the operational and maintenance environment, in one release or in phases, and confirms user acceptance; closing a project also makes sure the business can support the products after the project ends (see manual 19.2 and 19.4.3).

n.0: Post-project benefits reviews are planned during the project but carried out by the business after closure.
n.2: Phased handover is allowed, but acceptance of the project product as a whole is still confirmed at closure.
n.3: Users, through the senior user, accept the products; the supplier delivers them.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'closing a project' process. Ellie Chandran is comparing the project's performance with its baselined project initiation documentation and preparing the end project report and the lessons report, consulting Tim Rawlings, the senior supplier, and Neil Ashworth, who carries out business assurance. Which role is accountable for the 'evaluate the project' activity, and why?
o: The project manager, because Ellie compares performance and prepares the end project report.
The senior supplier, because Medivault's work is a major part of what is being evaluated.
Project assurance, because Neil Ashworth reviews the project's performance for the board.
The executive, because the executive is accountable for this activity and for the project's success.
5.w: In the closing a project RACI, the executive is accountable for evaluating the project, the project manager is responsible, and the senior supplier and project assurance are consulted (see manual 19.4.4).

n.0: Ellie is responsible for the work; the executive is accountable.
n.1: The senior supplier is consulted on the evaluation, not accountable for it.
n.2: Project assurance is consulted; it is not accountable.

5.q: The SPA project is in the 'closing a project' process. The trust board asked for a written record of what the project learns, as nobody recorded why the 2021 central booking attempt failed. Ellie Chandran reviews the lessons log, talks to Gareth Pugh and hub nurses about what helped Moorside adopt the SPA, and produces a lessons report for the trust. Is this an effective way to carry out closing a project, and why?
o: Yes, because evaluating the project includes reviewing lessons and producing a lessons report for future work.
Yes, because the lessons report replaces the end project report when the project closes on time and budget.
No, because lessons reports are for the project's own use and are archived with the project log at closure.
No, because lessons should come from the project management team rather than from staff outside it.
5.w: Evaluating the project reviews the project log for lessons and produces a lessons report, in consultation with the project management team, so that lessons can be passed on to future projects (see manual 19.4.4 and 2.2). Drawing on the nurses' experience captures knowledge held across the wider project ecosystem.

n.1: Both reports are produced when evaluating the project; the lessons report does not replace the end project report.
n.2: A lessons report exists to pass lessons on to the business and future projects, not to sit in the archive.
n.3: Much valuable knowledge sits with people across the project ecosystem; learning from experience draws on them too.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the development stage. Greendale Ready Meals will not reduce its 150,000-meal minimum, and the latest consumer panel results suggest the two pan-fried recipes will sell far fewer meals than that in year one. Rob Hennessy, the executive, says there is no point reviewing the business case again: the £180,000 listing fee has already been paid and cannot be recovered, so the project must carry on as planned. How well does this apply the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because stopping now would mean losing a listing fee that Harbridge's will not refund.
It applies it well, because the board has stated that the launch week in February cannot move.
It applies it poorly, because the justification must be revalidated against the remaining costs, risks and benefits.
It applies it poorly, because the business case should be confirmed through a benefits review before the trials stage.
6.w: Justification must remain valid and be revalidated throughout the project; if it is no longer justified, the project should be stopped (see manual 2.1). The listing fee is spent whichever way the board decides, so it cannot justify continuing. What matters is whether the costs still to come, including the Greendale minimum, and the risks are outweighed by the expected benefits. Rob is refusing to check the business case just as new information has emerged.

n.0: The fee is lost whether the project continues or stops, so it cannot justify the remaining investment; the principle looks forward at future costs, risks and benefits.
n.1: The fixed launch week is a constraint on the plan, not evidence that the project is still worth doing.
n.3: Benefits are confirmed mainly after closure; during the project the business case is maintained and checked at stage boundaries and when significant issues arise (manual 5.3.1).

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'starting up a project' process. One of the six recipes uses sesame, which has never been handled on the Fernhollow site. Nadia Osei asks Luke Barraclough to arrange visits to two other food manufacturers that have brought sesame onto their sites, reads the lessons reports from Fernhollow's last factory line upgrade, and records what she finds in the lessons log. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Learn from experience, because handling sesame is new to the business, so seeking lessons from other organizations matters more.
Focus on products, because the allergen controls found on the visits will become quality specifications for the sesame recipe.
Manage by exception, because the board has a very low appetite for allergen risk and wants early warning of any problem.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because Luke is responsible for allergen control and is building links with other firms.
6.w: Learn from experience: lessons are sought, recorded and acted on from the start, and when the work is a first for the business it is even more important to learn from others, including external organizations (see manual 2.2). Reviewing earlier lessons reports and recording findings in the lessons log is the 'assess previous lessons' activity of starting up a project (13.4.2).

n.1: The findings may later shape product descriptions, but the action described is gathering and recording lessons, not defining products or their quality specifications.
n.2: The low appetite explains why lessons matter here, but manage by exception is about setting tolerances and escalating forecast breaches; nothing here delegates authority or sets limits.
n.3: Luke is the means, not the purpose: the visits gather lessons rather than agree roles or build working relationships for the project.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process. Nadia Osei maps the people the project depends on who are not on the project board, including Tariq Javed at Harbridge's, Shona Mackintosh at Greendale and Jen Pascoe of the employee forum. She agrees with the board who will build and manage each relationship: Charlotte Vane will be the single contact for Tariq, and Dariusz Nowicki will meet Jen every fortnight. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Manage by exception, because decisions about each stakeholder are being made at the most local level where the knowledge resides.
Focus on products, because the relationships are organized around the products that each stakeholder will receive or supply.
Ensure continued business justification, because the value of the Harbridge's listing depends on a good relationship with its buyer.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the team is agreeing who builds and maintains each key stakeholder relationship.
6.w: The principle covers agreed roles and responsibilities, and it also requires the project management team to initiate and build relationships with and between internal and external stakeholders (see manual 2.3). Mapping stakeholders outside the board and agreeing who will manage each relationship applies it directly.

n.0: Deciding at the most local level is about delegated decision-making within tolerances; agreeing who owns each stakeholder relationship is about roles and relationships.
n.1: The relationships are assigned to people according to their links with each stakeholder, not structured around product definitions or quality expectations.
n.2: The listing matters to the business case, but the action is about who manages relationships, not about checking whether the project remains desirable, viable and achievable.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process. Nadia Osei proposes that the concept and recipe stage should end before the order for the tray-sealing line is placed and before the Greendale supply agreement is signed. This lets the board see the final recipe choice and an updated business case before it commits to the line and to the 150,000-meal minimum. How well does this apply the 'manage by stages' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because ending the stage there reduces the number of decisions the board must make in the development stage.
It applies it well, because the stage boundary gives the board a decision point before the largest commitments are made.
It applies it poorly, because the line order should be placed in initiation to protect the 14-week lead time and the launch week.
It applies it poorly, because stage boundaries should be set at equal intervals so that the board can plan its meetings.
6.w: Stages give the board review and decision points at which it assesses viability, and stage ends can be aligned with key decisions and external influences (see manual 2.4 and 7.2.3). Placing the boundary before the line purchase and the Greendale commitment means the board decides on those commitments with the recipe choice and an updated business case in front of it.

n.0: The boundary does not reduce the board's decisions; it places a decision point where it matters most.
n.2: Initiation plans the project; committing large sums to delivery before the board has authorized the project would undermine the controlled start that initiation provides.
n.3: Stage length should reflect decision points, risk and complexity, not a fixed calendar interval.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process. With the business layer's agreement, the project plan sets no time tolerance on the launch week, a cost tolerance of plus or minus 5% of the £2.3 million budget, and a scope tolerance that allows the launch to go ahead with four of the six recipes. Nadia Osei will escalate if any of these is forecast to be exceeded. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Manage by exception, because tolerances set the limits of the authority delegated to each management level.
Focus on products, because the scope tolerance defines which of the six recipes will be in the launch range.
Manage by stages, because tolerances are set for each stage so that the board can review them at stage ends.
Ensure continued business justification, because the cost tolerance protects the margin forecast in the business case.
6.w: Setting tolerances for the aspects of performance, and escalating when they are forecast to be exceeded, establishes the limits of delegated authority (see manual 2.5). Allowing as few as four recipes is a scope tolerance: the permitted range is manage by exception, even though the recipes themselves are defined under focus on products.

n.1: Defining the recipes and their requirements is focus on products; the permitted variation in how many are delivered is a tolerance.
n.2: These are project-level tolerances agreed with the business layer; stage-by-stage planning and decision points are a different principle.
n.3: The action sets limits of delegated authority for the plan; it does not review whether the project is still desirable, viable and achievable.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the concept and recipe stage. The consumer panel liked a dessert that one of the chefs made for a tasting, so Megan Cho asks two chefs to spend the next two-week cycle developing it as a seventh recipe. The project product description lists six ready meals, and Harbridge's has not asked for a dessert. How well does this apply the 'focus on products' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because co-creating products with the consumer panel improves their adoption by users.
It applies it well, because an extra recipe gives the launch a fallback if one of the six meals fails.
It applies it poorly, because chef time is going on a product that is outside the agreed scope of the project.
It applies it poorly, because a new recipe has to be approved by the Harbridge's buyer before work on it starts.
6.w: A PRINCE2 project defines and delivers agreed products and does no more work than needed to deliver them, which controls scope creep (see manual 2.6). A seventh recipe is not in the project product description; if it is wanted, it should be raised as a request for change rather than worked on informally.

n.0: Co-creation with users is good practice for agreed products, but it does not justify spending effort on a product outside the agreed scope.
n.1: A dessert cannot stand in for a ready meal in a range of six meals, and any fallback should be agreed through the plan and change control, not created informally.
n.3: Harbridge's is a customer stakeholder, not the authority for the project's scope; changes to scope are decided through the project's own change control.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process. Nadia Osei proposes that the review notes Mint and Tallow produces at the end of each two-week cycle serve as its checkpoint reports, that highlight reports to the board take the form of a one-page dashboard, and that stage boundaries be called 'gate reviews', the term the directors already use for capital projects. The changes are recorded in the project initiation documentation. Is this an appropriate application of the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
o: Yes, because the managing director signs off all investment over £250,000 and so can decide how the method is applied.
Yes, because reporting formats and terms are adapted to the delivery approach and the organization, and this is documented.
No, because checkpoint reports need to follow the standard PRINCE2 format so that work packages can be compared.
No, because replacing PRINCE2 terms with the organization's own terms weakens the method's common language.
6.w: Tailoring adapts processes, management products and terminology so that controls fit the project and the organization, and it must be documented and agreed, normally in the PID (see manual 2.7 and 15.4.1). Using the agency's cycle reviews as checkpoint reports, a lighter highlight format and the directors' own terms are all legitimate tailoring; the principles still apply in full.

n.0: Imogen Fairley's sign-off limit is a financial control in the business layer; tailoring is led by the project manager, documented in the PID and approved by the board.
n.2: Management products can be merged, renamed or given different formats; what matters is that they carry the information needed for control.
n.3: Terminology is one of the things PRINCE2 expects to be tailored, so that the method fits the organization's own language.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the concept and recipe stage. Mint and Tallow's designers work remotely, while Megan Cho's chefs are in the Fernhollow kitchen. At the last two tastings the pack designs did not reflect the recipes, and each side blamed the other. Nadia Osei arranges for the lead designers to join the chefs in the kitchen on every tasting day, with an informal lunch afterwards, and sets up a shared online board for work between tastings. Is this an appropriate approach to leading the team, and why?
o: Yes, because a hybrid team needs deliberate ways to build social cohesion and trust across the silos.
Yes, because the senior supplier is accountable for the quality of the products that suppliers deliver.
No, because the agency is a contracted supplier, so its people are managed by its own team manager.
No, because team-building activities are a matter for each organization's line managers, not the project.
6.w: Virtual, remote and hybrid teams do not share information organically; they need deliberate methods, such as synchronized co-location days for key people, to build social cohesion and trust across project silos (see manual 3.3.3). Bringing designers and chefs together on tasting days, with a shared board in between, focuses on the relationship that is failing.

n.1: It is true that the senior supplier is accountable for supplier quality, but that does not explain why bringing the two groups together is the right response.
n.2: The agency's team manager directs its own team's work, but building cohesion across the wider project ecosystem is part of leading the project team.
n.3: Leading and building the temporary project team, including across organizational boundaries, is part of the project manager's role.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the concept and recipe stage. None of Megan Cho's four chefs has worked with sesame or under strict allergen segregation. To save time, Dariusz Nowicki suggests that the chefs start trial batches of the sesame recipe next week and that Luke Barraclough's team tests the batches afterwards for cross-contact. Is this an appropriate approach to managing the team, and why?
o: Yes, because quality control by a team independent of production gives the board confidence in the results.
Yes, because the chefs' training is a line management matter that sits outside the project manager's remit.
No, because the board's very low appetite for allergen risk means the sesame recipe should be dropped.
No, because the chefs lack a competence the work needs, and the gap should be closed by training or reassigning work.
6.w: Building an effective team includes understanding the competencies people need, identifying gaps and mitigating them, for example by upskilling or by shifting responsibilities to more suitable people (see manual 3.3.2). A clear competency gap has been found in a high-risk area, and testing the batches afterwards does not close it.

n.0: Independent testing is quality control of the output; it does not give the chefs the competence they lack before they start handling sesame.
n.1: Some motivators such as pay sit outside the project manager's remit, but identifying and closing the competency gaps that project work depends on is part of building the team.
n.2: Dropping a recipe would be a scope decision for the board; a low appetite calls for strong allergen controls and competent people, not removal of the recipe by default.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the development stage. Night shift operators have stopped volunteering for training on the new tray-sealing line, and rumours are spreading that it will cut jobs. Dariusz Nowicki wants to tell them that the line is going in whatever they think. Instead, Nadia Osei and Dariusz meet Jen Pascoe, who represents the operators on the employee forum, to find out what lies behind the resistance before deciding how to respond. Is this an appropriate approach to leading change, and why?
o: Yes, because Jen Pascoe's views must be recorded in the issue register as a concern before any action is taken.
Yes, because resistance should be investigated to understand its causes, working with key influencers such as Jen.
No, because Jen holds no role in the project management team, so engagement should go through the senior user.
No, because the line has been ordered and the change will happen, so the priority is to announce the decision clearly.
6.w: Pockets of resistance show where communication and engagement should focus: the project should find out why stakeholders resist rather than sideline them, and identify key influencers, who may hold no formal role (see manual 3.2.2 and 3.4). Jen influences the night shift, so working with her to understand the concerns is the right first step.

n.0: A concern could be logged, but logging it is not what makes the approach appropriate; the value lies in understanding the resistance through a key influencer.
n.2: Projects must involve key people who are critical to success even if they hold no formal role, and Jen is such a person.
n.3: Announcing the decision without understanding the resistance risks deepening it; the change still needs the operators' support to work.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the trials stage. After launch the range will be run by the normal operations team, and every production run of the sesame recipe will need a full allergen clean-down that the operators have never carried out. Nadia Osei wants to move the factory from its current ways of working to this target state. Which action is MOST LIKELY to achieve this?
o: Issue detailed written clean-down procedures to every operator a week before the first production run.
Ask Luke Barraclough to audit operators after launch and record each failure in the issue register.
Have Dariusz Nowicki announce the new shift routines at the employee forum once the line is commissioned.
Involve the operators and Jen Pascoe in designing and testing the clean-down routines during the trials.
6.w: Co-creation involves users and key influencers in designing products and ways of working so that they are adopted by the organization (see manual 3.3). Enabling activities before and during transition, such as trials and training, help move people from the current state to the target state (3.2.1). Designing the routines with the operators during trials builds understanding and ownership before launch.

n.0: Written procedures issued late, without involvement, do not build the understanding or commitment that a new way of working needs.
n.1: Auditing after launch finds failures once the transition has happened; it does not prepare people for the target state.
n.2: Announcing routines after they are fixed tells people what will change but does not involve them in shaping it.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the development stage. Charlotte Vane has already told Tariq Javed, the Harbridge's buyer, that all six recipes will launch. Two recipes are now at risk, and Tariq has heard rumours from the packaging supplier. The communication management approach names Charlotte as Tariq's single contact, with a call every fortnight. Which action BEST applies the communication management approach?
o: Send Tariq the project's highlight reports so that he sees the same information as the project board.
Wait until the factory trials are complete so that Tariq is given a firm list of recipes at one time.
Have Charlotte use the next fortnightly call to give Tariq an honest view of readiness and invite his questions.
Ask Megan Cho to call the Harbridge's technical team directly to explain the problems with the two recipes.
6.w: The communication management approach sets the means and frequency of communication with, and feedback from, each stakeholder, giving a controlled two-way flow that avoids misconceptions (see manual 3.4). Using the agreed channel and contact, with an honest message and a chance for Tariq to respond, follows the approach and deals with the rumours.

n.0: Highlight reports are written for the project board; sending internal reports to a customer is not the agreed channel and may share sensitive information.
n.1: Delaying lets the rumours shape Tariq's view; the approach relies on regular two-way communication, not silence until there is certainty.
n.3: Bypassing the agreed single contact risks mixed messages to a key customer; Charlotte owns the relationship.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process, and Nadia Osei is drafting the communication management approach. She notes that the night shift operators will be affected both by the three-week shutdown and by the new line, and that Jen Pascoe, through the employee forum, has strong influence over whether they support the change. Under which heading of the communication management approach should this be recorded?
o: Communications schedule and procedures
Stakeholder analysis
Supporting tools and techniques
Resources
6.w: Stakeholder analysis identifies who is affected by the outcome or by the way the project is delivered, and who can influence its success or failure (communication management approach, see manual 3.4). The operators' exposure and Jen's influence belong there.

n.0: The schedule and procedures set out how, when and through which channels each group is communicated with; this entry identifies who is affected and who has influence.
n.2: Supporting tools and techniques covers platforms and tools such as communications or analytics software.
n.3: Resources covers the people and budget needed to carry out communication activities, not the analysis of stakeholders.

6.q: Matching set (business case). Nadia Osei is preparing the full business case for Fernhollow Kitchen. Which heading of the business case should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 1 of 3: Branded sales are forecast to reach £6 million a year by year three, at a gross margin of 28%.
o: Reasons
Expected benefits
Expected dis-benefits
Costs
6.w: Expected benefits sets out the measurable improvements the project is expected to bring, assessed against the current situation (business case composition, see manual 5.5). Forecast branded sales and margin are those improvements.

n.0: Reasons explain why the project is needed and how it supports business objectives; this statement gives the measurable result expected.
n.2: Dis-benefits are measurable declines that stakeholders see as negative; higher branded sales and margin are improvements.
n.3: Costs covers project and running costs and their funding, not the income the range will generate.

6.q: Matching set (business case). Nadia Osei is preparing the full business case for Fernhollow Kitchen. Which heading of the business case should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 2 of 3: The new tray-sealing line will cost £640,000 to buy and install, and servicing it will cost £35,000 a year from the operations budget.
o: Reasons
Expected benefits
Expected dis-benefits
Costs
6.w: Costs covers the project's costs and the ongoing operations and maintenance costs, together with how they will be funded (business case composition, see manual 5.5).

n.0: The purchase and servicing costs are not why the project is being undertaken.
n.1: These are costs of the investment, not improvements that it delivers.
n.2: A dis-benefit is a negative outcome of the change, such as lost sales elsewhere; buying and servicing equipment is a cost of the investment.

6.q: Matching set (business case). Nadia Osei is preparing the full business case for Fernhollow Kitchen. Which heading of the business case should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 3 of 3: Own-label sales have been flat for three years with falling margins, and the board's strategy is to build a brand of its own.
o: Reasons
Expected benefits
Expected dis-benefits
Costs
6.w: Reasons explains why the project is needed and how it enables the organization's business objectives, here flat own-label sales and the strategy of building a brand (business case composition, see manual 5.5).

n.1: These are the drivers for the project, not measurable improvements that it will produce.
n.2: Falling own-label margins describe the situation before the project, which is why it is needed; dis-benefits are negative results caused by the project's outcomes.
n.3: No cost or funding information is given.

6.q: Matching set (organizing). The project management team for Fernhollow Kitchen is being appointed. Imogen Fairley, who issued the mandate, will stay in the business layer, and Charlotte Vane has agreed to be one of the senior users. Using the additional information about the people, which individual would be most appropriate for each role? Statement 1 of 3: Executive.
o: Luke Barraclough
Rob Hennessy
Felix Haddad
Dariusz Nowicki
6.w: The executive is the single point of accountability for the project, secures its funding and owns the business case (see manual 6.2.4 and appendix B). Rob Hennessy, the finance director, controls funding and is already focused on cash flow and value, so he suits the role.

n.0: Luke Barraclough is independent of production and responsible for food safety, which suits an assurance role rather than ownership of the business case.
n.2: Felix Haddad works for the design agency and would represent a supplier interest, not Fernhollow's business interest.
n.3: Dariusz Nowicki will run the new line and the factory that uses it, which makes him a user representative rather than the owner of the investment.

6.q: Matching set (organizing). The project management team for Fernhollow Kitchen is being appointed. Imogen Fairley, who issued the mandate, will stay in the business layer, and Charlotte Vane has agreed to be one of the senior users. Using the additional information about the people, which individual would be most appropriate for each role? Statement 2 of 3: Senior user, alongside Charlotte Vane.
o: Luke Barraclough
Rob Hennessy
Felix Haddad
Dariusz Nowicki
6.w: The senior user represents those who will use or operate the products and is accountable for specifying the benefits and making sure the products deliver them (see manual 6.2.4 and appendix B). Dariusz Nowicki runs the factory and will own the new line after launch, so he represents the operational users.

n.0: Luke's independence from production makes him valuable for assurance; he is not the person who will operate the products.
n.1: Rob is better placed as executive, holding the business interest and funding, not as a user representative.
n.2: Felix represents the agency that designs the packs, which is a supplier interest.

6.q: Matching set (organizing). The project management team for Fernhollow Kitchen is being appointed. Imogen Fairley, who issued the mandate, will stay in the business layer, and Charlotte Vane has agreed to be one of the senior users. Using the additional information about the people, which individual would be most appropriate for each role? Statement 3 of 3: Project assurance on food safety and quality.
o: Luke Barraclough
Rob Hennessy
Felix Haddad
Dariusz Nowicki
6.w: Project assurance must be independent of the project manager and cannot be given to the project manager, team members or project support (see manual 6.2.4 and appendix B). Luke Barraclough is responsible for food safety and supermarket audits and is independent of production, so he can assure the board on these matters.

n.1: Rob is better suited to executive; board members are accountable for assurance in their area but usually delegate the work to someone with the right expertise.
n.2: Felix is part of a supplier delivering products, so he could not independently assure the quality of that work.
n.3: Dariusz runs production, so he is not independent of the work that food safety assurance would check.

6.q: Matching set (plans). Fernhollow Kitchen is preparing and approving its plans. Which role should carry out each planning action? Statement 1 of 3: Provide the company's standards for planning capital projects, which every plan in the project must follow.
o: Business layer
Executive
Project manager
Team manager
6.w: In the plans practice the business layer provides the planning standards that the business requires (plans roles, see manual table 7.1).

n.1: The executive defines stage tolerances and approves stage plans; company-wide planning standards come from the business layer.
n.2: The project manager applies the planning standards when preparing plans but does not set them for the business.
n.3: Team managers plan their own work packages within the standards they are given.

6.q: Matching set (plans). Fernhollow Kitchen is preparing and approving its plans. Which role should carry out each planning action? Statement 2 of 3: Prepare the schedule for the packaging design work package that Mint and Tallow will deliver.
o: Business layer
Executive
Project manager
Team manager
6.w: Team managers prepare the schedules for each work package they take on, and may prepare team plans (plans roles, see manual table 7.1).

n.0: The business layer sets planning standards and project tolerances, not schedules for individual work packages.
n.1: The executive approves stage plans and sets stage tolerances; it does not schedule work packages.
n.2: The project manager prepares the stage plan and work package descriptions; the schedule for the work within a package is prepared by its team manager.

6.q: Matching set (plans). Fernhollow Kitchen is preparing and approving its plans. Which role should carry out each planning action? Statement 3 of 3: Define the tolerances for the trials stage and approve the trials stage plan.
o: Business layer
Executive
Project manager
Team manager
6.w: The executive defines the tolerances for each stage and approves stage plans (plans roles, see manual table 7.1).

n.0: The business layer sets project-level tolerances; stage tolerances are set on the board by the executive.
n.2: The project manager prepares the stage plan and works within its tolerances; approving it and setting its tolerances is for the executive.
n.3: Team managers work within work package tolerances set by the project manager.

6.q: Matching set (quality). Nadia Osei is drafting the quality management approach for Fernhollow Kitchen. Which heading of the quality management approach should each statement be recorded under? Statement 1 of 3: Fernhollow's existing food safety management system and Mint and Tallow's own design quality procedures apply to the project.
o: Standards
Supporting tools and techniques
References
Responsibilities
6.w: References lists associated documents and products, such as the business's or the supplier's quality management systems, that the approach relies on (quality management approach composition, see manual 8.5).

n.0: Standards sets out the standards that apply to quality management itself, such as legal requirements and the format of quality records; existing management systems are referenced documents.
n.1: Supporting tools and techniques covers the systems and techniques used for quality planning and control, such as testing or inspection.
n.3: Responsibilities names who does what in quality planning, control and acceptance; no roles are given here.

6.q: Matching set (quality). Nadia Osei is drafting the quality management approach for Fernhollow Kitchen. Which heading of the quality management approach should each statement be recorded under? Statement 2 of 3: Luke Barraclough will approve the allergen controls for each recipe, and Charlotte Vane will accept the finished range on behalf of the users.
o: Standards
Supporting tools and techniques
References
Responsibilities
6.w: Responsibilities defines who is responsible for quality planning and control activities, including assurance and acceptance authorities (quality management approach composition, see manual 8.5).

n.0: No standard is stated; the entry assigns approval and acceptance to named people.
n.1: No tool or technique is described; the entry says who approves and who accepts.
n.2: No external document is cited; the entry sets out quality responsibilities.

6.q: Matching set (quality). Nadia Osei is drafting the quality management approach for Fernhollow Kitchen. Which heading of the quality management approach should each statement be recorded under? Statement 3 of 3: Every label must comply with food labelling and allergen law, and all quality records must follow the company's standard register format.
o: Standards
Supporting tools and techniques
References
Responsibilities
6.w: Standards covers any standards that apply to quality management, including legal requirements for published material and the composition and format of the quality register and other quality records (quality management approach composition, see manual 8.5).

n.1: Labelling law and record formats are standards to comply with, not tools or techniques for carrying out quality control.
n.2: References points to associated documents such as quality management systems; these are standards the project must meet.
n.3: No person or role is named; the entry sets out standards.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process. Nadia Osei's draft full business case assesses a single option: launching all six recipes, with two made by Greendale. Rob Hennessy asks her to compare three options instead: doing nothing differently, launching the four recipes that can be made in-house, and launching all six. Each option is to show its costs, benefits and risks. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the executive is accountable for the business case and so can decide what it contains.
Yes, because comparing options, with doing nothing as the baseline, shows the value each investment would buy.
No, because paying the £180,000 listing fee has committed the board to launching at least four recipes.
No, because options are assessed in starting up, so the full business case should cover the chosen option.
6.w: Developing the business case includes analysing options: do nothing differently (assessed first, as the baseline), do the minimum and do more than the minimum. The difference between them is the benefit the investment buys (see manual 5.3.1). Four in-house recipes is Harbridge's accepted minimum, so it is a realistic option alongside six.

n.0: Rob is accountable for the business case, but that does not explain why comparing options is good practice.
n.2: Paying the fee does not commit the board to continue: the fee is lost under every option, and doing nothing differently stays the baseline against which the other options are quantified.
n.3: The outline business case is developed in starting up, but it is refined into the full business case in initiation, when options can be assessed with better cost and risk information.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'managing a stage boundary' process at the end of the development stage. The tray-sealing line has cost £70,000 more than planned, and Greendale has confirmed its 150,000-meal minimum, which is now above the sales forecast for its two recipes. Nadia Osei updates the project plan and the trials stage plan but leaves the business case as it was approved in initiation, because the launch week cannot move. How well does this apply the business case practice, and why?
o: It applies it well, because the business case was approved by the board when it authorized the project.
It applies it well, because the fixed launch week means the business case cannot change the plan.
It applies it poorly, because the business case should be updated with actuals and forecasts for the board to check.
It applies it poorly, because the business case should be confirmed by a benefits review at each stage end.
6.w: The business case is maintained at the end of each stage: the project manager updates it with progress data and the latest forecasts, and the board checks it is still desirable, viable and achievable before authorizing the next stage (see manual 5.3.1). Higher line costs and a co-manufacturing minimum above forecast sales directly affect the justification.

n.0: Approval at authorization creates a baseline, but the business case must then be maintained and checked throughout, not frozen.
n.1: A fixed date constrains the plan but does not make the costs, benefits and risks irrelevant to the decision to continue.
n.3: Benefits are confirmed mainly after closure; at stage ends the business case is updated and checked, not confirmed.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the development stage. Before Gerrit Vos's installation engineers arrive for the factory shutdown, Nadia Osei arranges a site induction, a food hygiene certificate and allergen awareness training for each of them, and pairs each engineer with a Fernhollow maintenance fitter for the first week. Which step of the organizational design and development technique is being applied?
o: Understand the organizational ecosystem
Design the project ecosystem
Develop the project ecosystem
Transition the project into the organizational ecosystem
6.w: Developing the project ecosystem is the ongoing development of people and relationships as needs and membership change, including onboarding such as site visits, induction and certification (see manual 6.3.1).

n.0: Understanding the organizational ecosystem examines existing structures, governance and policies before the project ecosystem is designed.
n.1: Designing the project ecosystem decides how work and people will be organized; the onboarding of new members follows once that design is in place.
n.3: Transition hands products, people and learning back to the business at closure; the engineers are joining the project, not leaving it.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process. To keep costs down, Rob Hennessy, the executive, proposes that Amy, the project coordinator who maintains the project log and prepares board papers for Nadia Osei, should also carry out business assurance and report directly to him. How well does this apply the organizing practice, and why?
o: It applies it well, because the board decides how project assurance is done and may appoint anyone from the business.
It applies it well, because Amy would report to Rob, which keeps business assurance independent of the project manager.
It applies it poorly, because project support and project assurance should be kept separate.
It applies it poorly, because project assurance has to be carried out by an organization outside Fernhollow.
6.w: Project assurance cannot be given to the project manager, team members or project support, and project support must be kept separate from assurance (see manual 6.2.4 and appendix B). Amy maintains the project log for Nadia, so she would be assuring her own work.

n.0: The board does decide how assurance is done, but it cannot give it to someone who already holds the project support role.
n.1: A reporting line to the executive does not make Amy independent: she prepares the material that assurance would check.
n.3: Assurance can be done by board members, by people appointed from the business or by external parties; an outside organization is not required.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process. Working with Megan Cho and Dariusz Nowicki, Nadia Osei draws a product flow diagram. It shows that the carbon label cannot be finalized until the recipes are fixed, and that the Harbridge's audit result, an external product, depends on the line being commissioned. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the product flow diagram replaces the need for a product breakdown structure on a hybrid project.
Yes, because it shows the sequence and dependencies of the products, including external ones, before scheduling.
No, because external products such as the audit result are outside the project's control and are not planned.
No, because dependencies should be shown in the work breakdown structure, not in a product flow diagram.
6.w: In product-based planning the product flow diagram shows the sequence in which products are developed and the dependencies between them, including intermediate and external products (see manual 7.3.1). Identifying these early lets the schedule reflect them, here the link between commissioning the line and passing the audit.

n.0: The product breakdown structure is still created; the product flow diagram builds on it rather than replacing it.
n.2: External products are outside the project's control, which is exactly why they are shown as dependencies in the plan.
n.3: The work breakdown structure is a hierarchy of work linking products to work packages; product sequence and dependencies are shown in the product flow diagram.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process. Nadia Osei's draft project plan contains a day-by-day schedule for all five stages, including every factory trial run nine months from now. Charlotte Vane praises the detail and asks for it to be baselined so that progress can be tracked against it. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the fixed launch week means all of the work should be scheduled in detail from the start.
Yes, because a detailed baseline gives the board the clearest basis for managing by exception.
No, because the project plan should be prepared by the team managers who will carry out the work.
No, because the near future can be planned in detail, and later stages are detailed in their own stage plans.
6.w: The planning horizon limits how far ahead detailed planning is reliable. PRINCE2 uses a high-level project plan and a detailed plan for the current stage, with each later stage plan prepared near the end of the stage before it (see manual 7.2.1 and 7.2.2). A day-by-day schedule for trials nine months away is likely to be wrong and costly to maintain.

n.0: A fixed end date makes planning important but does not extend the planning horizon; detail is added stage by stage.
n.1: Tolerances need a realistic plan; a detailed but unreliable schedule creates false deviations rather than better control.
n.2: The project manager prepares the project plan; team managers prepare team plans and work package schedules.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the trials stage. Fernhollow's group food safety auditor, who reports to Imogen Fairley and has no role in the project, reviews whether the shelf-life tests, allergen swabbing and metal detection checks planned for the trials are adequate for a supermarket launch. Which part of the quality practice is being applied?
o: Quality assurance
Quality control
Project assurance
Quality planning
6.w: Quality assurance gives confidence that products will meet their quality specifications when tested. It is carried out independently of the project management team, typically by a business function, and checks that the project's quality control measures are appropriate (see manual 8.2.3).

n.1: Quality control is carrying out the checks on the products themselves; the auditor is reviewing whether the planned checks are adequate.
n.2: Project assurance is the project board's responsibility and sits within the project; the auditor has no project role and works for the business.
n.3: Quality planning defines the quality specifications and methods; the auditor is reviewing the planned checks independently, not planning them.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'starting up a project' process. While the project product description is being prepared, Charlotte Vane asks for 'Fernhollow Kitchen recognized by 30% of Harbridge's shoppers within a year of launch' to be listed as an acceptance criterion for the range. Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because acceptance criteria should be measurable, and a 30% recognition target can be measured.
Yes, because the senior user provides the acceptance criteria for the project product.
No, because brand recognition is an outcome of using the products, not something the range must meet to be accepted.
