No, because acceptance criteria are set out in each product description rather than in the project product description.
6.w: Acceptance criteria are a prioritized list of measurable attributes that the project product must meet before the users accept it (see manual 8.1.1). Shoppers recognizing the brand is a result of the change after launch, an outcome, and cannot be checked when the range is handed over.

n.0: Being measurable is necessary but not enough: the criterion must describe the product, not the result of using it.
n.1: Acceptance criteria do come from the users, through the senior user role, but this entry is an outcome, and who proposes it does not make it a valid criterion.
n.3: Acceptance criteria belong in the project product description; quality specifications belong in product descriptions.

6.q: Matching set (risk). Nadia Osei is adding a risk about the new tray-sealing line to the risk register. Which heading of the risk register should each statement be recorded under? Statement 1 of 3: Because the line has a 14-week lead time, a late purchase order could delay commissioning, leaving too little time for factory trials before launch.
o: Risk owner
Risk description
Risk action owner
Proximity
6.w: The risk description sets out the cause, the uncertain event and its effect on objectives (risk register composition, see manual 9.5). Here the cause is the lead time, the event is a late order delaying commissioning, and the effect is squeezed trials.

n.0: The risk owner is the person responsible for managing the risk; no person is named here.
n.2: The risk action owner carries out agreed actions for the risk owner; no person is named here.
n.3: Proximity records how soon the risk might occur; this statement describes its cause, event and effect.

6.q: Matching set (risk). Nadia Osei is adding a risk about the new tray-sealing line to the risk register. Which heading of the risk register should each statement be recorded under? Statement 2 of 3: The risk could occur within the next six weeks, when the purchase order for the line must be signed.
o: Risk owner
Risk description
Risk action owner
Proximity
6.w: Proximity records how close in time the risk might occur (risk register composition, see manual 9.5).

n.0: No person is assigned; the statement is about timing.
n.1: The statement gives when the risk might occur, not its cause, event and effect.
n.2: No person or action is assigned; the statement is about timing.

6.q: Matching set (risk). Nadia Osei is adding a risk about the new tray-sealing line to the risk register. Which heading of the risk register should each statement be recorded under? Statement 3 of 3: Dariusz Nowicki will be responsible for managing the risk and deciding how to respond to it.
o: Risk owner
Risk description
Risk action owner
Proximity
6.w: The risk owner is the person responsible for managing the risk and deciding its response (risk register composition, see manual 9.5).

n.1: The statement names who manages the risk, not the risk's cause, event and effect.
n.2: A risk action owner carries out specific agreed actions on behalf of the risk owner; Dariusz is managing the risk as a whole and deciding the response.
n.3: No timing is given.

6.q: Matching set (issues). Amy provides project support for Fernhollow Kitchen, and Felix Haddad is the team manager for packaging design. Which role should carry out each action? Statement 1 of 3: Decide on an escalated request to replace one of the six recipes, focusing on whether the expected branded sales are protected.
o: Project manager
Senior user
Project support
Team manager
6.w: When issues are escalated to the board, the senior user makes decisions with a focus on safeguarding the expected benefits (issues roles, see manual table 10.2).

n.0: The project manager manages the issue procedure and recommends options; an escalated issue is decided at board level.
n.2: Project support administers the issue procedure; it does not decide on escalated issues.
n.3: Team managers implement corrective actions in their work packages; they do not decide on escalated issues.

6.q: Matching set (issues). Amy provides project support for Fernhollow Kitchen, and Felix Haddad is the team manager for packaging design. Which role should carry out each action? Statement 2 of 3: Write new product descriptions and a new work package after the board approves an extra 'high protein' claim on two of the packs.
o: Project manager
Senior user
Project support
Team manager
6.w: The project manager implements corrective actions arising from issues, for example new product descriptions and work packages for agreed extra scope (issues roles, see manual table 10.2).

n.1: The senior user decides on escalated issues; preparing product descriptions and work packages is the project manager's work.
n.2: Project support maintains the issue register; it does not create work packages.
n.3: Team managers implement corrective actions within work packages they have accepted; creating a new work package is done by the project manager.

6.q: Matching set (issues). Amy provides project support for Fernhollow Kitchen, and Felix Haddad is the team manager for packaging design. Which role should carry out each action? Statement 3 of 3: Enter a new request for change from Charlotte Vane in the issue register and update its status as it is assessed.
o: Project manager
Senior user
Project support
Team manager
6.w: Project support administers the issue and change control procedures by maintaining the issue register (issues roles, see manual table 10.2).

n.0: The project manager runs the issue procedure and keeps the register when there is no project support; here Amy provides support.
n.1: The senior user decides on escalated issues; keeping the register is administration.
n.3: Team managers implement corrective actions in their work packages; they do not keep the issue register.

6.q: Matching set (progress). Fernhollow Kitchen is in the development stage. Which report or log should each item be recorded in? Statement 1 of 3: Ordering pack proofs in batches of six cut two weeks from the design cycle, and Nadia Osei wants later stages and future projects to use the idea.
o: Highlight report
Lessons log
Daily log
Exception report
6.w: The lessons log is the project's record of lessons that can be applied later in this project or in future projects (see manual 11.5).

n.0: Highlight reports summarize stage status for the board; lessons are first captured in the lessons log.
n.2: The daily log holds informal issues, actions and notes; a lesson to be reused is recorded in the lessons log.
n.3: Nothing is forecast to exceed tolerance.

6.q: Matching set (progress). Fernhollow Kitchen is in the development stage. Which report or log should each item be recorded in? Statement 2 of 3: The stage is now forecast to finish four weeks late, beyond its two-week time tolerance, and Nadia Osei sets out options and a recommendation for the board.
o: Highlight report
Lessons log
Daily log
Exception report
6.w: An exception report is produced by the project manager when a stage plan is forecast to exceed its tolerances, and it gives options and a recommendation (see manual 11.5).

n.0: A highlight report gives routine stage status; a forecast breach of stage tolerance needs an exception report.
n.1: This is not a lesson; it is a forecast breach of tolerance that must be escalated.
n.2: A forecast breach of stage tolerance needs formal escalation to the board, not an informal note.

6.q: Matching set (progress). Fernhollow Kitchen is in the development stage. Which report or log should each item be recorded in? Statement 3 of 3: Nadia Osei's fortnightly summary for the board of the stage's progress, including the results of the latest consumer panel.
o: Highlight report
Lessons log
Daily log
Exception report
6.w: A highlight report summarizes stage status for the project board at the intervals the board has set (see manual 11.5).

n.1: The lessons log records lessons, not routine status reports to the board.
n.2: The daily log is the project manager's informal record, not a report to the board.
n.3: Nothing is forecast to exceed tolerance; this is routine time-driven reporting.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the concept and recipe stage. Sesame has never been handled on the Fernhollow site, and a cross-contact incident there could lead to a recall that puts the own-label contracts at risk. Greendale Ready Meals already handles sesame under audited controls. The board agrees to Nadia Osei's proposal that Greendale should make the sesame recipe, so that no sesame enters the Fernhollow site. Which risk response is being used, and why?
o: Reduce, because Greendale's audited controls make a cross-contact incident less likely.
Transfer, because Greendale takes on the financial impact of any sesame incident under the agreement.
Avoid, because moving production removes the cause of the threat from the Fernhollow site.
Share, because Fernhollow and Greendale will split the costs and gains of making the sesame recipe.
6.w: Avoiding a threat makes the uncertain situation certain by removing the risk, for example by removing its cause (see manual 9.2.3, table 9.1). With no sesame on the Fernhollow site, the threat of cross-contact there can no longer occur.

n.0: Reducing a threat changes its probability or impact while a residual risk remains; here the cause of the threat is taken off the Fernhollow site.
n.1: Transfer passes part of the financial impact to a third party, for example through insurance or a contract clause; nothing here moves financial liability.
n.3: Sharing is a pain and gain arrangement with a partner; the scenario describes no split of costs or gains.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process. Imogen Fairley has made clear that the company has a very low appetite for food safety and allergen risks. Nadia Osei is drafting the risk management approach and needs a measurable threshold for the allergen-related risk exposure that can be accepted before it must be escalated. Who should set this risk tolerance?
o: Imogen Fairley, as the business layer, because she has set the company's risk appetite.
Nadia Osei, as project manager, because she is writing the risk management approach.
Luke Barraclough, because he is responsible for allergen control and food safety audits.
The project board, applying the risk appetite that the business has set.
6.w: Risk appetite is the business's attitude to risk, set here by Imogen Fairley for the company. Risk tolerance is the measurable threshold for each objective at risk, and it is set by the project board based on the business's overall risk appetite (see manual 9.2.1).

n.0: The business layer determines the appetite; the project board turns it into measurable tolerances for the project.
n.1: The project manager documents the tolerance in the risk management approach but does not set it.
n.2: Luke's expertise can inform the threshold, but setting risk tolerance is a project board decision.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process. At a risk workshop, Dariusz Nowicki says the line installation after the Christmas peak will go to plan because his team has not missed a shutdown deadline in ten years. The other directors agree without discussion, and the risk that trials will be squeezed into five weeks is scored as low probability. Nadia Osei records the score in the risk register. Is this an effective application of the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the operations director knows the factory best, so his view should decide the score.
Yes, because the board has said it is willing to take commercial risk to build the brand.
No, because the assessment shows groupthink, with the directors agreeing rather than testing the estimate.
No, because the timing of the line should be recorded as an issue, since the Christmas peak is certain.
6.w: Decision bias can distort risk assessment, and groupthink, valuing group cohesion over dissent or the right decision, is one of the named biases (see manual 9.2.4). The directors accepted one confident view without challenge, so the probability score is unreliable; Nadia should test it, for example with data on past shutdowns and the supplier's commissioning record.

n.0: Expert knowledge is valuable, but an unchallenged view from one person is how bias enters an assessment.
n.1: The appetite for commercial risk does not excuse a poor assessment of a risk that threatens the fixed launch week.
n.3: The peak is certain, but whether trials will be squeezed is still uncertain, so it is a risk; the problem is how it was scored.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the development stage. The product description for the meal sleeves requires them to be recyclable at the kerbside. The packaging supplier's first production batch uses a film that cannot be recycled at the kerbside, and the supplier says a compliant film would add three weeks. How should Nadia Osei treat this?
o: As an off-specification, handled through change control, with options to correct it or grant a concession.
As a request for change, because the board will need to relax the recyclability requirement for the launch.
As a risk, recorded in the risk register, because the three-week delay to the compliant film may not happen.
As an informal problem, recorded in the daily log and settled between Nadia and the packaging supplier.
6.w: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications. It is a formal issue that goes through change control, where the decision may be to correct it or to grant a concession (see manual 10.1 and 10.2.3). The batch has already failed the recyclability requirement, so it is an issue, not a risk.

n.1: A request for change proposes a change to a baseline; here a product has failed an existing specification, which is an off-specification whatever is later decided.
n.2: The non-compliant batch already exists, so this is an issue; the possible delay is part of its impact.
n.3: A product failing a board-level sustainability requirement needs formal handling through the issue register, not an informal note.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the concept and recipe stage. The fortnightly tastings produce frequent requests to change recipes and pack designs. The board appoints Charlotte Vane as change authority for recipe and packaging changes costing up to £8,000 each, gives her a change budget of £50,000 for the stage, and records the arrangement in the issue management approach. Larger changes still come to the board. Is this an effective application of the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the senior user is accountable for the business case and so should approve changes.
Yes, because delegating approval within limits, backed by a change budget, suits frequent iterative changes.
No, because the project board is the authority for requests for change and cannot pass this to one member.
No, because approved changes should be funded from the risk budget so that costs are tracked in one place.
6.w: The project board is the ultimate authority for changes but may delegate approval to a change authority within limits, and delegated authority should come with a change budget so that approved changes can be funded (see manual 10.2.4 and 10.2.5). With changes arising every two weeks, this keeps decisions quick while larger changes still reach the board.

n.0: The executive, not the senior user, is accountable for the business case.
n.2: The board is the ultimate authority but may delegate the approval of changes within limits, which is what it has done.
n.3: The risk budget funds responses to risks; approved changes are funded from the change budget.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is about to start the trials stage. Factory trials, shelf-life tests and the Harbridge's audit all fall within a few weeks, and two team managers will be reporting for the first time. The board asks for highlight reports every week during this stage instead of every month, and Nadia Osei asks the team managers for checkpoint reports twice a week. Which statement BEST explains why this is an appropriate use of the progress practice?
o: Highlight and checkpoint reports are event-driven controls, so they should be triggered by each trial run.
More frequent highlight reports remove the need for exception reports during a high-risk stage.
Reporting frequency should reflect the control needed, and inexperienced teams need more frequent reports.
The frequency of highlight reports is set in each work package description, so team managers can agree it.
6.w: Reporting frequency should reflect the level of control required, and an inexperienced team needs more frequent reporting until confidence grows (see manual 11.2.4). A short, high-risk stage with new team managers justifies weekly highlights to the board and more frequent checkpoints.

n.0: Highlight and checkpoint reports are time-driven controls produced at agreed intervals, not triggered by events.
n.1: Exception reports are still needed if stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded; routine reports do not replace them.
n.3: Highlight report frequency is set by the board; work package descriptions set the frequency of checkpoint reports.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the development stage, which has a time tolerance of two weeks. Gerrit Vos warns Nadia Osei that, on the current shipping schedule, the line is likely to arrive five weeks late. Nadia decides not to tell the board until the delay actually happens, because the supplier's forecasts have been wrong before. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager is expected to resolve problems before involving the board.
Yes, because the board should be given confirmed facts rather than uncertain forecasts.
No, because the line supplier's penalty clause should be enforced before any escalation.
No, because a forecast breach of stage tolerance is an exception and should be escalated now.
6.w: An exception is a situation where it can be forecast that tolerances will be exceeded, and the project manager should alert the board as early as possible through an exception report (see manual 11.1, 11.2.6 and 16.4.7). A credible forecast of five weeks against a two-week tolerance is enough to escalate; waiting removes the board's options.

n.0: The project manager acts within tolerance; a forecast breach of stage tolerance is outside her authority and goes to the board.
n.1: Manage by exception relies on forecasts so that the board can act before the breach occurs.
n.2: Contract penalties may recover some costs but do not change the forecast breach of the stage's time tolerance.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'starting up a project' process. Nadia Osei compares ways of delivering the range: making all six recipes in-house after adding pan-frying equipment, or using a co-manufacturer for the two pan-fried recipes; buying a new tray-sealing line or adapting an old one; and developing recipes in fixed phases or in two-week cycles with tastings. She recommends a hybrid approach using Greendale and a new line. Is this an appropriate application of the 'select the project approach' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because it decides how the work will be done: in-house or by third parties, build or buy, and the delivery method.
Yes, because the choice of suppliers is recorded in the project plan, which is baselined when initiation is authorized.
No, because the project approach is agreed in initiation as one of the nine management approaches.
No, because choosing co-manufacturers and equipment suppliers is a commercial decision for the business layer.
6.w: Selecting the project approach in starting up decides how the work will be approached, for example in-house or through third parties, building or buying, and the delivery method (see manual 13.4.5). Comparing these options before initiation gives the board a sound basis for authorizing initiation.

n.1: The project plan is prepared in initiation and baselined when the project is authorized; the project approach is selected earlier, in starting up.
n.2: The nine management approaches (risk, quality, issue and so on) are agreed in initiation; the project approach is a different product, selected in starting up.
n.3: The business layer commissions the project and sets its constraints; deciding how the work will be delivered is part of starting up the project.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'starting up a project' process. Imogen Fairley, who commissioned the project, has appointed Rob Hennessy as executive and Nadia Osei as project manager. The senior users, the senior supplier and the people who will provide project assurance now need to be chosen and appointed. Which role should be responsible for the 'appoint the project management team' activity?
o: The business layer, represented by Imogen Fairley.
The project manager, Nadia Osei.
The executive, Rob Hennessy.
The project board, acting together.
6.w: In the recommended RACI for 'appoint the project management team', the executive is responsible for making the appointments and the business layer is accountable; the project manager is not involved (see manual 13.4.4 and table 13.2).

n.0: Imogen, as the business layer, is accountable for the appointments, but the executive carries them out.
n.1: The project manager is not involved in appointing the project management team.
n.3: The board does not yet exist as a whole; its members are being appointed through this activity, which the executive carries out.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'starting up a project' process. To be thorough, Nadia Osei spends eight weeks preparing detailed recipe specifications, running full tenders with three line suppliers and producing a week-by-week plan for every stage before she requests project initiation. The launch week is eleven months away. Is this an effective way to carry out the 'starting up a project' process, and why?
o: Yes, because detailed specifications stop time being wasted in initiation on unsound assumptions.
Yes, because the fixed launch week makes it important to finish as much planning as possible early.
No, because the tenders should be run by the business layer before the project mandate is issued.
No, because starting up should do the minimum needed to decide whether initiation is worthwhile.
6.w: Starting up is a lighter process than initiation: it does the minimum necessary to decide whether the project is viable and worthwhile enough to initiate (see manual 13.1). Detailed specifications, tenders and full planning belong in initiation and later stages; spending eight weeks of an eleven-month timetable before initiation even starts puts the fixed launch week at risk.

n.0: Starting up should check key assumptions, but it does so at outline level, not through detailed specifications and tenders.
n.1: The fixed date makes time precious, so starting up should be quick; detailed planning is done in initiation and stage by stage.
n.2: The mandate comes from the business layer, but procuring suppliers is project work, carried out once the project is under way.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'directing a project' process. The three board members, Rob Hennessy, Charlotte Vane and Dariusz Nowicki, each review the project brief and the initiation stage plan by email, and all agree that initiation should go ahead. Rob, the executive, then emails Nadia Osei a written instruction to start initiation. Is this an appropriate application of the 'authorize initiation' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the executive holds the authority to start initiation without consulting the other members.
Yes, because initiation can be authorized without a meeting if all members agree and the executive instructs in writing.
No, because authorizing initiation requires a formal board meeting to approve the project initiation documentation.
No, because the business layer must approve the initiation stage plan before any initiation work starts.
6.w: 'Authorize initiation' reviews and approves the project brief and the initiation stage plan. It can be done with or without a formal meeting, as long as all board members agree and the project manager receives a documented instruction from the executive (see manual 14.4.1).

n.0: Authorizing initiation is a board decision; it could be done without a meeting here because all members agreed, with the executive then giving the written instruction.
n.2: The project initiation documentation is approved later, in 'authorize the project'; this activity approves the brief and the initiation stage plan, and no meeting is required.
n.3: The project board, not the business layer, approves the initiation stage plan in 'authorize initiation'.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'directing a project' process at the end of the development stage. Nadia Osei has submitted the end stage report and the trials stage plan, and the board is deciding whether to authorize the trials stage. Rob Hennessy is the executive and Charlotte Vane is a senior user. Which role should be accountable for this decision in the 'authorize a stage or exception plan' activity?
o: The project manager, Nadia Osei.
The senior user, Charlotte Vane.
Project assurance.
The executive, Rob Hennessy.
6.w: In the recommended RACI for 'authorize a stage or exception plan', the executive is accountable (and responsible), the senior user and project assurance are consulted, and the project manager is informed (see manual 14.4.4 and table 14.2).

n.0: The project manager prepares the plan and is informed of the decision; she is not accountable for it.
n.1: The senior user is consulted on the decision; accountability rests with the executive.
n.2: Project assurance is consulted and advises the board; it is not accountable.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the concept and recipe stage. The directors, used to running the factory hands-on, ask Nadia Osei to attend a weekly board meeting where they review every tasting result and approve each change to the work packages, even though the stage is forecast to finish within its tolerances. Is this an effective way to carry out the 'directing a project' process, and why?
o: Yes, because closer involvement helps directors who are new to projects learn how the project is run.
Yes, because the board is accountable for the project's success, so it should approve each change.
No, because the board should make key decisions and manage by exception, leaving day-to-day control to Nadia.
No, because the weekly meetings should be replaced by daily checkpoint reports sent directly to the board.
6.w: Directing a project lets the board be accountable through key decisions and overall control while delegating day-to-day management to the project manager; the board manages by exception and is not burdened with routine control (see manual 14.1 and 14.3). Approving work package changes within tolerance is the project manager's job in controlling a stage.

n.0: Learning is valuable, but it can come from briefings or coaching without the board taking over day-to-day control.
n.1: The board's accountability is exercised through decision points and tolerances, not by approving every change.
n.3: Checkpoint reports go from team managers to the project manager; the board receives highlight reports.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process. Before asking the board to authorize the project, Nadia Osei checks the parts of the project initiation documentation against each other. She finds that the project plan allows twelve weeks of trials, but the line delivery date in the commercial management approach and the supplier's contract leaves five. She resolves the conflict with Dariusz Nowicki before the PID is submitted. Is this an appropriate application of the 'assemble the project initiation documentation' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the elements of the PID should be cross-checked for consistency before it is baselined.
Yes, because the commercial management approach takes precedence over the project plan when they conflict.
No, because conflicts between products should be raised as issues and resolved after the PID is approved.
No, because the line delivery date is a matter for the operations director, not for the initiation documentation.
6.w: Assembling the PID includes cross-checking its elements for compatibility; the version used to gain authorization is then baselined and placed under change control (see manual 15.4.6). Finding the clash between the trials time and the line delivery date now avoids baselining an unworkable plan.

n.1: No management product takes precedence by default; the conflict has to be resolved so that both are consistent.
n.2: Resolving known conflicts before approval is the point of cross-checking; baselining a known inconsistency would push it into change control for no reason.
n.3: The line delivery date is a key planning constraint and must be shown consistently in the PID; the operations director's preference does not take it out of the project's control.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process. Nadia Osei creates a product breakdown structure for the whole launch, a work breakdown structure that groups the work into packages for the chefs, Mint and Tallow, Greendale and the line supplier, and a product flow diagram showing the order in which the products are needed. Which practice is being applied?
o: Organizing
Plans
Quality
Progress
6.w: Developing the product breakdown structure, the work breakdown structure and the product flow diagram is how the plans practice is applied in initiating a project (see manual table 15.3, and product-based planning in 7.3.1).

n.0: The work breakdown structure helps decide team structure, but producing these planning products applies the plans practice; organizing in initiation updates the project management team structure.
n.2: Quality in initiation is applied through the quality management approach and quality specifications, not the breakdown structures.
n.3: Progress in initiation concerns the project controls and reporting arrangements, not the breakdown of products and work.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen has just been authorized for initiation. Worried about the fixed launch week, Rob Hennessy tells Megan Cho's chefs to start the two-week recipe cycles and asks the design agency to begin branding work straight away, while Nadia Osei writes the project initiation documentation over the next four weeks. Is this an effective way to carry out the 'initiating a project' process, and why?
o: Yes, because iterative recipe and design work produces learning that will improve the initiation documentation.
Yes, because the executive is accountable for the project and can start delivery when time is short.
No, because the design agency's contract should be signed by the business layer before any work starts.
No, because delivery work and spending should wait until the board has authorized the project on solid foundations.
6.w: Initiating a project establishes solid foundations so that the business understands the work needed before committing significant expenditure; delivery starts once the board authorizes the project (see manual 15.1 and 14.4.2). Starting the chefs and the agency now commits money and effort before the plan, business case and controls are agreed.

n.0: Early learning can be useful, but committing delivery resources before authorization bypasses the board's decision point.
n.1: The executive is accountable, but authorizing the project is a board decision in directing a project, made on the PID.
n.2: Contracting is handled through the commercial management approach agreed in initiation; the problem is starting delivery before the project is authorized.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the development stage. Nadia Osei and Felix Haddad of Mint and Tallow work through the packaging artwork work package together. They agree the products, the constraint that sleeves must be kerbside-recyclable and carry the carbon label, tolerances of one week and £6,000, fortnightly checkpoint reports to match the agency's cycles, and how finished artwork will be approved. Felix confirms he can deliver it, and Nadia then authorizes the start. Is this an appropriate application of the 'authorize a work package' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the work package is co-created with the team manager and his acceptance is confirmed before work starts.
Yes, because the work package description should also hold benefits and quality tolerances for the artwork.
No, because the checkpoint frequency should follow the board's highlight reporting cycle, not the agency's cycles.
No, because a fixed-price supplier's work is controlled through its contract rather than through a work package.
6.w: Authorizing a work package involves defining it, building the relationship with the team manager, co-creating and reviewing it with them, confirming their acceptance and then authorizing the start (see manual 16.4.1). The description carries scope, cost and time tolerances, constraints, reporting arrangements and how the products will be approved.

n.1: Work package descriptions carry scope, cost and time tolerances; benefits and quality tolerances are not agreed in a work package description.
n.2: Checkpoint frequency is agreed for the work package and can sensibly follow the team's own working cycle.
n.3: External suppliers' work is still passed to them formally through work packages, which sit alongside the contract.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the development stage, and the fortnightly report to the board is due. The latest checkpoint reports from the team managers, the project log and the revised stage plan are pulled together, the corrective actions taken are listed, and the report is issued to the board. Which role should be responsible for the 'report highlights' activity?
o: The team managers, who produce the checkpoint reports.
Project support, which maintains the project log.
The project manager.
Project assurance, which checks that reporting is fair.
6.w: In the recommended RACI for 'report highlights', the project manager is responsible, with team managers, project support and project assurance consulted (see manual 16.4.8 and table 16.2).

n.0: Team managers are consulted; their checkpoint reports feed the highlight report, but they do not produce it.
n.1: Project support is consulted and may help to compile the report, but the project manager is responsible for it.
n.3: Project assurance is consulted; it does not produce the project manager's report to the board.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the development stage, which has a time tolerance of two weeks. Gerrit Vos phones to say that a component shortage might delay the shipment of the line. Without recording the problem or finding out how long the delay could be, Nadia Osei immediately sends the board an exception report recommending an exception plan. Is this an appropriate way to carry out the 'controlling a stage' process, and why?
o: Yes, because a possible delay to the line threatens the fixed launch week, so the board should be involved early.
Yes, because the executive is accountable for the project and should decide on any threat to the line.
No, because the line supplier's project engineer should have escalated the delay directly to the board.
No, because the issue should first be captured and assessed to see whether stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded.
6.w: In 'capture issues and risks' each issue or risk is registered and then assessed before a course of action is decided (see manual 16.4.5). An exception report is raised only when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded (16.4.7); otherwise the project manager deals with the matter within the stage.

n.0: Early warning matters, but escalation is for a forecast breach of stage tolerance, and that has not been assessed.
n.1: The executive is accountable, but decisions within stage tolerance are delegated to the project manager.
n.2: Team managers and suppliers raise issues with the project manager, not directly with the board.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the development stage. Gerrit Vos reviews the installation work package with Nadia Osei. He points out that the commissioning tests cannot fit inside the three-week shutdown, so they agree to move the tests into the first week of trials and to adjust the constraints. Gerrit then agrees to deliver the work package and prepares a team plan. Is this an appropriate application of the 'accept a work package' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the team manager can change the stage plan so that it fits the work package.
Yes, because the team manager agrees what will be delivered and confirms it is achievable before accepting.
No, because a team plan should be prepared by the project manager before the work package is offered.
No, because the constraints of a work package are fixed once the project manager has issued it.
6.w: In 'accept a work package' the team manager agrees with the project manager what is to be delivered, the reporting requirements, constraints and procedures, and whether it is achievable, before agreeing to deliver it; a team plan may be produced (see manual 17.4.1).

n.0: The team manager does not change the stage plan; changes are agreed with the project manager, who updates the stage plan.
n.2: Team plans are optional and are produced by team managers, not the project manager.
n.3: Work packages are agreed jointly; raising constraints that make the work unachievable is exactly what acceptance is for.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the development stage. Felix Haddad's team at Mint and Tallow is producing the packaging artwork under its work package, reporting progress through checkpoint reports and recording completed quality checks. Which role should be accountable for the 'execute a work package' activity?
o: The team manager, Felix Haddad.
The senior supplier.
The executive.
The project manager.
6.w: In the recommended RACI for 'execute a work package', the project manager is accountable while the team manager's team carries out the work; project assurance is consulted, and the business layer and executive are not involved (see manual 17.4.2 and table 17.2).

n.0: Felix's team does the work; accountability for the activity sits with the project manager.
n.1: The senior supplier commits supplier resources at board level, and the project board is not involved in managing product delivery.
n.2: The executive is not involved in executing work packages.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the development stage. After a call with the Harbridge's buyer, Charlotte Vane emails Felix Haddad directly and asks Mint and Tallow to make the brand logo larger on all six sleeves. Felix tells his team to make the change and mentions it to Nadia Osei in his next checkpoint report. Is this an appropriate way to carry out the 'managing product delivery' process, and why?
o: Yes, because the senior user represents the users and can ask for changes to products that affect them.
Yes, because the change can be made within the work package tolerances agreed with the agency.
No, because the team manager should take instructions from the project manager and raise the request as an issue.
No, because changes to the sleeve design should be approved by the Harbridge's buyer before work starts.
6.w: In managing product delivery the team manager works to the work package agreed with the project manager, notifies the project manager of new issues and takes any action the project manager requires, rather than instructions directly from board members (see manual 17.4.2). Charlotte's request is a request for change to an agreed product and should go through Nadia and the issue procedure.

n.0: The senior user can raise a request for change, but through the project's issue procedure, not by instructing a team manager.
n.1: Tolerances limit deviation in delivering agreed products; they do not let a team manager accept new requirements from a board member.
n.3: The buyer is a customer stakeholder; changes to the project's products are controlled through the project's own change control.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in week 2 of its 16-week development stage. To get ahead, Nadia Osei prepares the detailed trials stage plan now, including a date for every trial run, and asks the board to approve it with her next highlight report. Is this an appropriate application of the 'prepare next stage plan' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because preparing the plan early gives the line supplier more time to arrange its engineers.
Yes, because the trials stage is the most critical stage and so needs the longest planning time.
No, because the next stage plan should be prepared by the team managers who will run the trials.
No, because it should be prepared near the end of the current stage, when its detail is more reliable.
6.w: The next stage plan is prepared near the end of the current stage, close to when the work happens, so that it reflects what has been learned and stays within the planning horizon (see manual 7.2.2 and ch 18). It is then approved by the board in 'authorize a stage or exception plan' at the stage boundary.

n.0: The supplier's needs can be met through the project plan; detailed stage planning this early will be unreliable.
n.1: How critical a stage is does not change the planning horizon; the trials detail depends on what happens in development.
n.2: The project manager prepares stage plans; team managers prepare team plans.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'managing a stage boundary' process at the end of the development stage. During the three-week shutdown, the maintenance staff and Gerrit Vos's engineers worked long night shifts. Nadia Osei reviews how the teams performed and how their health and well-being held up, and records the findings for the lessons log and the end stage report. Which practice is being applied?
o: Organizing
Progress
Quality
Business case
6.w: In managing a stage boundary, the organizing practice is applied by reviewing the project team's performance, health and well-being for lessons and for the end stage report (see manual table 18.3).

n.1: Progress is applied by creating and issuing the end stage report; reviewing team performance and well-being applies organizing.
n.2: Quality is applied by checking the quality register for the stage's quality activities.
n.3: Business case is applied by updating the business case and benefits management approach; the review here is of the teams' performance and well-being.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'managing a stage boundary' process at the end of the trials stage. Tariq Javed confirms that Harbridge's will list the range in 300 stores at launch rather than 400. This lowers forecast year-one sales but keeps the forecast within the benefits tolerance. Nadia Osei updates the business case and the benefits management approach and reports the change in the end stage report, so that the board can decide whether to authorize the final stage. Is this an appropriate way to carry out the 'managing a stage boundary' process, and why?
o: Yes, because the senior user specifies the benefits and so can approve the lower forecast.
Yes, because changes to forecast benefits are handled by updating the business case at the stage boundary.
No, because a fall in forecast benefits should be handled by preparing an exception plan.
No, because benefits are confirmed after closure, so forecasts should not change during the project.
6.w: At a stage boundary the business case is updated to reflect changes in the project and its environment, the benefits management approach is updated, and the end stage report gives the board what it needs to decide on the next stage (see ch 18). A change in forecast benefits within tolerance is handled here, not through an exception plan.

n.0: The senior user specifies the benefits and shows the business that they are on track, but the decision to continue on the updated business case is the board's.
n.2: Exception plans respond to a forecast breach of tolerance; this change is within the benefits tolerance.
n.3: Benefits are confirmed mainly after closure, but forecasts are maintained throughout and updated at every stage boundary.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'closing a project' process after the first eight weeks of sales. Nadia Osei arranges for the range to pass to the normal sales and operations teams, checks that the line has a maintenance contract and trained operators, and obtains confirmation from the senior users that the range has been accepted. She also checks that post-project benefits reviews have been planned. Is this an appropriate application of the 'confirm project acceptance' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the products pass to the operational environment and acceptance is confirmed, with support in place.
Yes, because confirming acceptance includes carrying out the first benefits review before the project closes.
No, because acceptance should be confirmed by the business layer once the first benefits review is complete.
No, because the maintenance contract for the line is an operational matter that is not part of closing a project.
6.w: Confirming project acceptance passes the products to the operational and maintenance environment and confirms that they have been accepted; closing a project also makes sure the business can support the products afterwards (see manual 19.4.3 and 19.2). Checking that post-project benefits reviews are planned is part of this activity.

n.1: Benefits reviews after closure are planned during the project, but carrying them out is not a project activity.
n.2: Acceptance is confirmed during closing, before the project ends, on behalf of the users; benefits reviews come after closure, so waiting for one would keep the project open.
n.3: Making sure the business can support the products after closure is an objective of closing a project.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'closing a project' process. Nadia Osei checks that every product in the plans, from the six recipes and the packaging to the line and the co-manufacturing agreement, is recorded as approved and handed over, and then closes the register that lists the products and their status. Which practice is being applied?
o: Quality
Plans
Issues
Progress
6.w: In closing a project the plans practice is applied by checking and closing the product register, which lists the products of the plans and their status (see manual table 19.3).

n.0: Quality is applied by checking and closing the quality register of quality activities; the product register records product status.
n.2: Issues would be applied by reviewing open issues and recommending follow-on actions; this is about the products' status.
n.3: Progress is applied through the end project report and lessons report; closing the product register applies plans.

6.q: Fernhollow Kitchen has completed its launch stage. Rob Hennessy asks Nadia Osei to keep the project open, with its board and reports, for three more years until the forecast £6 million of annual branded sales has been confirmed. Is this an appropriate way to carry out the 'closing a project' process, and why?
o: Yes, because the project is not complete until its benefits have been realized and confirmed.
Yes, because the executive is accountable for the business case, including its benefits.
No, because later benefits are confirmed by post-project reviews that the business carries out.
No, because the senior user, not the executive, decides when the project closes.
6.w: A project is finite, and a clear end is better than a slow drift into use. In closing, the benefits management approach is updated to plan post-project benefits reviews, which the business carries out after closure; running them is not a project activity (see manual 19.3, 19.4 and 5.3.1).

n.0: Most benefits are realized after the project; the project ends when its products are accepted, and benefits are confirmed afterwards.
n.1: The executive is accountable for the business case, but that does not mean the project should stay open while benefits accrue.
n.3: Closure is authorized by the project board in directing a project, on the project manager's request; it is not a decision for the senior user alone.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Cllr Yvonne Price has announced the race in the local media. She tells Kezia Oduya that, because the cabinet is committed and the date is fixed with the national athletics body, the business case needs to be written once to secure authorization and will not need updating at stage boundaries. How well does this apply the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because political commitment and a fixed date are valid reasons for the project and belong in the business case.
It applies it well, because the executive, not the project manager, decides how often the business case is reviewed.
It applies it poorly, because the justification must stay valid throughout, so the business case is updated and checked each stage.
It applies it poorly, because the cabinet member should own the business case as the event's public champion.
7.w: The justification must remain valid and be revalidated throughout the project; if it is lost, the project should be changed or stopped (see manual 2.1). The project manager maintains the business case at each stage end and the board checks it before authorizing the next stage (5.3.1). Entries, sponsorship and costs against the £300,000 cap can all change, so a one-off business case applies the principle poorly.

n.0: Commitment and the fixed date explain why the project was started; they do not remove the need to revalidate the justification as costs, entries and sponsorship change.
n.1: The executive is accountable for the business case, but the principle requires it to be maintained and checked throughout; no role can decide to stop revalidating it.
n.3: The executive owns the business case (Andrew Mallory holds the budget); in any case the weakness here is that the case would not be revalidated, not who owns it.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'starting up a project' process. The council has never run an event of this size. Kezia Oduya arranges calls with the organizers of two established half marathons in other cities, reads the independent review of the collapse at Paceline's 10k race, and records what she learns in the lessons log. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Learn from experience, because the event is a first for the council, so seeking lessons from outside organizations matters even more.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the review concerns how Paceline carried out its medical role at the 10k.
Ensure continued business justification, because other cities' experience shows whether a half marathon brings in enough local spending.
Manage by exception, because the lessons will help Kezia decide which problems she can deal with herself and which to escalate.
7.w: Learn from experience: lessons are sought, recorded and acted on from the start, and when a project is a first for the organization it is even more important to learn from others, including outside organizations (see manual 2.2). Reviewing earlier reports and consulting people with experience of similar projects is the 'assess previous lessons' activity, recorded in the lessons log (13.4.2).

n.1: The review is one of the sources of lessons; Kezia is gathering and recording lessons, not agreeing roles or building relationships.
n.2: Kezia is not checking whether this project is still desirable, viable and achievable; she is collecting experience from other events.
n.3: Manage by exception is about tolerances and escalation; nothing here sets limits of delegated authority.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Kezia Oduya sets up a monthly liaison group with Inspector Ravi Sandhu of the safety advisory group, Colin Mayfield of the traders' association, Rev Judith Akers and a residents' representative. She agrees with each of them who their contact in the project team is and what they can expect to hear, and when. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Learn from experience, because the liaison group will collect lessons from people who have lived through earlier road closures.
Tailor to suit the project, because a liaison group adapts the method to the council's usual way of working with communities.
Manage by stages, because the group will meet at fixed intervals that give the board regular points to review the project.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the team is building relationships with external stakeholders.
7.w: The principle covers agreed roles and responsibilities and also the project management team initiating and building relationships with and between internal and external stakeholders (see manual 2.3). Kezia is setting up a relationship with each external group and agreeing what each can expect from the project.

n.0: The group may surface useful experience, but its purpose here is to build and manage relationships, not to gather lessons.
n.1: Tailoring adapts processes, products, roles or terms to the project; setting up stakeholder relationships is not a tailoring decision.
n.2: Manage by stages concerns stage-by-stage planning and board decision points; a monthly liaison group is not a stage boundary.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. The draft plan has a 16-week build-up stage. Kezia Oduya proposes splitting it into two stages, with a boundary straight after the safety advisory group's decision eight weeks before race day, so that the board decides whether to commit the largest infrastructure spending once it knows the event can go ahead. How well does this apply the 'manage by stages' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because shorter stages let the board set tighter tolerances for Kezia to work within.
It applies it well, because stage boundaries are decision points and can be aligned with key external events.
It applies it poorly, because adding a stage increases the time that senior managers spend directing the project.
It applies it poorly, because the number of stages was settled when the board authorized initiation.
7.w: Stages give the board review and decision points at which it assesses viability, and stage ends can be aligned with external influences (see manual 2.4). Without the safety advisory group's approval the event cannot go ahead, so a boundary after that decision lets the board commit the largest spending at the right moment.

n.0: Setting tolerances is manage by exception; the reason for this boundary is to create a decision point around the approval.
n.2: It is true that more stages add to the board's burden, but with a go or no-go approval and a low appetite for safety risk, more control here is justified.
n.3: Stages are decided as the project plan is prepared in initiation; the brief and initiation stage plan approved earlier do not fix them.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the build-up stage, which has a cost tolerance of plus or minus £15,000. The barrier hire contract comes in £8,000 above the stage plan. Kezia Oduya finds a matching saving in printing costs, adjusts the stage plan and reports both changes in her next highlight report, without asking the board for a decision. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Manage by stages, because the board will review the changed costs when it next authorizes a stage.
Ensure continued business justification, because keeping to the cost plan protects the council's £300,000 cap.
Manage by exception, because the forecast stays within the stage tolerance that the board delegated to Kezia.
Focus on products, because the barriers are a product whose cost is set in their product description.
7.w: Manage by exception sets limits of delegated authority through tolerances; while the stage is forecast to stay within tolerance the project manager can adjust without escalating, and the board is kept informed through highlight reports (see manual 2.5 and 11.2.6).

n.0: The board does review costs at stage ends, but Kezia's freedom to act now comes from the tolerance delegated to her, not from the next stage boundary.
n.1: Protecting the cap matters, but the action shows a decision taken within delegated limits rather than a check of whether the project is still worth doing.
n.3: A product description sets a product's purpose and quality, not its cost; the decision rests on the stage cost tolerance.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Kezia Oduya's draft plan for the build-up stage is a list of tasks such as 'sort volunteers', 'do marketing' and 'meetings with Paceline', each with a duration and an owner. Andrew Mallory likes it because the events team plans its markets this way. Nothing describes what each piece of work must produce or the standard it must meet. How well does this apply the 'focus on products' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because a simple task list is a reasonable way of tailoring the method for an in-house events team.
It applies it well, because each task has a named owner, which makes clear who is responsible for the work.
It applies it poorly, because the plan should be reviewed by the safety advisory group before the build-up stage starts.
It applies it poorly, because the plan is task-based and does not define the products and the quality they must meet.
7.w: The principle requires the project to be output-oriented: products are defined, with their quality expectations, in product descriptions, and these drive planning, quality and scope control (see manual 2.6). A list of tasks with no defined outputs is work-oriented and leaves scope and standards unclear.

n.0: Tailoring can simplify products and formats, but it cannot remove a principle; the plan still needs defined products.
n.1: Named owners clarify who does the work, but they do not define what must be delivered or to what standard.
n.2: The safety advisory group approves the event safety plan, not the project's stage plans; this does not explain the weakness.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Kezia Oduya proposes that highlight reports be a two-page summary every four weeks in the planning and approvals stage, then every two weeks in the build-up stage and daily during event week, when the pace and the safety risks are highest. The board would review them online instead of meeting. Is this an appropriate application of the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
o: Yes, because frequent highlight reports keep Cllr Yvonne Price ready for questions from the local media.
Yes, because the frequency and formality of reporting are matched to the pace and risk of each stage.
No, because the reporting frequency should stay the same in every stage once the board has set it.
No, because tailoring decisions are approved by the business layer rather than by the project board.
7.w: Tailoring makes project controls fit the project's scale, complexity, importance and risk, for example the frequency and formality of reports and reviews (see manual 2.7). Reporting more often as risk rises, and letting a busy board review online, is proportionate tailoring recorded in the PID.

n.0: Highlight reports are for the project board; media briefings are planned through the communication management approach, so this is not a tailoring reason.
n.2: Reporting frequency can be varied to suit the control needed at different points in the project.
n.3: Tailoring is documented in the PID, which the project board approves when it authorizes the project.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the planning and approvals stage. Paceline's operations team works from its head office in another city, and the council's events officers contact them mainly by email. Misunderstandings about road closure times have twice caused rework. Kezia Oduya arranges a joint planning day every fortnight on the riverside, where Lisa Ventnor's team and the events officers walk parts of the course together and agree actions. Is this an appropriate way to manage the project team, and why?
o: Yes, because working side by side lets Kezia direct Paceline's staff without going through Lisa Ventnor.
Yes, because regular, purposeful meetings build trust and social cohesion between teams from different organizations.
No, because Paceline's staff are accountable to Greg Halloran, so their ways of working are a matter for Paceline.
No, because joint team building should wait until the build-up stage, when the volunteers join the project.
7.w: Bringing teams together means building social cohesion through people meeting purposefully and regularly, creating trust across silos; teams that are not co-located need deliberate methods such as planned joint days (see manual 3.3.3). Here two organizations' teams are misunderstanding each other by email.

n.0: Kezia should work through the team manager; the value of the days is shared understanding, not bypassing Lisa.
n.2: Greg Halloran commits Paceline's staff, but the problem lies between the two teams, which the project manager should help to work together.
n.3: Delaying would let the rework continue; cohesion is needed now between the teams already working together.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the build-up stage. The events officer booking grandstands, barriers and toilets has booked equipment only for park concerts before. Two bookings have been late and one supplier delivered the wrong barriers. Lisa Ventnor's logistics team at Paceline has made bookings of this kind for many races. Which action is MOST appropriate for Kezia Oduya to take?
o: Pair the officer with Paceline's logistics team for the remaining bookings, arrange training and review progress at each checkpoint.
Ask Andrew Mallory, as executive, to approve each booking personally so that mistakes are caught before orders are placed.
Record the late bookings in the lessons log for future events and leave the work with the officer until race day.
Widen the officer's work package tolerances so that late bookings no longer need to be reported to her.
7.w: Building effective teams means understanding people's capabilities, identifying competency gaps and mitigating them, for example by upskilling or shifting responsibilities to more suitable people (see manual 3.3.2). Pairing the officer with experienced Paceline staff and arranging training closes the gap while keeping the work moving.

n.1: The executive directs the project and does not manage day-to-day bookings; this adds a bottleneck without closing the gap.
n.2: Recording a lesson is useful, but leaving the gap unaddressed risks more errors before race day.
n.3: Widening tolerances hides the problem from the project manager rather than dealing with the capability gap.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the planning and approvals stage. Rev Judith Akers has sent a joint letter from local churches, including the two on the route, saying the closures will stop worshippers reaching Sunday morning services. Cllr Yvonne Price wants to reply that the date is fixed and the closures are lawful. Which action is MOST LIKELY to reduce the churches' resistance to the event?
o: Ask Cllr Yvonne Price to explain the event's economic and charity benefits in an interview with the local paper.
Send each church a copy of the road closure order and the communication management approach for reference.
Record the joint letter in the risk register and review it again when the safety plan is submitted for approval.
Meet Rev Judith Akers and the church leaders to understand their needs and design crossing points and timings with them.
7.w: Pockets of resistance show where engagement should focus: find out why stakeholders resist rather than sidelining them, and co-create solutions with key influencers so they are adopted (see manual 3.2.2 and 3.4). Rev Akers organized the joint letter, so she is a key influencer for the churches.

n.0: Promoting benefits in the media does not address the churches' specific concern and may harden their position.
n.1: Sending documents informs the churches but does not engage them or address why they object.
n.2: The objection is already happening, so it is an issue to engage with now, not a matter to review later.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Kezia Oduya's stakeholder analysis lists the cabinet, Paceline, the building society, the police, the ambulance service, the traders' association and residents on the route. Zara Quinn points out that the route crosses the main access road to Carrowford Royal Infirmary and passes two churches holding morning services. Is Kezia's stakeholder analysis appropriate, and why?
o: Yes, because the police and ambulance service sit on the safety advisory group, which will consider hospital access.
Yes, because the traders' association and residents already speak for everyone living or working near the route.
No, because the hospital's patients, staff and visitors and the churches' congregations are affected and are missing.
No, because the stakeholder analysis should be written by the communication team once the project is authorized.
7.w: A stakeholder is anyone who can affect, is affected by, or perceives themselves to be affected by the project, and engagement starts by identifying all stakeholders and key influencers, including those with no formal role (see manual 3.2.2). People using the hospital and the church congregations are affected by the closures but have been missed.

n.0: The safety advisory group considers emergency access, but it does not represent patients, visitors or hospital staff, whose concerns differ.
n.1: Residents and traders have their own interests; they do not represent hospital users or church congregations.
n.3: The communication management approach, including stakeholder analysis, is agreed during initiation, before the project is authorized.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the build-up stage. Zara Quinn is recruiting about 1,200 volunteers, most of whom have never helped at a race. To save time, Kezia Oduya proposes emailing each fortnightly highlight report to every volunteer as their main source of information about their roles and race-day arrangements. Is this an appropriate application of the communication management approach, and why?
o: Yes, because sending the same report to everyone keeps the whole project ecosystem equally well informed.
Yes, because a highlight report is issued at regular intervals, which suits a large group of volunteers.
No, because highlight reports are confidential to the project board and should not leave the board.
No, because volunteers need role information through channels and at times that suit them as an audience.
7.w: The communication management approach sets the means and frequency of communication for each stakeholder group, with purpose, channels and messages suited to that audience (see manual 3.4). A board-level stage status report does not tell new volunteers what they need to do; they need targeted role briefings, for example through the volunteering programme.

n.0: Different groups need different messages; one board report does not inform volunteers about their roles.
n.1: Regular timing does not make the content right; highlight reports summarize stage status for the board.
n.2: Highlight reports can go to other stakeholders where useful; the problem is that this one does not meet volunteers' needs.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Kezia Oduya is drafting the communication management approach and writes this entry: 'Residents on the route: affected for five hours on race day; active on social media; individually low influence but able to create media pressure through residents' groups.' Under which heading of the communication management approach should this entry be recorded?
o: Stakeholder analysis
Communications schedule and procedures
Supporting tools and techniques
Resources
7.w: Stakeholder analysis identifies who is affected by the project's outcome or delivery and who can influence its success or failure (communication management approach contents, manual 3.4). The entry describes how residents are affected and how much influence they have.

n.1: The schedule and procedures set out what will be communicated to each group, how often and through which channels; the entry gives none of this.
n.2: Supporting tools and techniques are things such as communication platforms or analytics tools, not an assessment of a stakeholder group.
n.3: Resources are the people and budget for communication activities, not a description of a stakeholder group.

7.q: Matching set (business case). Kezia Oduya is preparing the business case practice products for the Carrowford Half Marathon. Which product should each piece of information be recorded in? Statement 1 of 3: No single-use plastic bottles on the course, 70% of event waste recycled, free bus travel for runners, and a carbon footprint report published within two months of the event.
o: Business case
Benefits management approach
Sustainability management approach
Communication management approach
7.w: The sustainability management approach defines the actions, reviews and controls that will ensure the project's sustainability performance targets are met, with reference to the organization's environmental goals (see manual 5.2.2 and 5.5).

n.0: The business case sets out the reasons, benefits, costs and time for the investment; the council's sustainability targets and their controls belong in the sustainability management approach.
n.1: The benefits management approach covers how benefits will be measured and reviewed, not sustainability performance targets.
n.3: The communication management approach covers communication with stakeholders; publishing a carbon report is one of the sustainability targets, not a communication procedure.

7.q: Matching set (business case). Kezia Oduya is preparing the business case practice products for the Carrowford Half Marathon. Which product should each piece of information be recorded in? Statement 2 of 3: Local spending may fall up to 10% below the £2.5 million target before the shortfall must be escalated; it will be measured by an independent economic impact study six weeks after race day.
o: Business case
Benefits management approach
Sustainability management approach
Communication management approach
7.w: The benefits management approach defines how benefits will be measured and reviewed and records the benefits tolerance, the permitted deviation in benefit targets before escalation (see manual 5.2.2 and 5.5).

n.0: The business case states the expected benefits themselves; the tolerance and the way they will be measured and reviewed belong in the benefits management approach.
n.2: Local spending is an economic benefit target, not one of the event's sustainability performance targets.
n.3: The statement sets a benefits tolerance and a measurement method, not how stakeholders will be informed.

7.q: Matching set (business case). Kezia Oduya is preparing the business case practice products for the Carrowford Half Marathon. Which product should each piece of information be recorded in? Statement 3 of 3: The event will cost £900,000, partly offset by £45 entry fees and £150,000 of sponsorship, with the council's net contribution capped at £300,000.
o: Business case
Benefits management approach
Sustainability management approach
Communication management approach
7.w: The business case records the costs of the project and how they are funded, weighed against the expected benefits and risks (business case costs heading, manual 5.5).

n.1: The benefits management approach covers measuring and reviewing benefits, not the project's costs and funding.
n.2: No sustainability target or control is given; these are costs and funding arrangements.
n.3: Costs and funding are not communication arrangements.

7.q: Matching set (organizing). The project management team for the Carrowford Half Marathon is being appointed. Using the additional information (people), which individual is most appropriate for each role? Statement 1 of 3: Executive, accountable for the business case and for securing the project's funding.
o: Cllr Yvonne Price
Andrew Mallory
Bernadette Lowe
Greg Halloran
7.w: The executive is the single point of accountability, owns the business case and secures funding (see manual 6.2.4). Andrew Mallory received the mandate from the cabinet and holds the events budget.

n.0: Cllr Price is the event's political champion and part of the cabinet that commissioned it; she does not hold the budget or the mandate.
n.2: Bernadette Lowe is an internal auditor, independent of the project, which suits an assurance role rather than accountability for it.
n.3: Greg Halloran runs the contracted supplier; he represents the supplier interest, not the council's business interest.

7.q: Matching set (organizing). The project management team for the Carrowford Half Marathon is being appointed. Using the additional information (people), which individual is most appropriate for each role? Statement 2 of 3: Senior supplier, able to commit the supplier's people and accountable for the quality of what it delivers.
o: Cllr Yvonne Price
Andrew Mallory
Bernadette Lowe
Greg Halloran
7.w: The senior supplier represents the suppliers, commits their people and resources, and is accountable for the quality of supplier products (see manual 6.2.4). Greg Halloran commits Paceline's staff and is accountable for its race-day operations.

n.0: Cllr Price champions the event for the council; she has no authority over Paceline's resources.
n.1: Andrew Mallory represents the council's business interest; he cannot commit Paceline's staff.
n.2: Bernadette Lowe audits for the council and has no authority over the supplier.

7.q: Matching set (organizing). The project management team for the Carrowford Half Marathon is being appointed. Using the additional information (people), which individual is most appropriate for each role? Statement 3 of 3: Business assurance, checking on the executive's behalf and independently of Kezia Oduya that the project is being run properly.
o: Cllr Yvonne Price
Andrew Mallory
Bernadette Lowe
Greg Halloran
7.w: Project assurance is independent of the project manager and can be provided by people appointed from the business (see manual 6.2.4). Bernadette Lowe is a senior auditor who has audited two council events and whose team has said it will review the project.

n.0: Cllr Price is the event's public champion and wants to start the race, so she is not well placed to give independent assurance.
n.1: Andrew Mallory is the executive; this role acts on his behalf, so it needs someone else.
n.3: Greg Halloran represents the supplier, so he cannot give the council independent business assurance.

7.q: Matching set (plans). Kezia Oduya is drafting the work package description for Paceline's course set-up work on the Carrowford Half Marathon. Which heading of the work package description should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 1 of 3: Crews may work on the roads between 10pm and 5am only under police escort, and every marshal must have completed the council's safety briefing.
o: Techniques and procedures
Constraints
References
Targets and tolerances
7.w: Constraints are restrictions or limits on the work, such as authorized working hours, safety and security measures (work package description contents, manual 7.5).

n.0: Techniques and procedures describe how the work is to be done; permitted hours and safety conditions are limits on the work.
n.2: References point to applicable higher-level plans; these are restrictions on how the work may be carried out.
n.3: Targets and tolerances set permitted deviations in scope, cost and time; these are limits on hours and safety, not tolerances.

7.q: Matching set (plans). Kezia Oduya is drafting the work package description for Paceline's course set-up work on the Carrowford Half Marathon. Which heading of the work package description should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 2 of 3: The dates and the certified route set out in the build-up stage plan and the project plan.
o: Techniques and procedures
Constraints
References
Targets and tolerances
7.w: References list the applicable references from higher-level plans that the team manager needs (work package description contents, manual 7.5).

n.0: The statement points to higher-level plans rather than describing how the work is to be done.
n.1: No restriction such as hours or safety measures is given; it identifies the plans the work must follow.
n.3: No permitted deviation in scope, cost or time is given.

7.q: Matching set (plans). Kezia Oduya is drafting the work package description for Paceline's course set-up work on the Carrowford Half Marathon. Which heading of the work package description should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 3 of 3: The work may finish up to two days late or cost up to £3,000 more before Lisa Ventnor must raise it with Kezia.
o: Techniques and procedures
Constraints
References
Targets and tolerances
7.w: Targets and tolerances set the permissible deviations for scope, cost and time for the work package, beyond which the team manager raises the matter with the project manager (work package description contents, manual 7.5 and 11.2.1).

n.0: The statement sets limits of delegated authority, not working methods.
n.1: Constraints are restrictions on how the work is done, such as hours or safety; time and cost deviations are tolerances.
n.2: No higher-level plan is referred to; these are the work package's own tolerances.

7.q: Matching set (quality). Kezia Oduya is drafting the quality management approach for the Carrowford Half Marathon. Which heading should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 1 of 3: Paceline's own quality management system for race operations, which the project will refer to for its timing and course checks.
o: References
Responsibilities
Supporting tools and techniques
Standards
7.w: The references heading points to associated documents or products, such as the business's or a supplier's quality management system (quality management approach contents, manual 8.5).

n.1: No person or role is given a quality duty; the statement points to the supplier's existing system.
n.2: Supporting tools and techniques are methods such as testing or inspection; the statement identifies a document to be referred to.
n.3: Standards are the standards that apply to quality management on the project; a supplier's own system is recorded as a reference.

7.q: Matching set (quality). Kezia Oduya is drafting the quality management approach for the Carrowford Half Marathon. Which heading should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 2 of 3: Bernadette Lowe will provide business assurance on quality, and Lisa Ventnor will approve the race-day marshal guide before it is printed.
o: References
Responsibilities
Supporting tools and techniques
Standards
