7.w: The responsibilities heading defines who does what in quality planning and control, including project assurance responsibilities and who approves products (quality management approach contents, manual 8.5).

n.0: No associated document or quality system is referred to; the statement assigns quality duties to people.
n.2: No testing, inspection or other technique is described; the statement names who assures and who approves.
n.3: No standard is set; the statement assigns roles.

7.q: Matching set (quality). Kezia Oduya is drafting the quality management approach for the Carrowford Half Marathon. Which heading should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 3 of 3: Everything published for the event, from the entry website to the race-day guide, must comply with data protection legislation.
o: References
Responsibilities
Supporting tools and techniques
Standards
7.w: The standards heading records standards that apply to quality management across the project, such as legal compliance required of all published material (quality management approach contents, manual 8.5).

n.0: The statement sets a requirement that applies to every published item, not a pointer to an associated quality system.
n.1: No person or role is assigned a quality duty.
n.2: No testing, inspection or other technique is described; this is a standard all published items must meet.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. In the full business case Kezia Oduya compares three options: holding no event, which shows what would happen without the investment; a 10k race with no festival; and the full half marathon with the riverside festival. She quantifies the costs, risks and local spending of the last two against the first. Is this an appropriate application of the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the 'do nothing differently' option is the baseline against which the value of the others is measured.
Yes, because the cabinet's mandate names the half marathon, so the comparison will confirm that choice is right.
No, because holding no event is not a real option once the date has been agreed with the national athletics body.
No, because benefits cannot be quantified until the event has run and the economic impact study is complete.
7.w: Business options always start with 'do nothing differently', which is the baseline for quantifying the other options; the difference between the options is the benefit the investment buys (see manual 5.3.1). Comparing the 10k and the full event against no event shows which option gives the best value.

n.1: The comparison is meant to show which option gives the best value, not to confirm a choice already made.
n.2: Even when a project is expected, the 'do nothing differently' option is kept as the baseline for measuring the others.
n.3: Benefits are forecast in the business case to support decisions; they are confirmed later through benefits reviews.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the build-up stage. Harriet Bloom tells Kezia Oduya that the building society will cut its sponsorship from £150,000 to £100,000 because entries are behind target. Kezia logs the news but decides that the business case can wait for her end stage update in eight weeks' time, when the board will review it. Is this an effective way to apply the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the business case is maintained at the end of each stage with the latest costs and forecasts.
Yes, because sponsorship income is a commercial matter for Andrew Mallory as executive, not for Kezia.
No, because Kezia should assess the effect of issues on the business case as they arise, as this threatens the cap.
No, because the sponsor's change should be confirmed through a benefits review before it is accepted.
7.w: The project manager checks the business case when assessing issues and risks for their impact on the justification, not only at stage ends (see manual 5.3.1). Losing £50,000 of income could push the council's net contribution past the £300,000 cap, so the board may need to act before the stage ends.

n.0: It is true that the business case is maintained at stage ends, but this does not remove the need to assess a major issue when it arises.
n.1: The executive owns the business case, but the project manager assesses issues for their impact on it on the executive's behalf.
n.3: Benefits reviews confirm whether benefits have been realized, mostly after closure; they are not used to assess a change in funding.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in its final stage. Kezia Oduya plans how the race know-how, the volunteer database, Paceline's contract contacts and the events officers who gained experience on the project will pass to the council's events team, which will run the race each year as normal business. Which step of the organizational design and development technique is she applying?
o: Develop the project ecosystem, as the events officers' new skills are recorded for later events.
Manage ongoing changes to the project ecosystem, as people move off the project when it ends.
Understand the organizational ecosystem, as the events team's current structure must be known.
Transition the project into the organizational ecosystem, as people, products and learning return.
7.w: The final step of the technique transitions the project into the organizational ecosystem: products, people and learning are handed back to the business at closure (see manual 6.3.1). Here the event is being handed to the events team to repeat as normal business.

n.0: Developing the project ecosystem is ongoing onboarding, skills and culture work while the project runs, not the handover at the end.
n.1: Managing ongoing changes covers moving people on and off as needs change during the lifecycle; handing the event to the business is the transition step.
n.2: Understanding the organizational ecosystem happens first, before the project ecosystem is designed.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. To save money, Andrew Mallory proposes that Martin Cole, the council's corporate risk and insurance manager, provide business assurance for the project and also act as project support, keeping the risk register, the issue register and the project log up to date for Kezia Oduya. Is this an effective way to apply the organizing practice, and why?
o: Yes, because Martin Cole is independent of Kezia Oduya, which project assurance requires.
Yes, because roles can be combined to suit the project, and the council saves the cost of a support officer.
No, because project assurance should be carried out by a board member rather than delegated to others.
No, because project support should be kept separate from project assurance so that assurance stays objective.
7.w: Project support is the project manager's responsibility and must be kept separate from project assurance, which is the board's; support staff cannot carry out assurance (see manual 6.2.4). Maintaining Kezia's registers would put Martin Cole inside the work he is meant to assure.

n.0: Independence from the project manager is needed, but combining assurance with support breaks the rule that the two roles are kept apart.
n.1: Roles can be combined, but not these two; the saving does not make the combination acceptable.
n.2: Board members are accountable for assurance but may delegate the work to people from the business or outside it.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. After writing the product breakdown structure, Kezia Oduya and Lisa Ventnor draw a product flow diagram. It shows that the course certificate must exist before entries open, and that the safety advisory group's approval and the police road closure order, which the project does not produce, are needed before race-day set-up. Is this an appropriate application of the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the diagram lets the team estimate each product's cost before the product descriptions are written.
Yes, because a product flow diagram shows the sequence and dependencies of products, including external ones.
No, because products that the project does not create, such as the approval, should be left off the diagram.
No, because product flow diagrams are drawn by team managers for team plans, not for the project plan.
7.w: In product-based planning the product flow diagram defines the sequence in which products are developed and the dependencies between them, including intermediate and external products (see manual 7.3.1). The approval and road closure order are external products the event depends on.

n.0: Estimates come after the products are defined and analysed; the diagram's purpose is sequence and dependencies, not costing.
n.2: External products are shown on the diagram because the project depends on them.
n.3: Product-based planning is used for project, stage and team plans; the project plan needs it during initiation.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Before the board sets stage tolerances, Kezia Oduya runs a short workshop with its members. They agree that race day cannot move, that public safety standards cannot be lowered and that the council's £300,000 cap is firm, so any flexibility must come from the scope of the riverside festival. Is this an effective way to apply the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because knowing which constraints take precedence is needed to choose approaches and set suitable tolerances.
Yes, because the project manager sets the stage tolerances and needs the board's views before doing so.
No, because stage tolerances are set by the business layer, so the board's views on constraints are not needed.
No, because scope tolerance belongs in work package descriptions rather than in stage plans.
7.w: Understanding which constraints take precedence is a crucial part of planning, used to select approaches and set tolerances (see manual 7.2.4). The board then allocates stage tolerances to the project manager, here leaving flexibility in festival scope.

n.1: The project board sets stage tolerances; the project manager sets work package tolerances.
n.2: The business layer sets project tolerances; the board sets stage tolerances within them.
n.3: Scope tolerance is set for plans at each level, including stage plans, as well as in work package descriptions.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'starting up a project' process. Kezia Oduya is drafting the project product description with Andrew Mallory and Greg Halloran. Under the user's quality expectations she writes: 'The event will bring about £2.5 million into local businesses over the weekend.' Is this an appropriate application of the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because quality expectations should show how the event supports the council's Active Carrowford strategy.
Yes, because user's quality expectations are high-level statements that do not need to be measurable.
No, because local spending is a benefit expected from the event, not the quality expected of what is delivered.
No, because quality expectations belong in the quality management approach, not the project product description.
7.w: The user's quality expectations describe the quality expected of the project product, captured in the project product description; an outcome or benefit such as more local spending is not a quality expectation (see manual 8.1.1 and 5.1). Expectations here would cover, for example, a safe, certified and well-marshalled course.

n.0: Alignment with strategy is shown in the business case; quality expectations describe the quality of the product itself.
n.1: It is true that expectations are high-level and may not be measurable, but this does not make a benefit into a quality expectation.
n.3: The user's quality expectations are recorded in the project product description; the quality management approach describes how quality will be achieved.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the build-up stage. Because Paceline's medical response at an earlier race was criticized, Andrew Mallory wants confidence in the medical plan. Lisa Ventnor's team checks the plan against its product description, and Kezia Oduya asks the council's health and safety unit, which is independent of the project, to review whether those checks are adequate. Is this an effective way to apply the quality practice, and why?
o: Yes, because quality control by the producers is backed by quality assurance from a function outside the project.
Yes, because project assurance must be independent of the project manager, which the health and safety unit is.
No, because the senior supplier is accountable for the quality of Paceline's products, so the council should not review them.
No, because quality assurance should be carried out by project support, who maintain the quality register.
7.w: Quality control checks products against their specifications, while quality assurance, carried out independently of the project management team by a business function, gives confidence that the quality controls are appropriate (see manual 8.2.2 and 8.2.3).

n.1: Project assurance is the board's responsibility and is independent of the project manager only; a unit outside the project is providing quality assurance.
n.2: The senior supplier is accountable for supplier product quality, but the business can still seek independent assurance that quality controls are adequate.
n.3: Project support administers quality records; it is part of the project management team, so it cannot provide independent quality assurance.

7.q: Matching set (risk). Kezia Oduya is recording a risk about race-day medical cover for the Carrowford Half Marathon in the risk register. Which heading of the risk register should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 1 of 3: Because Paceline's medical response was criticized at an earlier race, help for a runner who collapses could be slow, leading to serious harm and damage to the council's reputation.
o: Risk description
Proximity
Risk action owner
Risk owner
7.w: The risk description sets out the cause, the uncertain event and its effect on objectives (risk register contents, manual 9.2 and 9.5). Here the cause is the earlier criticism, the event a slow response and the effect harm and reputational damage.

n.1: Proximity is how near in time the risk might occur; the statement describes the risk itself.
n.2: A risk action owner carries out agreed actions for the risk owner; no person or action is given here, only cause, event and effect.
n.3: No person is named to manage the risk.

7.q: Matching set (risk). Kezia Oduya is recording a risk about race-day medical cover for the Carrowford Half Marathon in the risk register. Which heading of the risk register should each piece of information be recorded under? Proximity

Risk owner

n.1: No timing is given.
n.2: A risk action owner carries out specific agreed actions on the risk owner's behalf; Greg is managing the response as a whole, which makes him the risk owner.

7.q: Matching set (risk). Kezia Oduya is recording a risk about race-day medical cover for the Carrowford Half Marathon in the risk register. Which heading of the risk register should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 3 of 3: The risk could occur on race day, Sunday 14 September, about 30 weeks from now.
o: Risk description
Proximity
Risk action owner
Risk owner
7.w: Proximity records how close in time the risk might occur (risk register contents, manual 9.2 and 9.5).

n.0: The statement gives timing only, not the cause, event and effect.
n.2: No person is named to carry out an action.
n.3: No person is named.

7.q: Matching set (issues). The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the planning and approvals stage. Where should each item be recorded or described? 7.q: Matching set (issues). The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the planning and approvals stage. Where should each item be recorded or described? Statement 2 of 3: The effect on the plan, the course certificate and the business case of moving the route away from St Mary's, with the options and a recommended decision for the board.
o: Issue register
Daily log
Issue report
Issue management approach

7.q: Matching set (issues). The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the planning and approvals stage. Where should each item be recorded or described? Statement 3 of 3: Colin Mayfield's formal request to move the start time to 8am, with its type, priority, current status and issue owner.

Daily log
Issue report
Issue management approach

7.q: Matching set (progress). Which report or log of the Carrowford Half Marathon project should each item be recorded in? Statement 1 of 3: After the event, a comparison of the actual cost, entries and timescales with the version of the PID that the board authorized, with follow-on actions for the events team.

Checkpoint report
Lessons log
End project report

n.2: The lessons log records lessons as they arise, not a review of overall performance.

7.q: Matching set (progress). Which report or log of the Carrowford Half Marathon project should each item be recorded in? Statement 2 of 3: During the build-up stage, Zara Quinn notes that briefing volunteers by short video took far less time than face-to-face sessions, which future events could copy.
o: Highlight report
Checkpoint report
Lessons log
End project report
7.w: The lessons log is the informal repository of lessons that could be applied on this or future projects, recorded as they are identified (see manual 11.5).

n.0: A highlight report gives stage status to the board; a lesson noted during the stage is recorded in the lessons log.
n.1: A checkpoint report gives work package status to the project manager; lessons are recorded in the lessons log.
n.3: The end project report is written at closure; the lesson is captured now in the lessons log.

7.q: Matching set (progress). Which report or log of the Carrowford Half Marathon project should each item be recorded in? Statement 3 of 3: The status of the build-up stage against its tolerances, sent to the board every two weeks.
o: Highlight report
Checkpoint report
Lessons log
End project report
7.w: The highlight report is a time-driven summary of stage status that the project manager sends to the board at intervals the board defines (see manual 11.2.2 and 11.5).

n.1: A checkpoint report goes from a team manager to the project manager about a work package; stage status for the board is a highlight report.
n.2: The lessons log records lessons, not stage status.
n.3: The end project report is produced at closure.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the build-up stage. Harriet Bloom says the building society would value the event far more if it were shown on regional television, which is possible but not certain. To raise the chance of coverage, Kezia Oduya invites the regional broadcaster to a site visit and offers it free camera positions at the start and finish. Which type of risk response is being applied, and why?
o: Exploit, because the action makes sure that the television coverage will take place.
Enhance, because the action increases the probability of the opportunity without making it certain.
Share, because the broadcaster and the building society both gain if the coverage goes ahead.
Accept, because the project will wait to see whether the broadcaster decides to cover the race.
7.w: Enhance is a response to an opportunity that takes definite action now to increase its probability or impact; exploit would make the opportunity certain (see manual 9.2.3, table 9.1). An invitation and free positions make coverage more likely but do not guarantee it.

n.0: Exploit removes the uncertainty; the broadcaster may still decline, so coverage is not made certain.
n.2: Share is a pain or gain arrangement with a partner, usually through a contract; no such arrangement is made here.
n.3: Accept means taking no action now, but Kezia is acting to raise the chance of coverage.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. The council's risk management policy sets a low appetite for risks to public safety and reputation and a moderate appetite for financial risk on events. Kezia Oduya's draft risk management approach uses one probability and impact scale for every risk, and lets her accept any risk scored below 'high' without referring it to the board. Is this an effective way to apply the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because using one scale for every risk makes it easier to compare and prioritize risks across categories.
Yes, because the project manager sets the risk tolerances when writing the risk management approach.
No, because the low appetite for safety and reputation risk calls for tighter thresholds than for financial risk.
No, because the risk management approach should list each identified risk together with its owner and response.
7.w: The business sets the risk appetite and the project board sets risk tolerances based on it (see manual 9.2.1). With a low appetite for safety and reputation risk, the thresholds for escalating those risks should be tighter than for financial risk, not the same single cut-off.

n.0: A common scale helps comparison, but it ignores the different appetites the council has set for different kinds of risk.
n.1: Risk tolerance is set by the project board based on the business's risk appetite, not by the project manager.
n.3: Specific risks, owners and responses belong in the risk register; the approach describes procedures, scales and responsibilities.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the planning and approvals stage. The product description for the course requires a certified distance of 21.0975 km. The accredited course measurer reports that the route designed by Paceline is 40 metres short, so it cannot be certified until it is changed. Entries are due to open in three weeks. How should Kezia Oduya classify this issue, and why?
o: As a request for change, because the route design will have to be altered before entries open.
As a concern, because its effect on the date for opening entries still has to be assessed.
As a problem, because it has an immediate negative effect on the planning and approvals stage.
As an off-specification, because a product will not meet the specification in its product description.
7.w: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications (see manual 10.1, issue types). The route design is a product whose product description requires the certified distance, and it falls short.

n.0: A request for change proposes changing a baseline; here the baseline (the required distance) stays the same and the product fails to meet it.
n.1: The impact will be assessed, but the issue is already known to be a product failing its specification.
n.2: It is negative, but PRINCE2 classifies a product that will not meet its specification as an off-specification.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. The board agrees that Kezia Oduya may approve requests for change costing up to £5,000 each from a change budget of £20,000, and that any change affecting the route or the event safety plan comes to the board. The arrangement is written into the issue management approach and Kezia's role description. Is this an effective way to apply the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the board may delegate approval of changes within limits, with a budget to fund approved changes.
Yes, because the project manager is the ultimate authority for requests for change once the project is authorized.
No, because changes should be funded from the risk budget, which pays for responses to threats and opportunities.
No, because change authority should be given to a separate group, not the project manager, to keep it independent.
7.w: The project board is the ultimate authority for changes but may delegate approval within limits to a change authority or the project manager, with a change budget so approved changes can be funded; the delegation is documented in the issue management approach and role descriptions (see manual 10.2.4 and 10.2.5).

n.1: The board remains the ultimate authority; the project manager approves changes only within the limits delegated.
n.2: The risk budget funds risk responses; approved changes are funded from the change budget.
n.3: The board may delegate change authority to the project manager as well as to a separate person or group.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon build-up stage has a cost tolerance of plus or minus £20,000. Inspector Ravi Sandhu asks for an extra staffed crossing at the hospital access road, costing £12,000. This is above Kezia Oduya's £5,000 change limit but within stage tolerance. Kezia registers the request, assesses its effect on the plan, budget and safety plan, and sends the board her options and a recommendation. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because a request from the police is an external event, so the project manager may approve it herself.
Yes, because she captures and assesses the request and recommends options to those with authority to decide.
No, because a request from the safety advisory group should be treated as a risk rather than as an issue.
No, because a change above the project manager's limit should be raised with the board in an exception report.
7.w: The issues technique is capture, assess, recommend, decide and implement: the request is registered, its impact assessed, and options with a recommendation go to whoever holds the authority to decide (see manual 10.3.1). As the cost is within stage tolerance, an issue report is used rather than an exception report.

n.0: Its source does not change the approval rule: at £12,000 it is above Kezia's delegated limit, so the board decides.
n.2: The request has already been made, so it is an issue to be handled, not an uncertain future event.
n.3: An exception report is used when stage or project tolerance is forecast to be exceeded; this change is within stage tolerance.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the planning and approvals stage, and entries have just opened. Kezia Oduya sets up an online dashboard that takes entry numbers from the entry system each day, compares them with the planned entry curve and forecasts whether 6,000 entries will be reached by the end of June. Board members can view it between highlight reports. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because data and systems help compare actual progress with the plan and forecast likely outcomes.
Yes, because the dashboard can set the entry tolerances from the daily figures as they change.
No, because progress control compares actual achievement with the plan rather than forecasting results.
No, because the board should receive progress information in highlight reports rather than on a dashboard.
7.w: The progress practice compares actual achievements with the plan and forecasts the project's objectives and viability; data and systems support tracking, forecasting and presentation in stakeholders' preferred format (see manual 11.1, 11.2.5 and 11.2.7). The end-of-June forecast matters because of the 6,000-entry trigger.

n.1: Tolerances are set by the management levels, not by data or systems.
n.2: Forecasting is part of the purpose of the progress practice, not separate from it.
n.3: Highlight reports continue; data and dashboards can supplement them in the format stakeholders prefer.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon build-up stage has a cost tolerance of plus or minus £20,000. Three weeks into the stage, Kezia Oduya forecasts that higher prices for barriers and grandstands will push stage costs £35,000 over plan. None of the extra money has been spent yet, so she decides to report the position in the end stage report and look for savings in the meantime. Is this an effective way to apply the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the end stage report gives the board the information it needs to decide what to do next.
Yes, because tolerance is not exceeded until the extra money has actually been spent.
No, because a forecast breach of stage tolerance is an exception and should be reported to the board now.
No, because the extra costs should be approved by Cllr Yvonne Price as cabinet member for leisure.
7.w: An exception is a situation where a deviation beyond agreed tolerance can be forecast; the project manager escalates it to the board in an exception report as soon as it is forecast, so the board can decide in good time (see manual 11.1 and 11.3.1).

n.0: The end stage report supports the next-stage decision; waiting until then denies the board the chance to act on the exception now.
n.1: Exceptions are based on forecasts, not only on money already spent.
n.3: Stage tolerance breaches are decided by the project board; the cabinet member is not part of the board.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'starting up a project' process. Because race day cannot move, Kezia Oduya wants to save time. She proposes to send the board the project brief and to begin initiation as soon as it agrees, explaining the six weeks of initiation work as she goes rather than preparing an initiation stage plan. Is this an appropriate application of the 'plan the initiation stage' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the fixed race date means that any time saved in initiation can be used in the build-up stage.
Yes, because six weeks is short enough for the board to follow initiation through Kezia's highlight reports.
No, because initiation uses time and resources, so it should be planned and approved to avoid aimless work.
No, because the initiation stage plan is prepared in the 'managing a stage boundary' process, not here.
7.w: Initiating a project takes time and consumes resources, so the work is planned and approved to make sure initiation is not aimless and unstructured; starting up a project is not complete without the initiation stage plan (see manual 13.4.7 and 13.4.8).

n.0: The fixed date makes efficient initiation important, but an unplanned initiation is more likely to waste time than save it.
n.1: Highlight reports report against a stage plan; without an initiation stage plan there is nothing to control initiation against.
n.3: The initiation stage plan is the one stage plan produced in starting up a project; later stage plans are prepared at stage boundaries.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'starting up a project' process. The cabinet gave the mandate to Andrew Mallory, who has been appointed executive. Andrew is now choosing the other members of the project board and agreeing their role descriptions, including inviting Greg Halloran to represent Paceline. Which role is accountable for the 'appoint the project management team' activity?
o: The business layer, represented here by the council's cabinet
The executive, Andrew Mallory, who is choosing the members
The project manager, Kezia Oduya, who will lead the team
The senior supplier, Greg Halloran, who commits Paceline's staff
7.w: In the recommended RACI for 'appoint the project management team', the business layer is accountable and the executive is responsible; the project manager is not involved (see manual 13.4.4 and table 13.2). The cabinet commissioned the project, so it is the business layer here.

n.1: Andrew Mallory carries out the appointments, which makes him responsible; accountability sits with the business layer.
n.2: The project manager is not involved in appointing the project management team.
n.3: Greg Halloran is being appointed; he has no RACI role in making the appointments.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'starting up a project' process. Before asking the board for authority to initiate, Andrew Mallory asks Kezia Oduya to have Paceline produce a detailed course design, a full rota for 1,200 volunteers and a draft event safety plan, so that the board knows exactly what it is approving. This will take about three months. Is this an effective way to carry out starting up a project, and why?
o: Yes, because detailed products reduce the risk that the safety advisory group rejects the event later on.
Yes, because the board needs a full business case and detailed plans before it can authorize initiation.
No, because the course design and the volunteer rota are Zara Quinn's responsibility rather than Paceline's.
No, because starting up should do the minimum needed to decide whether initiation is worthwhile.
7.w: Starting up a project asks whether there is a viable and worthwhile project; it is a lighter process than initiation and does the minimum necessary to decide whether initiation is worth the investment (see manual 13.1). Three months of detailed delivery work before initiation is authorized is far more than this, and eats into a fixed timescale.

n.0: Reducing safety risk matters, but detailed delivery products belong in later stages after the project is authorized, not before initiation.
n.1: The board authorizes initiation on the project brief, with an outline business case, and the initiation stage plan; the full business case comes from initiation.
n.2: Course design is Paceline's contracted work; in any case the problem is doing detailed work too early, not who does it.

7.q: The project brief and the initiation stage plan for the Carrowford Half Marathon have been sent to the three board members. As their diaries make a meeting difficult, Andrew Mallory asks each member by email whether they are content. All three agree, and Andrew then sends Kezia Oduya a written instruction to begin initiation. Is this an appropriate application of the 'authorize initiation' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the executive can authorize initiation on his own once he has read the project brief.
Yes, because all board members agreed and the executive gave Kezia a documented instruction to begin.
No, because the brief and the initiation stage plan should be approved at a formal meeting of the board.
No, because initiation should be authorized by the cabinet, which issued the project mandate.
7.w: Authorize initiation can be done with or without a formal meeting, as long as all board members agree and the project manager receives a documented instruction from the executive (see manual 14.4.1). Both conditions are met here.

n.0: The decision is the board's, so all members must agree; the executive's documented instruction confirms it.
n.2: A formal meeting is not required for this activity when all members agree and the executive documents the instruction.
n.3: The cabinet, as the business layer, issued the mandate; the project board authorizes initiation in directing a project.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon planning and approvals stage is ending. Kezia Oduya has submitted the end stage report and the build-up stage plan, and the board is reviewing them in the 'authorize a stage or exception plan' activity. According to the recommended RACI, how is the project manager involved in this activity?
o: Responsible for the activity
Accountable for the activity
Consulted during the activity
Informed of the outcome
7.w: In the recommended RACI for 'authorize a stage or exception plan', the executive is accountable and responsible, the senior user and project assurance are consulted, and the project manager is informed (see manual table 14.2).

n.0: The executive is responsible for this activity; the project manager prepared the inputs in managing a stage boundary.
n.1: The executive is accountable; this is a board decision.
n.2: The senior user and project assurance are consulted; the project manager is informed of the decision.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the build-up stage. After a news story about medical cover at another race, Andrew Mallory phones Lisa Ventnor directly and tells her to add four more medical posts on the course. Lisa's team starts the work, and Kezia Oduya finds out a week later from the stage budget figures. Is this an effective way to carry out directing a project, and why?
o: Yes, because board members may give direction at any time, either collectively or individually.
Yes, because the executive is accountable for the project, including the safety of those taking part.
No, because the board should direct through the project manager, who instructs team managers.
No, because extra medical posts change the safety plan, which the safety advisory group should decide.
7.w: Directing a project lets the board stay accountable while delegating day-to-day management to the project manager; the board is not involved in managing product delivery, and team managers take their instructions from the project manager through work packages (see manual 14.1, 14.3 and 17.4.2). Direction should have gone to Kezia.

n.0: Ongoing direction can come from individual board members, but it is given to the project manager, not straight to a team manager.
n.1: The executive is accountable, but that does not mean bypassing the project manager to instruct suppliers' teams.
n.3: The safety advisory group approves the event safety plan, but the problem here is the board bypassing the project manager.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Kezia Oduya drafts the sustainability management approach from the council's targets for major events: refill stations instead of bottles, 70% of waste recycled, free buses for runners and a carbon report within two months. She also asks two other cities how their races met similar targets. Is this an appropriate application of the 'agree the management approaches' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the approaches draw on business standards the project must meet and on lessons from similar projects.
Yes, because the sustainability management approach is where the business layer sets out its environmental policy.
No, because sustainability targets are recorded in the business case, so a separate approach is not needed.
No, because the management approaches should be agreed in starting up a project, before the brief is approved.
7.w: The management approaches are derived from business strategies, standards and practices the project must comply with and from users' expectations, and lessons from similar projects are sought when agreeing them (see manual 15.4.2). The council's event targets and other cities' experience are exactly these inputs.

n.1: The approach describes how the project will achieve its sustainability targets; the business's own policy is an input to it, not its content.
n.2: Sustainability targets and tolerances are documented in the sustainability management approach, which supports the business case.
n.3: The management approaches are agreed during initiation; starting up produces the project brief.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Andrew Mallory is the executive, Kezia Oduya is the project manager and Bernadette Lowe has been appointed to provide business assurance. Which describes the recommended RACI for the 'prepare the full business case' activity?
o: Andrew responsible, Kezia accountable, Bernadette consulted
Kezia responsible, Andrew accountable, Bernadette consulted
Kezia responsible and accountable, Bernadette informed
Andrew responsible, the cabinet accountable, Kezia consulted
7.w: For 'prepare the full business case' the project manager is responsible, the executive is accountable, project assurance is consulted and the business layer is not involved (see manual 15.4.5 and table 15.2).

n.0: The roles are reversed: the project manager prepares the business case and the executive is accountable for it.
n.2: The executive is accountable for the business case; the project manager cannot hold that accountability, and assurance is consulted.
n.3: The business layer is not involved in this activity, and the project manager prepares the full business case.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Kezia Oduya hears that grandstand prices will rise next month. She proposes signing a £180,000 contract for grandstands and barriers now, two weeks before she asks the board to authorize the project, so that the lower price is secured. Is this an effective way to carry out initiating a project, and why?
o: Yes, because the fixed race date makes early booking essential, and initiation can include urgent delivery work.
Yes, because a lower price improves the business case, which the board reviews when it authorizes the project.
No, because infrastructure is booked in the event week stage, close to when it will be used on race day.
No, because initiation should lay solid foundations before significant spending is committed to the project.
7.w: Initiating a project establishes solid foundations so that the business understands the work needed before committing to significant expenditure (see manual 15.1). Committing £180,000 before the board has authorized the project bypasses that decision point.

n.0: The fixed date is a real pressure, but delivery spending waits for the board to authorize the project.
n.1: A saving may help the business case, but the board has not yet decided whether the project should go ahead.
n.2: In this plan infrastructure is booked in the build-up stage; in any case the issue is committing money before authorization.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the planning and approvals stage. Lisa Ventnor notifies Kezia Oduya that the course measurement work package is complete. Before updating the product register and the stage plan, Kezia checks that the accredited course measurer has signed the certificate, as the course's product description names the measurer as its approver. Is this an appropriate application of the 'receive completed work package' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because each product should have the approval required by the quality responsibilities in its product description.
Yes, because Greg Halloran, as senior supplier, has confirmed that Paceline's work met the terms of its contract.
No, because completed work packages should be approved by the project board before the stage plan is updated.
No, because acceptance of products is confirmed in the 'closing a project' process rather than during a stage.
7.w: In 'receive completed work package' the project manager makes sure each product has gained its requisite approval, as defined by the quality and sustainability responsibilities in its product description, then updates the product register and stage plan (see manual 16.4.3).

n.1: No such confirmation is described, and a contract sign-off does not replace the approval named in the product description.
n.2: The project board does not approve individual work packages; the approvers named in each product description do.
n.3: Closing a project confirms acceptance of the project product as a whole; individual products are approved as their work packages complete.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the build-up stage. Kezia Oduya is preparing her fortnightly highlight report in the 'report highlights' activity. Lisa Ventnor is Paceline's team manager, an events officer provides project support and Bernadette Lowe provides business assurance. According to the recommended RACI, whom should Kezia consult?
o: Lisa Ventnor, the events officer providing support and Bernadette Lowe
Andrew Mallory and the other members of the project board
Andrew Mallory, Bernadette Lowe and Inspector Ravi Sandhu
Cllr Yvonne Price and the cabinet, as the council's business layer
7.w: In 'report highlights' the project manager is responsible, and the team manager, project support and project assurance are consulted (see manual 16.4.8 and table 16.2).

n.1: The board receives the highlight report; it is not consulted in preparing it.
n.2: The executive receives the report and Inspector Sandhu has no role in the project management team; the team manager and support are missing.
n.3: The business layer is not consulted on highlight reports; the board decides what is reported onwards to it.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon build-up stage is forecast to finish within its tolerances, but volunteer sign-ups are 300 behind plan. Kezia Oduya agrees an amended work package with Zara Quinn that adds three recruitment events at the city's universities, paid for from within the stage budget, and reports the action in her next highlight report. Is this an effective way to control the stage, and why?
o: Yes, because volunteer recruitment is run by the volunteering programme, outside the project's control.
Yes, because the project manager can take corrective action within stage tolerance through a work package.
No, because any shortfall against plan should be escalated to the board in an exception report.
No, because corrective actions should be approved by the board before the work package is changed.
7.w: When evaluating stage status reveals a deviation, the project manager identifies and selects solutions within stage tolerance and triggers them through 'authorize a work package' (new or amended work packages), keeping the board informed through highlight reports (see manual 16.4.4 and 16.4.6).

n.0: Zara's programme is doing the work under a work package, so it is within the project's control; that is why the amended work package works.
n.2: Exception reports are for forecast breaches of stage or project tolerance; this stage is forecast to stay within tolerance.
n.3: Corrective action within stage tolerance is the project manager's decision; the board is told, not asked.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the build-up stage. Lisa Ventnor receives the draft work package for setting up the course, which requires every barrier and sign to be in place by 6am. Volunteers cannot reach the route before 5am because of the road closure times, so Lisa shows Kezia Oduya the work cannot be done in time, and they agree a later finish time and extra Paceline crew before Lisa accepts. Is this an appropriate application of the 'accept a work package' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the team manager may change a work package's constraints when they conflict with the team plan.
Yes, because the team manager agrees with the project manager what is required and whether it can be achieved.
No, because the team manager should accept the work package as issued and raise problems in checkpoint reports.
No, because the constraints in the work package were set by the project board, which would need to agree a change.
7.w: In 'accept a work package' the team manager agrees with the project manager what is to be delivered, the constraints and procedures, and whether the work is achievable, before agreeing to deliver it (see manual 17.4.1).

n.0: The team manager cannot change a work package alone; the change is agreed with the project manager.
n.2: Accepting work known to be unachievable would only defer the problem; the activity exists to agree an achievable work package first.
n.3: Work package constraints are agreed between the project manager and team manager; the board sets stage tolerances, not work package details.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the build-up stage. Lisa Ventnor's team has finished installing the timing mats and the results system, and Lisa is carrying out the 'notify work package completion' activity. According to the recommended RACI, which role should be informed?
o: Senior supplier
Senior user
Business layer
Project support
7.w: In the recommended RACI for 'notify work package completion', project support is informed; the business layer, senior user and senior supplier are not involved (see manual 17.4.4 and table 17.2).

n.0: The senior supplier is not informed in this activity, even though the team is a supplier team.
n.1: The senior user is not involved in notifying work package completion.
n.2: The business layer is not involved in managing product delivery.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the build-up stage. At a safety advisory group meeting, Lisa Ventnor learns that fewer paramedics than expected will be available on race day. Without involving Kezia Oduya, she agrees with Inspector Ravi Sandhu to merge two medical posts and changes her team's plan to match. Is this an effective way to manage product delivery, and why?
o: Yes, because the safety advisory group approves the safety plan, so agreeing changes with it directly is efficient.
Yes, because the team manager manages the development of products within the work package.
No, because the team manager should tell the project manager of new risks and act as the project manager directs.
No, because Lisa should have raised an exception report with the project board about the shortage.
7.w: In 'execute a work package' the team manager notifies the project manager of any new issues, risks or lessons and takes the action the project manager requires (see manual 17.4.2). Changing medical cover affects the safety plan and the stage, so Kezia must assess it.

n.0: The safety advisory group approves the plan, but changes to the project's products go through the project manager's control.
n.1: The team manager manages development within the agreed work package; merging medical posts goes beyond it.
n.3: Team managers do not raise exception reports to the board; work package problems go to the project manager.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon build-up stage is nearing its end. Kezia Oduya prepares the plan for the final stage, covering event week and the six weeks after it. The plan includes the debrief, the sponsor and carbon reports, the economic impact study, and the activities to hand the event over to the events team and close the project. Is this an appropriate application of the 'prepare next stage plan' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the business case is updated from the stage plan before the board authorizes the final stage.
Yes, because the next stage plan is prepared near the end of this stage, and closure is planned in the final stage.
No, because closing the project should be planned as a separate stage after the economic impact study.
No, because the final stage plan should be prepared after the board has authorized the final stage.
7.w: The plan for the next stage is produced near the end of the current stage, and closure activities are planned as part of the stage plan for the final stage; closing a project is not a stage of its own (see manual chapter 18 and 7.2.2.2).

n.0: The business case is updated using the revised project plan, but this does not explain why this stage plan is appropriate.
n.2: Closing a project is a process within the final stage, not a separate stage.
n.3: The board needs the plan to decide whether to authorize the stage, so it is prepared beforehand.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon planning and approvals stage is ending, and Kezia Oduya is preparing the end stage report in the 'evaluate the stage' activity. According to the recommended RACI, how should Lisa Ventnor, Paceline's team manager, be involved?
o: Responsible for preparing the report
Accountable for the report
Consulted on the report
Informed when it is issued
7.w: In 'evaluate the stage' the project manager is responsible, and the team manager, project support and project assurance are consulted (see manual table 18.2).

n.0: The project manager is responsible for preparing the end stage report.
n.1: A team manager is not accountable for the end stage report.
n.3: The team manager is consulted while the report is prepared, not just informed afterwards.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon planning and approvals stage is ending. Entries are open and the sponsorship contract is signed, but the volunteer plan, one of the stage's products, is only half finished. Kezia Oduya moves it into the build-up stage plan and asks the board to authorize the next stage, stating that the current stage's work is complete. Is this an effective way to manage the stage boundary, and why?
o: Yes, because the next stage plan should include any work that is carried forward from the current stage.
Yes, because the volunteer plan is produced by Zara Quinn's programme, which sits outside the project.
No, because an unfinished product means an exception plan must be approved before the next stage starts.
No, because the board should be told which of the stage's products are complete and approved, and which are not.
7.w: Managing a stage boundary assures the board that the products in the current stage plan are completed and approved, and gives it what it needs to judge continued viability (see manual 18.2). Hiding an unfinished product denies the board an accurate view before it commits to the next stage.

n.0: Carried-forward work can go in the next stage plan, but the board must be told about it rather than told the stage is complete.
n.1: The volunteer plan is one of the stage's products, so it is part of the project whoever produces it.
n.2: An exception plan follows a forecast breach of tolerance and a board request; an unfinished product is reported, not automatically treated as an exception.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'closing a project' process at the end of the final stage. Kezia Oduya confirms that the project can close, updates the project plan with actual figures, closes the project log, makes sure the project records are archived, and drafts closure messages for residents, churches, traders, volunteers and partner charities. Is this an appropriate application of the 'prepare planned closure' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because closing is prepared by updating the plan, closing the log, archiving records and drafting messages.
Yes, because the project manager authorizes closure of the project once its records have been archived.
No, because closure messages to stakeholders are drafted by the board after it has authorized closure.
No, because the project log should stay open until the post-project benefits reviews have been completed.
7.w: In 'prepare planned closure' the project manager confirms the project can close, updates the project plan with actuals, closes the project log, makes sure project information is secured and archived, and prepares closure communications (see manual 19.4.1).

n.1: The project board authorizes closure in directing a project; the project manager prepares and requests it.
n.2: Preparing closure communications is part of the project manager's preparation; the board then notifies the business layer that the project has closed.
n.3: Post-project benefits reviews happen after closure and are run by the business; the project log is closed in closing a project.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'closing a project' process. Andrew Mallory is the executive, Kezia Oduya the project manager and Greg Halloran the senior supplier. Kezia is preparing the end project report and the lessons report in the 'evaluate the project' activity. Which describes the recommended RACI for this activity?
o: Kezia responsible, the cabinet accountable, Greg informed
Andrew responsible, Kezia accountable, Greg consulted
Kezia responsible, Andrew accountable, Greg consulted
Kezia responsible and accountable, Andrew informed
7.w: For 'evaluate the project' the executive is accountable, the project manager responsible, the senior supplier and project assurance consulted, and the business layer not involved (see manual 19.4.4 and table 19.2).

n.0: The business layer is not involved in evaluating the project; the executive is accountable and the senior supplier is consulted.
n.1: The roles are reversed: the project manager prepares the reports and the executive is accountable.
n.3: The executive, not the project manager, is accountable, and the senior supplier is consulted.

7.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'closing a project' process. The economic impact study is complete, and the council has decided to repeat the event next year as normal business. Andrew Mallory proposes keeping the project open, with Kezia Oduya and the project log, until next year's race, so that benefits from the repeat event can be measured within the project. Is this an effective way to close the project, and why?
o: Yes, because the project should stay open until all of its expected benefits have been confirmed.
Yes, because the senior user is responsible for benefits realization, so the board must stay in place to see it through.
No, because benefits cannot be measured for an event that is repeated each year as normal business.
No, because the project should close and plan post-project benefits reviews that the business carries out.
7.w: Closing a project provides a fixed end point; benefits still to come are covered by updating the benefits management approach to plan post-project reviews, which the business carries out after closure (see manual 19.1, 19.2 and 19.4.3). Carrying out those reviews is not a project activity.

n.0: Most benefits are realized after a project closes; keeping it open adds cost and delays handover to the events team.
n.1: The senior user's responsibility for the continued realization of benefits carries on after closure, without the project board staying in place.
n.2: Benefits from repeated events can still be measured, through post-project reviews planned in the benefits management approach.

8.q: Project Skyline is at the end of the foundations stage. The cloud provider has raised its prices, and Mairi Campbell's updated forecast cuts the yearly running cost saving from £1.4 million to £1.1 million, which is still within the benefits tolerance. Before the board decides whether to authorize the wave migration stage, Fraser McIntyre asks Mairi to re-test the options, including keeping some applications at the Falkirk site, against the updated costs, risks and benefits. How well does this apply the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because the senior user is accountable for the business case and has to approve the revised saving.
It applies it well, because the justification is revalidated against the latest forecasts before the board commits to the next stage.
It applies it poorly, because a fall in forecast benefits should be escalated to the business layer in an exception report.
It applies it poorly, because the society's board approved the cloud strategy, so the options should stay closed during the project.
8.w: The principle requires the justification to remain valid and to be revalidated throughout the project, using the latest costs, risks and benefits; the board checks it at each stage boundary before committing to the next stage (see manual 2.1 and 5.3.1, the 'check' step). Re-testing the options when forecasts change is exactly this.

n.0: The executive, Fraser McIntyre, is accountable for the business case; the senior user specifies the benefits and demonstrates that forecast benefits are on track (see manual 6.2.4.2).
n.2: The reduced saving is within the benefits tolerance, so there is no exception; changes to benefits forecasts are handled when the business case is updated at the stage boundary.
n.3: Approval of a strategy does not fix the project's justification; it must be revalidated throughout, and a cheaper or better option may emerge as costs change.

8.q: Project Skyline is in the foundations stage. During the pilot wave, Arjun Menon's team finds that three applications failed their first switch-over because server addresses had been written into their code. Mairi Campbell records this in the lessons log, holds a short session in which the Pune engineers explain the problem to the Edinburgh team and to Hugh Bannerman's operations staff, and adds an address check to the migration checklist for wave 1. How well does this apply the 'learn from experience' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because the lesson is recorded, shared across the teams and acted on while the project is still running.
It applies it well, because a lessons report has to be issued to the project board after each migration wave is complete.
It applies it poorly, because lessons should be gathered at the end of the project so that they can be passed on in a lessons report.
It applies it poorly, because a failed switch-over should be raised as an issue rather than recorded and shared as a lesson.
8.w: Learning from experience means seeking, recording and acting on lessons throughout the project, not only at the start and end, and sharing them in ways that suit different people (see manual 2.2). Recording the lesson, sharing it across the three locations and changing the checklist before wave 1 does this well.

n.1: A lessons report can be produced when useful, but there is no requirement for one after every wave; the reason does not explain why this is good practice.
n.2: Lessons are sought, recorded and acted on throughout the project; waiting until closure would lose the benefit for the later waves.
n.3: Handling the failures as issues and learning from them are not alternatives; recording and sharing the lesson is a good application of the principle.

8.q: Project Skyline is in the foundations stage. Mairi Campbell finds that the Stratoshift engineers in Pune are taking requests directly from Steven Clarke, from Hugh Bannerman's operations staff and from Mairi herself, and their priorities are clashing. She agrees with Lena Fischer that Arjun Menon will be team manager for all migration work, records this in the role descriptions, and sets up a weekly joint call so that the Pune engineers get to know the operations staff they hand applications to. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because she clarifies who directs the work and builds links between the teams.
Manage by exception, because Arjun Menon can now make decisions within the tolerances set for his work packages.
Focus on products, because the joint call will help the operations staff to accept the migrated applications at handover.
Tailor to suit the project, because the team manager role is being adapted for a supplier based in another country.
8.w: The principle calls for agreed roles and responsibilities so that people know what is expected of them, and for the project management team to build relationships with and between internal and external stakeholders (see manual 2.3). Naming one team manager and creating a regular link between Pune and the operations staff applies both parts.

n.1: Nothing is said about tolerances or escalation; the problem being solved is unclear direction and weak relationships.
n.2: The call is set up so that the teams get to know each other, not to define or co-create products; the main action is clarifying who directs the work.
n.3: The team manager role is used as PRINCE2 describes it; nothing about the method is being adapted to the project.

8.q: Project Skyline is in the 'initiating a project' process. To reduce the number of board decision points, Fraser McIntyre proposes merging the wave migration stage and the core banking stage into one stage of 11 months. Moving core banking is the riskiest part of the project, and when it can start depends on the results of the earlier migration waves. How well does this apply the 'manage by stages' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because longer stages reduce the burden that the project places on the members of the board.
It applies it well, because the board can still control the project through the tolerances set for the longer stage.
It applies it poorly, because each stage of a PRINCE2 project should be of a similar length to the others.
It applies it poorly, because the board would lose a decision point to review viability before the riskiest work begins.
8.w: Stages give the board review and decision points at which to assess viability; shorter stages give more control and stage length should reflect risk and complexity (see manual 2.4). Removing the boundary before the core banking move takes away the decision point at the most critical moment, so the principle is applied poorly.

n.0: It is true that longer stages reduce the burden on senior managers, but this does not justify losing control at the project's riskiest point.
n.1: Tolerances support manage by exception; they do not replace the stage boundary at which the board decides whether to commit to the core banking move.
n.2: Stages can be of different lengths; their number and length depend on risk, complexity and decision points, not on matching each other.

8.q: Project Skyline is in the wave migration stage. Mindful of the board's very low appetite for outages, Fraser McIntyre proposes that the project board meets each month to approve the switch-over date of every application due to move in the following month, instead of setting tolerances for the stage and leaving the dates to Mairi Campbell. How well does this apply the 'manage by exception' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because a very low risk appetite means the board should take the day-to-day decisions on migrations.
It applies it well, because monthly meetings give the board regular, time-driven control over progress in the stage.
It applies it poorly, because the board should delegate within tolerances and be told when they are forecast to be exceeded.
It applies it poorly, because switch-over dates for individual applications should be approved by the business layer.
8.w: Manage by exception sets limits of delegated authority through tolerances; the board delegates day-to-day decisions to the project manager and is alerted when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, which saves senior time without removing control (see manual 2.5). The low appetite should be reflected in tight risk tolerances, not in the board approving every date.

n.0: Risk appetite shapes the tolerances the board sets; it does not mean the board should take over day-to-day management from the project manager.
n.1: Time-driven reporting such as highlight reports is useful, but approving each date is day-to-day management, not control by exception.
n.3: The business layer sets project tolerances and decides on project-level exceptions; it does not approve individual switch-over dates.

8.q: Project Skyline is in the wave migration stage. Aileen Docherty asks Arjun Menon's engineers to build parts of her proposed data platform while they are migrating the finance applications, saying it will be cheaper to do it now. The data platform is not one of the products in the approved plans and it has no product description. How well does this apply the 'focus on products' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because doing related work during a migration reduces the total cost of change to the society.
It applies it well, because the chief information officer can approve changes to the scope of the work packages.
It applies it poorly, because the team would be doing work that is not needed to deliver the project's agreed products.
It applies it poorly, because the data platform should have been added to the project product description in initiation.
8.w: Focus on products means the project does no more work than is needed to deliver its agreed products, which are defined by product descriptions; this controls scope creep (see manual 2.6). Building an unplanned, undefined product is work outside the agreed scope, so the principle is applied poorly.

n.0: Possible savings do not make unplanned work acceptable; the project should deliver its agreed products and nothing more.
n.1: Being chief information officer gives Aileen Docherty no authority over the project's agreed scope; changes to baselined products go through issue and change control.
n.3: The data platform has not been approved as part of the project, so there is no reason it should have been in the project product description; any addition should go through change control.

8.q: Project Skyline is in the 'initiating a project' process. Mairi Campbell proposes highlight reports every two weeks during the foundations, wave migration and core banking stages, and monthly during decommissioning, using the society's standard change portfolio template. One report each month will also serve as the written update the audit committee wants. The project board agrees, and the arrangement is recorded in the PID. How well does this apply the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because frequent highlight reports can take the place of end stage reports at stage boundaries.
It applies it well, because report frequency and format are matched to each stage's risk and to the society's governance.
It applies it poorly, because the format of highlight reports is set by PRINCE2 and should not be adapted.
It applies it poorly, because reports to the audit committee should be exception reports sent by the executive.
8.w: Tailoring makes project controls fit the project's scale, risk and environment, for example the frequency and formality of reports, and aligns the method with the business's own processes; tailoring decisions are documented and agreed in the PID (see manual 2.7). Reporting more often in the riskier stages and reusing the society's template is proportionate tailoring.

n.0: End stage reports support the board's decision at each stage boundary; highlight reports do not replace them, however often they are produced.
n.2: Management products may be adapted in format, merged or renamed; using the society's template is a normal tailoring choice.
n.3: Exception reports are for forecast breaches of tolerance and go to the project board; a regular update to the audit committee is a communication arrangement.

8.q: Project Skyline is in the foundations stage. The Pune engineers and Hugh Bannerman's operations staff have never met, and handovers of the pilot applications are causing friction and blame. Mairi Campbell arranges for Arjun Menon and two of his engineers to spend the first two weeks of the pilot wave in Falkirk, working alongside the operations staff, and sets up a short daily call in the hours when both countries are at work. Is this an appropriate approach to leading the team, and why?
o: Yes, because working side by side removes the need for checkpoint reports from the Pune team during the pilot.
Yes, because a team split across sites needs deliberate contact to build trust and social cohesion between its parts.
No, because team building is a matter for each supplier's own line managers rather than for the project manager.
No, because the Stratoshift engineers should be managed through the framework contract rather than by the project.
8.w: Virtual, remote and hybrid teams do not share information naturally, so the project should deliberately build social cohesion and trust across silos, for example through synchronized co-location days for key people and regular purposeful contact (see manual 3.3.3). Bringing key engineers to Falkirk and setting a shared daily call does this.

n.0: Checkpoint reports are still needed to report work package progress; co-location improves relationships but does not replace reporting.
n.2: Building an effective team is part of leading the project team; the project manager should act when friction between parts of the team harms the work.
n.3: The contract sets the commercial terms, but the engineers are still part of the project team and need to work well with the society's staff.

8.q: Project Skyline is in the 'initiating a project' process. Few of Brennan Mutual's IT staff have cloud skills, yet the society will run the new environment after the project closes. To save time, Mairi Campbell proposes that Stratoshift engineers write all the cloud operating procedures and run the migrated applications until closure, with cloud training for the operations staff arranged by the IT department after the project ends. Is this an appropriate approach to building the team's capability, and why?
o: Yes, because in a thin client delivery model the supplier carries out most of the work on the project.
Yes, because training staff for business as usual falls outside the scope of a PRINCE2 project.
No, because the capability gap should be closed during the project, for example by upskilling the operations staff.
No, because the senior supplier should write the operating procedures personally as a member of the board.
8.w: Leading successful teams includes understanding competencies and capabilities, identifying gaps and closing them, for example by upskilling or shifting responsibilities (see manual 3.3.2). The operations staff will run the new environment, so their skills gap should be addressed while the project is running, not left until it has closed.

n.0: A thin client model describes who does the work, but it does not remove the need for the society's own staff to be able to run the products after handover.
n.1: Preparing people to use and support the project's products is part of transition and of leading the team; enabling activities such as training belong in the project.
n.3: The senior supplier commits supplier resources and is accountable for the quality of supplier products; writing procedures is team work, and it would not close the society's skills gap.

8.q: Project Skyline is in the foundations stage. Ross Leckie, who is respected by the operations staff, has told colleagues that the promise of retraining will not be kept, and two engineers have asked about redundancy terms. Hugh Bannerman suggests leaving Ross out of the project's briefings and design workshops so that his doubts do not spread any further. Is this an appropriate way to lead the change, and why?
o: Yes, because Ross Leckie holds no formal role in the project management team for Project Skyline.
Yes, because resistance from staff should be handled by the society's HR team rather than by the project.
No, because Ross Leckie should be appointed as a senior user so that he represents the operations staff.
No, because Ross Leckie is a key influencer whose concerns should be explored and who should be involved.
8.w: Leading change means identifying stakeholders and key influencers, including people with no formal role, and treating pockets of resistance as a sign of where to engage: find out why people resist and involve them, for example through co-creation (see manual 3.2.2 and 3.4). Excluding the informal leader would deepen mistrust.

n.0: Projects must involve key people who are affected or critical to success even when they hold no formal role.
n.1: HR support may help, but the project is responsible for engaging the people affected by its change.
n.2: Engaging Ross does not require a board role; the senior user represents the users and must have the authority to commit them, which Ross does not have.

8.q: Project Skyline is in the 'initiating a project' process. Mairi Campbell drafts the change management approach. It describes how the IT operations function should look once both data centres have closed, and states that retraining for the operations staff will begin after decommissioning is complete. How well does this apply the guidance on leading successful change, and why?
o: It applies it well, because change management controls changes to the products in the project's baseline.
It applies it well, because the target state is the part of the approach that the board approves in the PID.
It applies it poorly, because retraining should be recorded as a risk in the risk register instead of in an approach.
It applies it poorly, because it should plan the move through interim states, with enabling activities before, during and after.
8.w: The change management approach sets out the target organizational state and how the business will move from the current state through any interim states, with enabling activities such as training before, during and after transition (see manual 3.2.1). As the data centre roles shrink wave by wave, retraining that starts after decommissioning comes too late.

n.0: In PRINCE2 7 change management is the organizational transition from current to target state; controlling changes to baselines belongs to the issues practice.
n.1: The whole approach is approved as part of the PID; describing only the end state leaves out how people will get there.
n.2: Concerns about retraining may give rise to risks, but planning the retraining itself is an enabling activity in the change management approach.

8.q: Project Skyline is in the foundations stage. Mairi Campbell's stakeholder analysis lists the project board, the IT department and Stratoshift. Joanne Pettigrew points out that the first switch-over weekends will affect branch staff, the contact centre and members who use online banking, and none of them have been told. What should Mairi do to apply the communication approach?
o: Add branch, contact centre and online banking users to the stakeholder analysis and plan messages for each before switch-overs.
Ask the audit committee to approve each message about the switch-over weekends before it is sent to staff and members.
Report the switch-over dates in the next highlight report so that the board members can brief their own teams.
Wait until the end of the foundations stage and add the affected groups when the approaches are reviewed.
8.w: The communication management approach should identify everyone affected by the project or its delivery, and set out the purpose, timing, channels and messages for each group, so that communication is planned and two-way across the project ecosystem (see manual 3.4). Branch staff, the contact centre and members are affected by switch-overs and need planned communication before they happen.

n.1: The audit committee receives a monthly update; it has no role in approving operational messages to staff and members.
n.2: Highlight reports keep the board informed of stage status; they are not the way to communicate with affected staff and members.
n.3: The switch-over weekends are imminent; a gap in the stakeholder analysis should be fixed now rather than left to a later review.

8.q: Project Skyline is in the 'initiating a project' process. Mairi Campbell is writing the communication management approach. She records that a shared collaboration platform, with a channel for each migration wave and recorded daily stand-ups, will be used between Pune, Edinburgh and Falkirk. Under which heading of the communication management approach should this be recorded?
o: Stakeholder analysis
Communications schedule and procedures
Supporting tools and techniques
Resources
8.w: The supporting tools and techniques heading records the platforms and tools used to communicate, such as collaboration platforms and analytics or automation tools (see manual 3.4). A shared collaboration platform is a tool.

n.0: Stakeholder analysis identifies who is affected by or can influence the project, not the tools used to reach them.
n.1: The schedule and procedures set out the purpose, frequency, channels and messages for each stakeholder group, not the platform itself.
n.3: Resources are the people and budget for communication activities; a collaboration platform is a tool, not a resource.

8.q: Matching set (business case). Mairi Campbell is preparing the full business case for Project Skyline. Which heading of the business case should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 1 of 3: The landlord of the Leeds data centre will not extend the lease, and the society's board has adopted a strategy of moving to public cloud hosting.
o: Reasons
